## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- Adam Smith is on this map for two reasons: he holds office, and he makes big decisions. He has been the U.S. Representative for Washington's 9th Congressional District since 1997. That is 15 terms in office.
- As Ranking Member (and former Chair) of the House Armed Services Committee, he shapes national defense policy and Pentagon spending. This affects Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM), the largest military base in Pierce County and one of the largest on the West Coast.
- His district covers parts of Tacoma, SeaTac, Tukwila, and other South King/North Pierce County communities. As Dean of the Washington House delegation, he carries extra weight.
- People near him who are not on the map: Washington's two U.S. Senators (Patty Murray, Maria Cantwell) have their own nodes. Other WA House members are not on the map. Smith's wife Sara Bickle-Eldridge (a UW/Seattle University Law graduate) is not on the map unless she holds her own power.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** David Adam Smith (goes by Adam Smith)
- **Aliases:** Rep. Adam Smith; @RepAdamSmith (X/Twitter)
- **Date and city of birth:** June 15, 1965, Washington, D.C. (age 61 as of 2026)
- **Current home:** Bellevue, WA area (LinkedIn lists Renton, Washington). Grew up in SeaTac, WA.
- **Family:** Married in 1993 to Sara Bickle-Eldridge (UW graduate, Seattle University School of Law). Daughter Kendall Charlotte (UW grad 2022). Son Jack Evers (student at Washington State University). Adopted as an infant by Leila June (née Grant) and maternal uncle Ben Martin Smith III. Father Ben worked as a ramp serviceman at SeaTac Airport (United Airlines) and was active in the Machinists' Union. Father died when Smith was 19. Mother Leila stayed at home. Two brothers.
- **Education:** Bow Lake Elementary, Chinook Middle School, Tyee High School (graduated 1983). One year at Western Washington University, then Fordham University — BA in Political Science (1987). University of Washington School of Law — JD (1990). Worked through college loading trucks for UPS.
- **Profession:** Attorney. Private practice at Cromwell, Mendoza & Belur (1992). Prosecutor for City of Seattle (1993–1995). Judge pro tempore (1996). Politician (1990–present).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Primary power basis:** Elected federal office. U.S. Representative, WA-9, since 1997 (15 terms). As the longest-serving WA House member (Dean of delegation), he has deep seniority and know-how.
- **Committee power:** Ranking Member of the House Armed Services Committee (HASC). That makes him the top Democrat on the committee that handles military policy, the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), and oversight of the Department of Defense. This is one of the most powerful committee spots in Congress. He was Chair during the 116th and 117th Congresses (2019–2023) when Democrats held the majority. He has served on HASC since 1997.
- **Defense and foreign policy reach:** Former chair of the Terrorism, Unconventional Threats and Capabilities subcommittee. Former chair of the Air and Land Forces subcommittee. Previously served on the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. Founded the bipartisan Congressional Caucus for Effective Foreign Assistance (CCEFA). Has traveled to the Middle East, North Africa, and other conflict zones.
- **Community Project Funding:** Smith secured $6,316,000 in community project funds for WA-09 in a House-passed package (Jan 2026). He also secured $24.6M for Puget Sound military projects in an earlier spending package. As Ranking Member of HASC, he has "traditionally been restrained in making requests of the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee."
- **District covered:** WA-9 includes parts of Tacoma, SeaTac, Tukwila, Renton, Kent, Bellevue, and other South King/North Pierce County communities. The district covers SeaTac Airport and parts of the Puget Sound industrial corridor.
- **Domain overlaps:** Government (congressman, HASC ranking member), Defense/Military (armed services policy, JBLM advocacy), Economic (transportation, trade, tech), Foreign Policy (national security, foreign aid reform).

## 3. Where their power comes from

JBLM and the South Sound military community benefit from his defense policy positions. WA-09 communities benefit from community project funding ($6.3M+ in 2026). Defense contractors with a Puget Sound presence benefit from his committee position. | #1, #2, #7, #9 |

He shapes the Democratic caucus position on defense issues. He has direct oversight authority over the Pentagon. | #2, #5, #8 |
| Who wins | Smith has won 15 straight elections since 1996. He went from state senator (youngest in the country) to HASC Chair — one of the most powerful positions in Congress. He secured $24.6M for Puget Sound military projects and $6.3M+ in community project funding for WA-09. He was inducted into the JBLM Civilian Hall of Fame. | #2, #7, #9, #10 |

## 5. How they touch government
- **Campaign finance (2026 cycle):** $1,882,001 total receipts. $1,583,206 spent. $869,549 cash on hand (as of July 15, 2026). Main campaign committee: ADAM SMITH FOR CONGRESS COMMITTEE (FEC ID H6WA09025). He also has sponsored leadership PACs.
- **Campaign finance (2024 cycle):** $1,677,916 raised. $1,701,114 spent. Won general election.
- **Campaign finance (historical):** 2022: $1,386,776 raised. 2020: $1,327,196 raised. 2018: $1,415,994 raised. He raises between $1.3M and $1.9M per cycle.
- **FEC candidate profile:** H6WA09025. Incumbent. Democratic Party. Statement of candidacy filed 11/14/2024.
- **Community Project Funding:** $6,316,000 for WA-09 communities (House-passed, Jan 2026). $24.6M for Puget Sound military projects (earlier spending package). FY26 requests accepted with an April 17, 2025 deadline. Only requests with direct WA-09 impact were put forward.
- **Lobbying:** As a congressman, Smith does not register as a lobbyist. He is lobbied by defense contractors, tech companies, local governments, and advocacy groups seeking his HASC and appropriations reach.
- **Federal funding to Pierce County:** Smith's HASC position directly affects JBLM (in Pierce County / 28th LD). JBLM is one of the largest military bases on the West Coast and a major economic engine for Pierce County. Defense policy moves Smith helps shape affect base operations, military housing, staffing, and contracts. All of these have a big economic impact on the county.
- **JBLM Civilian Hall of Fame:** Smith was inducted for supporting JROTC programs in area high schools and backing new leaders at JBLM.

## 6. Other seats they hold
- **JBLM** (`jblm`): Graph records armed_services_champion relationship (weight 6). Smith is the Ranking Member of HASC, which has direct reach over JBLM operations, funding, and policy. He has visited JBLM multiple times to observe war-fighting readiness (most recently Aug 20, 2025, with his wife Sara). Inducted into JBLM Civilian Hall of Fame. Weight 6 in graph — the highest weight in his connections.
- **Pierce County Council** (`county-council`): Graph records federal_funding relationship (weight 4). Federal funding decisions Smith shapes flow through to Pierce County government, especially for defense, transportation, and community projects.
- **House Armed Services Committee Democrats (HASCDemocrats):** Smith leads the Democratic caucus on HASC, giving him direct overlap with the national defense policy apparatus.
- **New Democrat Coalition:** Member. Provides centrist Democratic coalition ties.
- **Congressional Progressive Caucus:** Member. Provides progressive policy network ties (notable that Smith spans both New Dem and Progressive caucuses — an unusual ideological range).
- **Congressional Caucus for Effective Foreign Assistance (CCEFA):** Founder/co-chair (with Rep. Ted Yoho, R-FL, in 116th Congress). Bipartisan caucus on foreign aid reform.
- **Brookings Institution:** Participated in Brookings events on his memoir "Lost and Broken" about mental health and health care — provides think tank network ties.
- **University of Washington:** JD (1990). Daughter graduated from UW (2022). Provides higher education network ties.

## 1. Who they are
- **AIPAC / pro-Israel funding:** A third-party tracker (whofundsmyrep.com) reports Smith has received $638,554 from "pro-Israel committees." This figure needs verification against FEC filings. - **Defense contractor donations:** As HASC Ranking Member, Smith is a top recipient of defense industry contributions. Specific contractor-by-contractor breakdown requires OpenSecrets/FEC transaction-level analysis. This is a significant potential conflict-of-interest nexus.
- **WA-9 district boundaries and Pierce County overlap:** The 9th District includes parts of Tacoma but is primarily a South King County district. The exact portions of Pierce County within WA-9 and the population distribution need verification against current redistricting maps. The graph's edge to Pierce County Council (federal_funding, weight 4) implies significant county-level funding flows.
- **Leadership PAC:** Smith has "sponsored leadership PACs" per FEC filings. The name, donation patterns, and recipients of his leadership PAC need investigation — this is a common mechanism for congressional power-building.
- **Mental health advocacy:** Smith's memoir on chronic pain and anxiety (Brookings event) and his HASC role create a potential intersection with military mental health policy. Whether he has translated personal experience into specific legislative initiatives on military mental health warrants examination.
- **2028 outlook:** Smith declared candidacy and is on the ballot for 2026. His long tenure (15 terms) and committee seniority make him deeply entrenched, but the evolving political landscape of WA-9 and national politics may affect his future positioning.

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** Adam Smith holds one of the most powerful positions in the U.S. Congress as Ranking Member of the House Armed Services Committee. He shapes national defense policy, the annual NDAA, and oversight of the Pentagon. His power directly affects Pierce County through JBLM — one of the largest military bases on the West Coast, a major economic engine for the county, and the anchor of the 28th Legislative District. His 15-term tenure, dual caucus memberships (New Dem + Progressive), and Dean of delegation status give him deep institutional power. He has delivered real federal funding to the region ($6.3M+ community projects, $24.6M military projects).
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense-attorney counter-argument anticipated):** A defense attorney would flag the intersection of Smith's HASC role (shaping defense policy and acquisition) with defense industry campaign contributions as a structural conflict of interest. The $1.3–1.9M he raises per cycle inevitably includes significant defense contractor money. The counter: Smith has been a consistent advocate for Pentagon efficiency, fraud/waste/abuse reduction, and military personnel welfare — positions that sometimes run counter to contractor interests. His memoir on mental health and advocacy for military mental health services suggests genuine concern for service members rather than pure industry capture.
- **Analysis of alternatives:** The opposing view is that Smith's power is mostly national rather than local. His HASC role gives him huge reach over defense policy but limited direct control over Pierce County governance. Under this view, his connection to Pierce County is mainly through JBLM (a federal base, not a county agency) and community project funding (small compared to the county's $3B+ budget). His district is mostly in South King County, not Pierce County, and his local reach may be overstated by rank 44/163.
- **Confidence:** High — Smith's congressional record, committee positions, campaign finance data, and biographical details are well-documented in primary sources (House.gov, Congress.gov, FEC, HASC Democrats, DVIDS, JBLM). His JBLM tie and defense policy reach are well-established. The main gaps are in transaction-level defense contractor donation analysis and the exact scope of Pierce County overlap in WA-9.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- Alice Phillips is on this map because she runs labor in Pierce County. She is the elected President of the Pierce County Central Labor Council, AFL-CIO (PCCLC). That council is a federation of about 114 unions. Those unions cover about 44,000 workers.
- As President, she runs the union's endorsement process. Her union's political action committee (COPE) picks which Democrats to back. That endorsement matters a lot in close primaries.
- She is also a Labor Trustee on the Clover Park Technical College Board. The governor gave her that seat in 2021.
- **Adjacent but EXCLUDED:** Nathe Lawver (PCCLC Secretary-Treasurer). Vance Lelli (former PCCLC President). Adam Brinkman (current IBEW 483 Business Manager). All are nearby but not the same person on this map.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Alice Phillips.
- **Pronouns:** she/her (per PCCLC bio).
- **Education:** Clover Park High School. Clover Park Technical College, 1979.
- **Military:** US Navy. She rose to Hull Technician First Class. She won the Navy Medal of Achievement.
- **Family / residence:** South Sound resident. Her spouse's name is not in public records.
- **Career path:** US Navy → City of Tacoma electrical worker (10 years) → IBEW Local 483 (the local electricians' union). She moved up: shop steward, then Executive Board, then Vice President, then President, then Organizer, then Union Rep, then Assistant Business Manager, then Business Manager for 30 years. Now she is PCCLC President. She was the first woman in that role.
- **Sanctions / criminal / civil:** None found.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Domain = political.** Her power comes from running the biggest labor group in the county. That group gives endorsements in every election. The union's political action committee (COPE) endorsement is a strong signal in Democratic primaries.
- **Statutory:** None. This is an elected union role, not a public office.
- **Influence mechanisms:**
  - COPE endorsements: Phillips is the public face of PCCLC's vetting process. That process has 40+ hours of candidate questionnaires and interviews. In 2024, PCCLC backed Ryan Mello for County Executive, Marty Campbell for Auditor, Davida Haygood for Council District 2, and several Superior Court picks.
  - **Clover Park Technical College Board of Trustees** (Labor Trustee, appointed by the governor). This seat ties labor to workforce training.
  - Public advocacy: Phillips pushed the 2026 unanimous endorsement of Pierce Transit's sales-tax hike from 0.6% to 0.9%. She has spoken at labor rallies.
- **key facts answers:**
  - Who is funded and endorsed: about 44,000 workers' dues, through 114 affiliates, pay for PCCLC's political work.
  - PAC spending: PCCLC has its own COPE. The exact dollar amounts were not in public records.
  - Party-machinery control: She is the de facto gatekeeper for Democratic primary endorsements in Pierce County.
  - Candidate recruitment: Through the IBEW pipeline and PCCLC delegates.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | PCCLC affiliates and their about 44,000 members. Pro-labor Democrats who clear the COPE endorsement. The Clover Park TC workforce system. | 1, 2 |
| Who sits | **PCCLC President** (elected by delegates). **Clover Park Technical College Board of Trustees** (Labor Trustee, Governor Inslee–appointed, April 2021). | 1, 3 |
| Who governs | Influences Democratic primary endorsement slates in Pierce County. Advises labor trustees on workforce boards. Sits on broader labor committees (Tacoma Joint Labor Committee, Washington State Labor Council Education Committee). | 1, 2 |
| Who wins | Pro-labor candidates and incumbents. IBEW 483 (her long-time local). Labor-aligned civic groups (United Way of Pierce County, Paint Tacoma-Pierce Beautiful, Emergency Food Network). | 1, 2 |

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** Alice Phillips is the top elected officer of labor in Pierce County. As PCCLC President she controls COPE endorsements. Those shape Democratic primary outcomes. She also ties labor and workforce policy together through her governor-appointed seat on the Clover Park TC Board. Her power is real but narrow. It shows up through endorsements and coalition work, not a budget or a law.
- **Conflicts of interest (defense-attorney counter-argument anticipated):** A critic could say her dual role blurs the line. She is both PCCLC President and a governor-appointed public trustee at Clover Park TC. The defense is simple. The CPTC Labor Trustee seat exists to bring labor's view into workforce training. The dual role is built in, not a conflict.
- **Analysis of alternatives (investigative control document (ICD)-203):** One reading says labor-endorsement power is just symbolic. Real campaign cash comes from candidate PACs, not labor COPE. The opposite reading: in off-year and primary races, labor turnout is decisive. In those races the COPE endorsement decides the winner. Evidence supports tier3 placement at rank 148.
- **Confidence:** High on identity, role, and endorsements. Three primary sources back this up. Medium on personal-political reach. Vote totals are not in primary sources.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- Allan Belton is the 14th President of Pacific Lutheran University (PLU), a private Lutheran school in Parkland, Pierce County. He runs a school that brings in millions each year. He hires and fires top staff. He sets the school's direction.
- He is on the map because he holds this job. The PLU Board of Regents picked him. The board can also fire him. Board members are the power above the president.
- PLU is one of the largest private employers in the Parkland and Tacoma area. The school serves about 3,000 students each year.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Allan Belton.
- **Age:** 52 when appointed, per the News Tribune in 2019.
- **Residence:** Gig Harbor, WA (per his PLU bio).
- **Family:** Married to Melinda Krotz Belton (PLU Class of 1991). They have three children.
- **Education:**
 - B.A. in Business Administration from Washington State University.
 - M.B.A. (Master of Business Administration) from Washington State University.
- **Career path:** 25 years at Bank of America Merrill Lynch (last role: Managing Director and Chief Operations Officer for Global Treasury Management) → PLU Chief Financial Officer (joined 2015) → PLU Senior Vice President and Chief Administrative Officer → PLU Acting President (around 2017) → **PLU 14th President** (April 3, 2019 to now, per PLU website in Fall 2025).
- **Sanctions or criminal record:** None found.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **The office itself:** He was chosen by the PLU Board of Regents. As president, he runs academic affairs, finances, advancement, and human resources. This is the standard power a private-university president holds.
- **Budget and contracts:** PLU is private. The exact yearly budget was not confirmed in primary materials (UNVERIFIED). PLU's endowment is reported in IRS (Internal Revenue Service) Form 990 filings, but those were not pulled.
- **Domain is institutional.** He is the steward of a private faith-based school. He connects academic, faith, and Tacoma/Parkland civic groups.
- **Key facts:**
 - Tax status: PLU is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit (a tax-exempt charity under the IRS code). Belton himself is not.
 - Board roster: The PLU Board of Regents governs the school. Belton sits on it by virtue of his role (ex officio).
 - Government funding share: PLU gets federal student aid (called Title IV) and research grants. Specific Pierce County government funding was not confirmed (UNVERIFIED).
 - Board overlaps: Member of the Washington Advisory Committee of the U.S. Global Leadership Coalition (USGLC). This shows his standing in business and civic circles.
 - Civic footprint: PLU runs Parkland-University partnerships and "Parkland's University" community programs in 2024 and 2025.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | PLU students (about 3,000 undergrad and grad, UNVERIFIED), faculty, staff; the Parkland and Tacoma community; WSU alumni network (his alma mater). | 1, 2 |
| Who sits | Sits on the PLU Board of Regents by virtue of his role; member of the USGLC Washington Advisory Committee. | 2, 3 |
| Who governs | Full control of PLU as 14th President. He served as Acting President around 2017. He became 14th President on April 3, 2019. | 1, 2 |

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why he is on the map:** Andrew Strobel is a key connector in Pierce County. He works in three places at once. He is the Tribal and Regional Affairs Advisor to the County Executive (Ryan Mello). He spent 15 years as the Planning and Land Use Director for the Puyallup Tribe of Indians. He also sits on the Tacoma Community College (TCC) Board of Trustees, where the governor appointed him. Because of these roles, he links county government, tribal government, and education.
- **Who is NOT on the map:** Other county staff are too low-level to map. Other TCC Board members are tracked separately or left out. Other Puyallup Tribe planning staff are not directors, so they do not get their own profile.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Andrew Strobel
- **Alias:** "strobelski" (his Threads handle)
- **Birth date and place:** Not found in public records.
- **Lives in:** Tacoma, Washington (per his LinkedIn page).
- **Family:** Not found in public records.
- **Education:** Two bachelor's degrees from the University of Puget Sound, in Economics and in International Political Economy. A master's degree (M.P.S., or Master of Professional Studies) in Natural Resource Management from Syracuse University.
- **Tribal ties:** A delegate of the Central Council of the Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska (from the Seattle area). He also has family ties to the Puyallup Tribe from his long career there.
- **Languages:** Japanese (per LinkedIn).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Appointed job:** Strategic Advisor of Tribal and Regional Affairs in County Executive Ryan Mello's office. This is an at-will job. That means he serves at the pleasure of the Executive. He advises Mello on regional policy and transit. He also acts as the main contact between the county and tribal governments. He works with the Puget Sound Regional Council (PSRC), the Pierce County Regional Council, and Sound Transit.
- **Picked by the governor:** Washington Governor Bob Ferguson chose Strobel for the TCC Board of Trustees. His five-year term started January 28, 2026. He took the seat that Pat Shuman used to hold.
- **Old job:** Planning and Land Use Director at the Puyallup Tribe, from April 2010 to January 15, 2025. That is almost 15 years. He moved up from Associate Planner to Director. He helped pass the tribe's full land use plan. He led the Tacoma Tideflats Subarea Plan, a seven-year project. He helped open the Emerald Queen Casino in 2020. He worked on road safety on tribal land.
- **Volunteer and civic jobs:** Vice-Chair of the Tacoma Planning Commission until at least June 2023. Chair of the Transportation Committee of the Central Council of Tlingit and Haida (term 2026–2028). He sat on the PSRC Growth Management Policy Board for the Puyallup Tribe (July 2024). He sat on the PSRC Transportation Policy Board for the Puyallup Tribe (December 2024).
- **How his roles overlap:**
 - **Government and tribal:** Main bridge between Pierce County and the Medicine Creek Treaty Tribes (Puyallup, Nisqually, Squaxin Island, Muckleshoot).
 - **Institutional and government:** TCC Board (education) plus Pierce County Executive staff (government).
 - **Government and transit:** Advises Mello on transit and works with Sound Transit and PSRC.

## 3. Where their power comes from

|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | His advisory job helps the Mello team build ties with tribal governments and regional planning groups. His TCC role helps the college's tribal partnerships. His old tribal job helped the tribe's land use and sovereignty work. | Sources 1, 3, 4 |
| Who sits | He sits on the TCC Board of Trustees (governor appointee). He was Vice-Chair of the Tacoma Planning Commission. He is Chair of the Central Council Tlingit and Haida Transportation Committee. He sat on the PSRC Growth Management Policy Board and the PSRC Transportation Policy Board for the Puyallup Tribe. | Sources 1, 4, 5, 6, 7 |
| Who governs | As Strategic Advisor to the County Executive, he runs the day-to-day tribal-county relations and advises on regional and transit policy. He does not govern on his own. His power comes from Mello. | Sources 1, 4 |
| Who wins | He won the governor's appointment to the TCC Board. He helped pass the tribe's land use plan and the Tideflats Subarea Plan. Moving from tribal to county work was a career step up. | Sources 1, 3, 4 |

## 5. How they touch government
- **Pierce County Executive's office:** Strategic Advisor. At-will job. He works with tribal governments, PSRC, Pierce County Regional Council, and Sound Transit.
- **TCC Board of Trustees:** Appointee of Governor Ferguson. Five-year term from January 28, 2026. TCC is a state-funded community college. The Board runs the school, sets the budget, and picks partners.
- **PSRC boards:** He spoke for the Puyallup Tribe on the PSRC Growth Management Policy Board (July 2024) and the PSRC Transportation Policy Board (December 2024). These boards shape how the central Puget Sound region grows and how people move around.
- **Tacoma Planning Commission:** Former Vice-Chair. He advised the City Council on planning, land use, zoning, and development rules under Tacoma Municipal Code 13.02.040. He left the Commission in June 2023.
- **Campaign money:** Not found. The state's campaign-finance agency (called the PDC, or Public Disclosure Commission) has no record of a campaign for Andrew Strobel. He is not elected and does not run campaigns.
- **Tribal contact:** He speaks for Pierce County with the Puyallup, Nisqually, Squaxin Island, and Muckleshoot tribes. These are the four Medicine Creek Treaty Tribes.

## 6. Other seats they hold
- **Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello:** Direct boss. Strategic Advisor. At-will job. Main institutional overlap.
- **Puyallup Tribe of Indians:** Former Planning and Land Use Director (15 years). Still has ties to tribal leaders.
- **TCC Board of Trustees:** Governor appointee. Sits with Chair Dona Ponepinto, Vice Chair LaTasha Wortham, Lois Bernstein, and Manny Santiago. Overlap with TCC President Ivan Harrell.
- **PSRC Growth Management Policy Board:** Spoke for the Puyallup Tribe as of July 2024.
- **PSRC Transportation Policy Board:** Spoke for the Puyallup Tribe as of December 2024.
- **Central Council of Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska:** Delegate. Chair of the Transportation Committee for 2026 to 2028.
- **Tacoma Planning Commission:** Former Vice-Chair. Served through mid-2023.
- **Tacoma Charter Review Committee:** Spoke for the Puyallup Tribe in the 2024 Charter Review process.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why it is on the map:** Banner Bank is on the map because it is well-connected and holds civic office through its leaders. Banner Bank is the main operating part of Banner Corporation (a company that trades on the NASDAQ stock exchange under the symbol BANR). It is a Washington-state-chartered commercial bank based in Walla Walla. Banner runs branches in Tacoma and across Pierce County. Two Tacoma branches are at 1015 A Street and 1211 South Pearl Street. Banner is on this map because one of its officers, AJ Gordon, was Board Chair of the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce. That gives Banner direct civic leadership ties.
- **Who is NOT on the map:** Umpqua Bank (a Pacific Northwest rival), Columbia Bank (now part of Umpqua), and big national banks like Wells Fargo, JPMorgan, and Bank of America. They have Tacoma branches but no specific Pierce County board ties in this research. Islanders Bank, a Banner subsidiary in the San Juan Islands, is not a separate entity.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name (operating part):** Banner Bank. It is a Washington-state-chartered commercial bank.
- **Parent company:** Banner Corporation. It is a Washington company that trades on the NASDAQ stock exchange under the symbol BANR. It started as a thrift in 1890 (per the Banner Bank About page).
- **Headquarters:** 10 South First Avenue, P.O. Box 907, Walla Walla, WA 99362.
- **Type:** Washington-state-chartered commercial bank. It is insured by the FDIC (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation). Its parent company files with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
- **Leadership:** President & CEO Mark J. Grescovich. He became President in April 2010 and CEO in August 2010. He held other banking jobs before that. His total pay for fiscal year 2025 was $3,590,983, per AFL-CIO PayWatch.
- **Subsidiaries:** Banner Bank (the operating bank) and Islanders Bank (3 branches in the San Juan Islands), per SEC filings.
- **Law that governs it:** Washington State banking code. The Washington State Department of Financial Institutions (DFI) supervises it. The SEC oversees the parent. The Federal Reserve oversees the holding company.
- **Size:** $16.34 billion in assets as of March 31, 2026 (per Banner's release on the Pacific Financial deal). Branches in Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and California. It calls itself one of the largest community banks in the Pacific Northwest.
- **Recent deal:** Banner plans to buy Pacific Financial Corporation of Aberdeen, WA. Pacific Financial is the parent of Bank of the Pacific. The deal was announced in 2026.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power from the law:** As a state-chartered commercial bank, Banner makes loans, takes deposits, and offers mortgages and treasury services. It is supervised by the Federal Reserve and the DFI. Banner is not a regulator itself.
- **Domain = economic.** Power comes from its market position as a Pacific Northwest bank and from its civic board ties.
- **Key facts:**
 - Revenue: FY 2025 CEO pay was $3.59 million (a rough scale measure). Full financial data is on SEC EDGAR (the SEC's public filing system).
 - Ownership: Public, traded on NASDAQ under BANR. Institutional and individual shareholders own it.
 - Market position: Pacific Northwest community-banking leader (about $16 billion in assets). One of the largest banks based in Washington.
 - Government contracts and deposits: Banner holds public funds in places where it serves as a bank for government. Its exact Pierce County depositary status was not confirmed.
 - Jobs: About 2,000+ employees across the Pacific Northwest. The exact number was not confirmed.
 - Real estate: Branch network in Tacoma (1015 A St, 1211 S Pearl St) and across Pierce County. Specific holdings were not confirmed.
- **Civic leadership:** AJ Gordon was Board Chair of the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce around 2021–2022, when the Chamber moved from Tom Pierson to Andrea Reay as President & CEO. Other Banner bankers in the area include Christopher Estrada (VP, Tacoma–Pierce County region), Doug Hedger (VP, Pierce & South King counties), and Michael Cruz (VP, Branch Manager in Tacoma). That is a deep bench for one bank in Pierce County.

## 3. Where their power comes from

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- Bill Robertson is on this map because he runs MultiCare Health System. MultiCare is the largest private employer in Pierce County. It is also the largest not-for-profit, locally owned health system in Washington State. He has been President and CEO since May 1, 2014.
- Under his leadership, MultiCare grew from a Tacoma-focused hospital group into the largest community-owned nonprofit health system in the region.
- He also chaired the Washington State Hospital Association (WSHA) board from 2020 to 2021. WSHA lobbies in Olympia on behalf of member hospitals.
- He plans to retire on December 31, 2026. Florence Chang will take over as President and CEO on January 1, 2027.

## 1. Who they are
- **Name:** William G. "Bill" Robertson.
- **Education:** B.S. in Accounting from Southern Adventist University. MBA from Texas Christian University. He is also a Certified Public Accountant (CPA).
- **Home:** Tacoma, WA area since May 2014. He and his wife moved to the South Sound when he joined MultiCare.
- **Career:** He was CEO of Shawnee Mission Medical Center near Kansas City, KS. Then he was President and CEO of Adventist HealthCare Inc. in Gaithersburg, MD. He became President and CEO of MultiCare Health System on May 1, 2014. He took over from Diane Cecchettini. In 2022 his title became CEO. Florence Chang was named President, then President and CEO starting January 1, 2027.
- **Family:** His wife was named in a 2014 announcement. Other family details are not public.

## 2. Their career and offices
- 2001–2003: AmeriCorps volunteer at United Way of Pierce County. Hired.
- Around 2003: Staffer for State Rep. Hans Dunshee. Hired.
- 2005–2010: Metro Parks Tacoma board. Elected.
- 2006: Pierce County director at Cascade Land Conservancy. Hired.
- 2010–2019: Tacoma City Council. Appointed, then elected.
- Around 2010s: Executive director at Pierce Conservation District. Hired.
- 2021–2025: Pierce County Council, District 4. Elected.
- 2025–now: Pierce County Executive. Elected.

He climbed a steady ladder of local offices over twenty years.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **MultiCare CEO.** Robertson runs a multi-billion-dollar health system. MultiCare is a 501(c)(3) not-for-profit. It is the largest not-for-profit, locally owned health system in Washington State. It runs four adult hospitals, one children's hospital (Mary Bridge Children's), and many clinics. MultiCare is the largest private employer in Pierce County.
- **System growth.** MultiCare grew from a Tacoma-focused hospital group into the largest community-based nonprofit health system in the state under Robertson. Decisions about new sites, partnerships, and service lines flowed through his office. Examples include the 2024 Pacific Lutheran University (PLU) Medical Center partnership and the 2022 Indigo Urgent Care buildout.
- **Statewide hospital leadership.** He chaired the WSHA board from 2020 to 2021. WSHA is the main statewide hospital trade group. The board chair role gives him power over WSHA's lobbying agenda. That covers state hospital policy, Medicaid and Medicare payments, and pandemic-era coordination.
- **Pay.** UNVERIFIED publicly. MultiCare is a private nonprofit. IRS Form 990 reports lag by about two years. Robertson's exact pay is not yet on the public record.

- **Chairman:** Has served as chairman and vice chairman several times. Most recently returned to chairman after re-election and a swearing-in (per TNT and tribal news). Current chairman as of 2024–2025.
- **Vice Chairman:** Has served as vice chairman at various points. Specific dates not confirmed.
- **Puyallup Land Claims Settlement (1980s):** Key negotiator. The Puyallup Tribe of Indians Settlement Act of 1989 led to a $162–163 million settlement, signed March 25, 1990. It was one of the largest 20th-century Indian land claims settlements. Sterud said in 2015 the talks "took four years of my life."
- **Economic development oversight:** Has been involved in every part of the Tribe's economic work since the 1980s, including:
 - Emerald Queen Casino (two locations: Fife and Tacoma on I-5; new $372–400M Tacoma casino facility).
 - Cannabis business.
 - Marina operations.
 - Development of "the only tribal-run deepwater port in the country" (per official bio).
- **Re-election:** Sterud and Annette Bryan were re-elected and sworn in to new three-year terms (per tribal news). Vice Chairwoman Sylvia Miller gave them the oath of office.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power he holds:**
 - **Sovereign governance:** As Chairman of the Puyallup Tribal Council, Sterud runs a federally recognized sovereign nation. The Tribal Council (7 elected members) oversees all tribal operations, programs, and businesses.
 - **Economic power:** The Emerald Queen Casino employs about 2,200 people. The new Tacoma casino cost about $372–400M. It is projected to bring $1.5 billion in economic impact over the next decade. Casino operations are the Tribe's largest single source of revenue.
 - **Legislative advocacy:** Sterud testified before the Washington State Senate Transportation Committee on Feb 7, 2025/2026. The bill would make it easier for tribes to reclaim land. He and EQC CEO Yale Rowe also testified for the college sports wagering bill that Gov. Ferguson signed.
 - **Cultural and institutional power:** Frequent speaker at UW Tacoma graduations and new-student events. Has led the Tribe in Canoe Journeys and cultural events.
- **How his power overlaps with Pierce County:** Tribal governance and sovereignty overlap with the casino economy, real estate, and state legislative work, campaign donations, and gaming compacts.
- **Key facts:**
 - **Tax status:** The Puyallup Tribe is a federally recognized sovereign nation (not a 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(6)). Tribal businesses have specific tax treatment under federal law and the tribal-state gaming compact. Sovereign immunity applies.
 - **Board roster:** Tribal Council has 7 members: Chairman Bill Sterud, Vice Chairwoman Sylvia Miller (Wikipedia lists Anna Bean as Vice Chair in one source and Sylvia Miller in another — not confirmed which is current), Annette Bryan, Amber Hayward, Tim Reynon, and Fred Dillon.
 - **Government funding share:** Not confirmed. The Tribe gets federal funding through the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA), Indian Health Service (IHS), and other programs, but specific amounts were not found.

- **Pay:** Not confirmed. Tribal Council pay is not public. The Tribe is a sovereign nation, so it does not have to follow state or PDC public-records rules for internal pay.

Sterud's personal donation record is not confirmed. Tribal donations are usually made by the tribal government, not by individual council members.

## 5. How they touch government
- **Campaign donations:** The Puyallup Tribe (not Sterud personally) donates to political candidates. The graph shows `puyallup-tribe → rosie-ayala (donated, weight 3)`. The Tribe has given $600,000+ to 47 local groups from 2023 Emerald Queen Casino revenue. That is charitable, not political. It also gave $200,000+ to 19 local groups.
- **Lobbying:** Sterud personally testified before the Washington State Senate Transportation Committee on Feb 7. The bill would help tribes reclaim land. He and EQC CEO Yale Rowe also testified for the college sports wagering bill that Gov. Ferguson signed. Those are direct legislative actions.
- **Gaming compact:** The Tribe operates under a tribal-state gaming compact with Washington State. The original compact was signed by Gov. Lowry on May 28, 1996. Seven amendments followed through 2025. The current restated compact was signed by Gov. Ferguson on Sept. 12, 2025. The 7th amendment restates and supersedes all prior amendments. The Puyallup Tribe is one of three tribes (with Muckleshoot and Tulalip) allowed up to 4,000 player terminals (most tribes get 2,500).
- **Federal recognition:** The Puyallup Tribe is a federally recognized Indian Tribe (Bureau of Indian Affairs). It has a self-governance compact with the U.S. Department of the Interior. The Tribal-State Gaming Compact was deemed approved by law and published in the Federal Register (91 FR 3213, Jan 26, 2026).

Robert Watson Ferguson, born February 23, 1965; 24th Governor of Washington, assumed office January 13, 2025 (source 1, 2, 3).
Served as 18th WA Attorney General (2013–2025); King County Council member (2004–2013) (source 1, 2).
Elected Nov 5, 2024: defeated Dave Reichert (R) 55.5% to 44.3% statewide; won Pierce County 50.79% to 48.96% (source 4, 5).
Appointed Doris Walkins to Pierce County Superior Court (Feb 25, 2026), filling vacancy from Judge Kirkendoll's retirement (source 6, 7).
Appointed Colleen Melody and Theo Angelis to WA Supreme Court (source 8, 9).
Budget priorities: public safety, housing, ferries, affordability; proposed $4B in cuts and $1.3B in new programs (source 10, 11).

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why he's on the map:** Bob Ferguson is the Governor of Washington State. He runs the state's executive branch. He picks judges for every court in the state, including Pierce County Superior Court. He also writes the state budget plan.
- **Direct Pierce County action:** In February 2026, he chose Doris Walkins to fill a Pierce County Superior Court seat. That was a direct use of his power over a Pierce County court.
- **Pierce County vote:** He won Pierce County in the 2024 governor's race with 50.79% of the vote. It was close — only about 8,000 votes separated him from Republican Dave Reichert.
- **Who is NOT on the map:** Lt. Gov. Denny Heck sits on the Governor's Economic Development Council but is profiled on his own page. Former Gov. Jay Inslee is out of office now.

## 1. Who they are
- **Full name:** Robert Watson Ferguson (source 1, 2).
- **Goes by:** Bob Ferguson (source 1, 3).
- **Born:** February 23, 1965, in Washington State. He is a fourth-generation Washingtonian (source 1, 2, 3).
- **Wife and kids:** Colleen Ferguson, a teacher. Twins Jack and Katie. They live in the Governor's Mansion in Olympia (source 1, 3).
- **Parents:** Murray Ferguson, who worked at Boeing. Betty Ferguson, a special education teacher. He is one of seven children (source 2, 3).
- **Education:** Bishop Blanchet High School; BA in Political Science, University of Washington (1989); JD, New York University School of Law (1995). He also served in the Jesuit Volunteer Corps after college (source 2, 3, 12).
- **Before office:** Law clerk for Chief Judge W. Fremming Nielsen in Eastern Washington and Judge Myron Bright on the 8th Circuit Court. After that, he worked as a lawyer at the firm Preston, Gates & Ellis, now called K&L Gates (source 2, 3, 12).
- **Personal:** Catholic. Chess master (rated 2232 by FIDE, the world chess body; twice won the Washington State Chess Championship). He likes to climb and backpack (source 1, 3).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **The office.** Ferguson is the 24th Governor of Washington. He took office on January 13, 2025. His term ends January 8, 2029. As governor, he runs state agencies, writes the budget plan, picks judges, signs laws, and sets the legislative agenda (source 1, 2, 3, 8).
- **The budget.** He proposed a 2026 supplemental budget with $4 billion in cuts and $1.3 billion in new programs. His priorities are housing, public safety, ferries, affordability, and education (source 10, 11). The 2025–27 two-year state budget added $9 billion or more in new or higher taxes to close a shortfall (source 11).
- **Judicial appointments.** He picks the judges for every state court seat. That includes the Washington Supreme Court, the Court of Appeals, and every Superior Court (source 8). He has chosen two WA Supreme Court justices (Colleen Melody and Theo Angelis) and several Superior Court judges, including Doris Walkins in Pierce County (source 6, 8, 9). He can also strike individual budget items with a line-item veto.
- **Executive orders.** He signs executive orders to direct state policy. Recent ones include EO 26-02 (the Governor's Economic Development Council, June 25, 2026), EO 26-01 (workplace rules for menopause, June 1, 2026), a license plate reader law (SB 6002, March 2026), wildfire emergency orders (August 2026), and a Medicaid executive order (September 2026) (source 13, 14, 15, 16).
- **Where his power reaches:** All 39 counties in Washington, including Pierce County.

## 3. Where their power comes from

| Who benefits | Washington residents gain from public safety, housing, and education funding. The Democratic Party keeps the governorship. Judges he picks get career wins. | 3, 10, 11 |
| Who sits | Ferguson is Governor. He chairs the Governor's Economic Development Council, a 26-member panel with Amazon, Microsoft, Boeing executives, labor leaders, tribal reps, and university presidents. Lt. Gov. Denny Heck is the only other elected official on the council. | 13, 14 |
| Who governs | He runs the state executive branch, which controls a $60 billion+ two-year budget. He also picks judges statewide. | 10, 11, 14 |
| Who wins | He beat Dave Reichert 55.5% to 44.3% statewide in November 2024. He won Pierce County 50.79% to 48.96%. His judicial picks are confirmed. | 4, 5, 8 |

## 5. How they touch government
- **Campaign money.** His 2024 governor's campaign raised a lot. He beat Reichert, who ran a $1.7 million+ operation (source 4). Full filings from the state campaign-finance agency (PDC) were not pulled in this pass.
- **Pierce County vote.** He won Pierce County 220,153 (50.79%) to Reichert's 212,218 (48.96%) in November 2024. About 443,447 ballots were cast, with 76.73% turnout (source 5).
- **Judicial picks.** He picked Doris Walkins for Pierce County Superior Court on February 25, 2026. She filled the seat left open by Judge Karena Kirkendoll's retirement in Department 17 (source 6, 7). He picked Colleen Melody for the Washington Supreme Court on November 24, 2025 (replacing Justice Mary Yu) and Theo Angelis on March 9, 2026 (replacing Justice Barbara Madsen) (source 8, 9).
- **Budget.** He proposed the 2025–27 state budget (signed May 2025) and the 2026 supplemental budget (proposed December 23, 2025). The plan includes $4 billion in cuts, $1.3 billion in new programs, and $9 billion+ in new taxes. It shapes Pierce County funding for housing, public safety, and schools (source 10, 11).
- **Orders that hit Pierce County.** His Economic Development Council order (EO 26-02) brought statewide planning. SB 6002 (the license plate reader law) led the Pierce County Sheriff to shut down Flock cameras. He also signed wildfire emergency orders (August 2026) and a Medicaid executive order (September 2026) (source 13, 14, 16).
- **PDC appointment.** He appointed Matt Segal of Pacifica Law Group to the Washington State Public Disclosure Commission (PDC) (source 17).

## 6. Other seats they hold
- **Governor's Economic Development Council.** A 26-member panel with senior Amazon, Microsoft, and Boeing executives; labor leaders (the State Labor Council and the Building and Construction Trades Council); tribal reps; and university presidents. Lt. Gov. Denny Heck is the only other elected official (source 13, 14).
- **Washington Supreme Court.** Two of his picks now sit there: Colleen Melody and Theo Angelis. Melody used to run the civil rights division at the Attorney General's office under Ferguson (source 8).
- **Pierce County Superior Court.** Doris Walkins, his February 2026 appointee (source 6, 7).
- **King County Superior Court.** Kent Liu, Daniel York, Benjamin Santos, and Tenaya Scheinman, all his picks (source 8).
- **Washington Court of Appeals.** Tyson R. Hill (Division III), his appointee (source 8).
- **Washington State Democratic Party.** He won as the Democratic candidate for governor (source 2, 4).
- **Past networks.** His former AG office staff (Colleen Melody led the civil rights division). Former King County Council member (2004–2013) (source 2).

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why Boeing is on the map.** Boeing's Frederickson plant is Boeing's only major factory in Pierce County. It has about 1,500 direct jobs. It gives Boeing a seat at the local economic-development table. Boeing is on the map for four reasons. (1) It holds a place in the county: a 500-acre factory in the Frederickson industrial zone. (2) It makes decisions: Boeing runs subcontracting, hiring, and capital spending at the site. (3) It has a strong reputation: Boeing is a global Fortune 100 aerospace company, and its Frederickson plant puts Pierce County on national aerospace supply chains. (4) It is well-connected: Boeing has links to Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM) as an aerospace partner, and seats on the Chamber of Commerce board and the Economic Development Board (EDB).
- **What is NOT on the map.** Boeing corporate (The Boeing Company, based in Arlington VA since 2022, formerly in Chicago) is the parent. It is the controlling entity here but is not a separate node. Other Boeing suppliers in the area (Toray Composites America in Frederickson; AIM Aerospace) are not separate entries. The Machinists Union (IAM District 751, SPEEA) is not on the map. Boeing's Federal Way office and Renton/Everett factories are out of Pierce County.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** The Boeing Company (operating unit: Boeing Fabrication — Frederickson).
- **Type:** Public industrial corporation (NYSE: BA). Incorporated in Delaware. Aerospace and defense maker.
- **Tax ID (EIN):** 91-0425694 (The Boeing Company). SEC CIK 0000012927. Files 10-K annual reports.
- **Parent and subsidiaries:** Parent is The Boeing Company. Frederickson is an operating site of Boeing Commercial Airplanes (BCA) and Boeing Defense, Space & Security (BDS). It builds skin and spar parts for BCA commercial wing programs. It also builds Apache-related parts for BDS.
- **Who owns it:** Public shareholders. Top holders include Vanguard, BlackRock, State Street, and Capital Group. CEO Kelly Ortberg (since Aug 2024).
- **Laws that apply:** Delaware General Corporation Law. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Part 21 (aircraft production approval). ITAR (defense articles). Securities Exchange Act.
- **Founded:** Boeing was founded in 1916 in Seattle. The Frederickson plant opened in the 1990s (the plant marked its 20th anniversary in the mid-2010s).
- **Pierce County location:** Frederickson Industrial Park, south of Puyallup near the Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM) military base. Bounded roughly by 176th St E and Frederickson Industrial Park Rd. In unincorporated Pierce County (the FRED 310 zoning case surrounds the plant).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power held:** Boeing Frederickson holds economic power in Pierce County through four channels. (1) Jobs: about 1,500 direct jobs, making it one of the county's largest private employers (6th-largest in the 2017 EDB list). (2) Land: 500 acres of dedicated aerospace manufacturing. (3) Supply chain: the plant builds wing skins, stringers, and tail surfaces for the 747, 757, 767, and 777. That makes it a single point of failure inside Boeing's production system. (4) Capital spending: the FRED 310 zoning case proposes 310 acres of adjacent industrial development, expanding Boeing's landholdings.
- **Economic overlap:** Boeing's 66,800 employees in Washington state (Dec 2023, Seattle Metro Chamber data) make it the state's largest private employer. Its Pierce County site is a key part of the regional aerospace cluster.
- **Government contracts:** Boeing Frederickson builds Apache helicopter parts for BDS under federal contracts with the US Army and international customers (UK, India, Saudi Arabia, and others). Boeing's $25 billion in losses since 2019 (per AP) put cash-burn pressure on the company, including the Frederickson site.
- **Jobs controlled:** About 1,500 employees in Frederickson (2017 EDB count). It was 1,575 in 2017, down from 1,750 in 2016. The October 2024 layoff announcement hit 17,000 Boeing employees company-wide. By November 2024, 2,199 Washington state Boeing workers had received layoff notices (per ESD filings). The exact Frederickson layoff count is UNVERIFIED.
- **Land and real estate:** 500-acre factory in Frederickson Industrial Park. The Pierce County FRED 310 zoning case (2021) proposed two adjacent parcels of about 310 acres for industrial, warehouse, and office development for lease. The site is south of 176th St E and east of Frederickson Industrial Park Rd, around the current Boeing plant.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Boeing shareholders benefit from continued production, though the company has lost $25 billion+ since 2019. Frederickson workers benefit from high-wage aerospace jobs (about $80K–$120K typical for machinists; the IAM 751 contract after the strike gave a 38% pay raise over 4 years). Pierce County benefits from Boeing's tax base, capital spending, and supply-chain ripple effects. Toray Composites America was drawn to Frederickson by Boeing's presence. | #1, #2, #4 |
| Who sits | Boeing corporate: CEO Kelly Ortberg (since Aug 2024); former CEO Dave Calhoun (2020–2024). Local site management is UNVERIFIED. Boeing holds seats on the EDB, the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber, and the Greater Seattle Chamber. IAM District 751 (machinists) and SPEEA (engineers) represent Frederickson workers. | #3, #4, #5 |
| Who governs | Boeing corporate runs hiring, capital spending, product mix, and facility decisions. The Boeing Company controls whether the Frederickson plant keeps operating, what products it makes, and how many people it employs. The IAM 751 strike (Sept 13 – Nov 5, 2024) showed that labor also has governance power. The strike idled Boeing's Renton, Everett, Auburn, **Frederickson**, and Portland/Gresham plants. | #4, #5 |
| Who wins | Boeing wins when it lands major defense contracts (Apache production runs through 2028) and when commercial production stabilizes (777X delayed to 2026; 767 cargo production ends 2027). Workers won the 2024 IAM 751 strike (38% pay raise over 4 years). Pierce County won the 2014 Boeing 777X competition (Frederickson got tail-fabrication work). | #4, #5 |

**Network analysis:** Boeing is a **structurally central** but **politically constrained** node in Pierce County. The aerospace_partner link to JBLM (weight 3) reflects Boeing's deep ties to the military economy of the South Sound. Boeing makes Apache helicopters (a US Army program that flies out of JBLM), and JBLM soldiers are a key end-user market. The board link to Chamber and EDB membership (weight 3 each) reflects Boeing's voice in regional economic-development policy. The graph may underweight Boeing's real economic power in Pierce County. With 66,800 employees statewide and the company's only major Pierce County factory in Frederickson, Boeing's structural importance to the county far exceeds what a "tier3" rank suggests.

## 1. Who they are
- **The bottom line.** Boeing's Frederickson plant is Pierce County's only major Boeing industrial site. It is a 500-acre aerospace factory with about 1,500 workers (down from 1,750 in 2016 to 1,575 in 2017, and likely lower after the 2024 layoffs). The plant's power base is its aerospace supply-chain role. Boeing Frederickson builds wing skins, stringers, and tail surfaces for the 737, 747, 757, 767, and 777. It also builds Apache helicopter parts for defense. That single-point-of-failure role gives Frederickson outsized weight inside Boeing's production system. The plant's economic weight in Pierce County far exceeds what the tier3 graph rank suggests. Boeing's Pierce County workforce is concentrated here, and the plant's fortunes after the 2024 layoffs will shape the county's economic path.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags.** Boeing Frederickson creates a structural conflict between private corporate interests and public Pierce County interests. Boeing's October 2024 layoff announcement (a 10% cut, 17,000 jobs company-wide) imposed real costs on Washington workers and on Pierce County's economic base. The 2024 IAM 751 strike and its 38% pay-raise deal shifted labor costs to Boeing. Boeing is now recouping those costs through layoffs. The 2024 FRED 310 zoning case proposed 310 acres of adjacent industrial development for lease. That suggests Boeing is planning for future growth, but it also creates land-use tension with neighbors. The defense reading: Boeing is a private company making market-driven choices. The 38% pay raise reflected workers' leverage. Layoffs reflect Boeing's $25B+ losses. The FRED 310 expansion would create jobs.
- **Two readings.** The opposing reading is that Boeing Frederickson's power is overstated. Boeing's $25B+ losses, FAA production caps on the 737 MAX, the 2024 IAM strike, and the deferred 777X program all threaten the plant's future. Under this view, Boeing Frederickson is on a downward arc and its about 1,500 jobs could shrink fast. The other reading: the 777X tail-fabrication work (announced 2014) and Apache helicopter production (runs through 2028) provide a stable floor. The FRED 310 zoning case shows Boeing is planning for future capacity. The 2025–2026 path is unclear, but the plant's role inside Boeing's production system gives it institutional protection.
- **Confidence:** Medium. Boeing Frederickson's existence, product mix, employment scale, and strategic role are confirmed by primary Boeing/EDB/Pierce County sources (reliability 0.85–0.95). Specific 2024–2025 employment at Frederickson is UNVERIFIED (likely lower than 1,500 due to layoffs, exact figure not located in this session). Pierce County-specific Boeing tax payments and contracts are UNVERIFIED. The plant's relationship to specific JBLM Apache operations is UNVERIFIED beyond general Apache production.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- Bruce Dammeier is on this map because he held the top elected job in Pierce County: Pierce County Executive from 2017 to 2024. The Executive runs the county's $1B+ budget, can veto Council laws, and hires the heads of about 30 county departments. He is a Republican. He left office in January 2025 after hitting his term limit. Democrat Ryan Mello took the seat.
- People NOT on the map: Pat McCarthy (a former Executive before him), Roger Bush (a Council Chair during his term), and Joe Stortini (an even earlier Executive).

## 1. Who they are
- **Full name:** Bruce Dammeier.
- **Born:** Not confirmed in this pass. No date of birth in the records reviewed.
- **School:** B.S. in Ocean Engineering from the U.S. Naval Academy, graduated with distinction. M.S. in Engineering from the University of Washington (UW).
- **Military:** 8 years as a U.S. Navy Civil Engineer Corps Officer. He went on relief missions.
- **Career:** Naval officer → ran a family printing business → community volunteer → WA House District 25 (2009–2013) → WA Senate District 25 (2013–2017, Senate Majority Caucus Vice Chair) → Pierce County Executive (2017–2024).
- **Family:** Married to Lauren Dammeier.
- **Home:** Pierce County native. He went to Curtis High School in the University Place area.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Elected executive power (from his office):** As Pierce County Executive from 2017 to 2024, Dammeier could veto Council laws. He hired the heads of about 30 county departments. He signed contracts and deals with other governments. He used the veto in public. His most public veto was Ordinance 2024-540s on large tent encampments in August 2024.
- **Budget power (decisions on money):** He wrote and negotiated the county's two-year budget, worth more than $1B for operations. He also decided how to spend federal ARPA funds, homelessness programs, and the Building Together Initiative.
- **Bridge role to nonprofits:** He sat on boards for community groups like Tacoma Goodwill and Mel Korum YMCA. As Executive, his seat on these boards linked county power to the local nonprofit world.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- The Candidate Academy is a candidate-training program run by the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber. The Chamber is the region's main business advocacy group. Its tax ID number (EIN) is 91-0434830 (Source 3). The Academy meets the bar for being well-connected. It bridges the business world and the electoral world by training future candidates. It also meets the bar for from holding office. It is a formal program of the Chamber, a gatekeeper in Pierce County politics. The graph shows a weight-5 edge from the Academy to the Pierce County Council. That marks its pipeline function.
- A few related Chamber programs sit outside this map. The Business Leadership Academy is a separate 10-week program, founded in 1978 (Source 5). It is not directly political, so it is excluded. Spaceworks Tacoma is a Chamber arts and business incubator. It is excluded. The Pierce County Business Accelerator is for BIPOC businesses. It is excluded.

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** The Candidate Academy is not a separate legal entity. It is a program of the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce. The Chamber's legal name is "Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce." Its EIN is 91-0434830 (Source 3).
- **Entity type:** The Chamber is a 501(c)(6) business league. It is a chamber of commerce (Sources 3 and 4, ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer: "Business leagues, chambers of commerce, real estate boards, etc., created for the improvement of business conditions"). Donations to the Chamber are not tax-deductible (Source 4).
- **EIN and registration:** 91-0434830 (Sources 3 and 4). Year formed: 1884 (Source 3, CauseIQ). The tax exemption was issued before 2012. ProPublica has filings from 2012 onward (Source 4). The fiscal year ends in September (Source 3).
- **Parent and subsidiaries:** The parent is the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce. The Chamber also runs a separate foundation: "Tacoma Pierce County Chamber of Commerce Foundation" (EIN 20-4962532, 501(c)(3), tax exemption issued August 2006, Source 6). The Candidate Academy is a program, not a subsidiary.
- **Ownership chain:** The Chamber is an independent nonprofit. It is run by a board of directors. The board has 31 voting members. All 31 are independent voting members per the most recent 990 (Source 3).
- **Governing law:** Washington state nonprofit corporation law. State law (RCW) 24.03. The federal tax agency (IRS) 501(c)(6) status.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power held:** The Candidate Academy holds cultural power and power from connections. It is a candidate-recruitment and training pipeline. It shapes who runs for local office. It does not hold legal or regulatory power. It does not have veto power. Its power is indirect. By teaching campaign operations, fundraising, and media messaging, it shapes who enters local politics. The program helps people "determine whether to throw their hat in the ring or how to otherwise get engaged" (Source 1).
- **Basis for power-domain overlap (political domain):** The program covers Civics 101, campaign strategy and operations, election filing, fundraising and event planning, media and messaging, and campaign management. Local political leaders teach these topics (Source 1). This puts the Chamber in the role of gatekeeper for business-aligned candidates.
- **Key facts:**
 - **Who is funded and endorsed?** The Candidate Academy does not directly fund or endorse candidates. It trains them. The Chamber's separate Voters Guide handles endorsements (Source 2). It is unverified whether Academy graduates get Chamber endorsements at higher rates.
 - **PAC spending?** UNVERIFIED. No Chamber PAC was found in this research. The Chamber's 501(c)(6) status allows political advocacy, but not direct candidate donations (Source 4).
 - **Party machinery control?** The program is nonpartisan in framing. It is open to "civic-minded individuals." But the Chamber's business focus means the training likely leans toward pro-business candidates. Inference: the program acts as a soft recruiting channel for business-aligned candidates. This is not stated openly.
 - **Candidate output?** UNVERIFIED. The Chamber does not publish a list of Academy graduates. It does not track how many graduates run or win. The 47th Business Leadership Academy graduated "more than twenty participants" in 2025 (Source 5). No similar number is available for the Candidate Academy.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Prospective candidates benefit from training and networking with "local elected officials and community advocates" (source #1). The Chamber benefits by expanding its network of politically engaged allies. Business-aligned candidates benefit from Chamber infrastructure and connections. | #1 |
| Who sits | The program features "speakers who are leaders in the political sphere around Tacoma and Pierce County" (source #1) — specific speaker roster UNVERIFIED. The Chamber's board (31 voting members per 990, source #3) governs the parent organization. | #1, #3 |
| Who governs | The Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber Board of Directors governs the Candidate Academy as a program of the Chamber. UNVERIFIED: whether the Academy has a separate advisory committee or program director. | #3 |
| Who wins | UNVERIFIED — no public data on Academy graduates who subsequently won elected office. The program's stated goal is to equip participants to "become better equipped to serve as a candidate and elected or appointed official" (source #1), but outcomes are not tracked publicly. | #1 |

## 5. How they touch government
- **Lobbying:** The parent Chamber, a 501(c)(6), engages in advocacy (Source 2: the Chamber lists "Advocacy" as a core function). The Candidate Academy is an educational program. It is not a lobbying vehicle. Specific L-2 lobbyist registrations for the Chamber are unverified.
- **Contracts and grants:** UNVERIFIED. No government contracts or grants were found for the Candidate Academy. The Chamber's 990 (Source 3) shows $3.1 million in revenue for FY2024. Program-level revenue is not available.
- **Campaign donations:** The Chamber, as a 501(c)(6), cannot make direct candidate donations. The Candidate Academy does not donate to candidates. It is unverified whether speakers or graduates have given money through other vehicles.
- **Voters Guide:** The Chamber publishes a Voters Guide (Source 2: listed under Resources on the Chamber website). This is a separate advocacy function from the Candidate Academy. It is the Chamber's interface with the electoral system.
- **Regulatory interactions:** None found. The Academy is an educational program. It has no regulatory role.

## 6. Other seats they hold
- **Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber (`chamber`):** This is the parent organization. The Candidate Academy is a Chamber program (Source 1). Graph edge: `runs`, weight 6.
- **Pierce County Council (`county-council`):** The Academy trains people who may run for offices like the County Council (Source 1 covers "various levels of government and elected positions"). Graph edge: `trains_candidates`, weight 5. It is unverified whether specific Council members have been Academy speakers.
- **Pacific Lutheran University (PLU):** The Chamber's separate Business Leadership Academy is "made possible through a partnership between the Chamber and Pacific Lutheran University" (Source 5). It is unverified whether PLU also partners on the Candidate Academy.
- **Local elected officials:** The Academy has "local elected officials and community advocates" as speakers (Source 1). This creates direct board overlaps between the Chamber and sitting officials. Specific names are unverified.

## 9. Who they are connected to
Graph connections (from `evidence/29-power-graph-v2.json`):

| Connected entity | Relationship | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| Chamber of Commerce (`chamber`) | runs | 6 |
| Pierce County Council (`county-council`) | trains_candidates | 5 |

**Network analysis:** The Candidate Academy is a two-edge node. It bridges the Chamber (economic and advocacy world) and the County Council (government and electoral world). The weight-6 `runs` edge to the Chamber is the main tie. The Academy is a Chamber program, not an independent body. The weight-5 `trains_candidates` edge to the County Council shows its pipeline function. It trains people who may later run for Council and other offices. The Academy ranks 36/163 with a composite power of 0.052. This reflects its indirect power. It does not govern or regulate. But it shapes who runs for office. That is a form of agenda-setting power.

| 6 | Tacoma Pierce County Chamber of Commerce Foundation: EIN 20-4962532; 501(c)(3); tax exemption issued August 2006; separate entity from the Chamber (501(c)(6)) | ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer — Chamber Foundation 990 | https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/204962532 | primary | 0.9 |

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** The Candidate Academy is a candidate-training program run by the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce. It does not directly govern, regulate, or donate to candidates. Its power comes from connections and culture. It shapes who enters local politics. It gives campaign skills and access to elected officials to future candidates. The program's 1-day format and lack of public graduate tracking limit its measurable impact. But its role as a gatekeeper for business-aligned candidates is structurally important. The Chamber also publishes a Voters Guide (Source 2) and runs the Academy. That creates a path from training to endorsement, though the Academy itself does not endorse.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags:** (1) The Chamber trains candidates through the Academy. It may then endorse them through its Voters Guide. That creates a path from training to endorsement that could favor Academy graduates. (2) The program is run by a 501(c)(6) business league. So training likely leans toward pro-business candidates, even if the program is nonpartisan. Defense: (1) No evidence shows that Academy graduates get special endorsement treatment. The Voters Guide and Academy are separate functions. (2) The program is open to all "civic-minded individuals" (Source 1). It covers neutral topics like civics and election filing. It does not cover ideology. No evidence of partisan filtering in participant selection was found.
- **Analysis of alternatives:** The other reading is that the Candidate Academy is a small educational program with limited reach. It runs for one day. It does not publish a graduate list. It has no measurable impact on who gets elected in Pierce County. Under this view, the weight-5 `trains_candidates` edge overstates the program's real influence. But the program's structural position matters. It is run by the region's main business advocacy group. It features sitting elected officials as speakers. It covers the full campaign toolkit. That gives it more agenda-setting power than its length suggests. The lack of outcome tracking is also telling. If the Academy did not work, the Chamber would publish its success numbers.
- **Confidence:** Medium. The program's existence, curriculum, and Chamber parentage are confirmed by primary sources (Chamber website, reliability 0.9). However, the program's actual impact — how many graduates ran for office, won, or received Chamber endorsements — is UNVERIFIED due to absence of published outcome data. The power assessment is structural/inferential rather than empirically demonstrated.

fields.graph_description: Roman Catholic metropolitan archdiocese covering western Washington (including all of Pierce County); canonically responsible for parishes, schools, and religious institutions in the case-study area, and ecclesiastical sponsor of major Pierce County healthcare systems (VMFH and, through CommonSpirit, Franciscan).

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
<!-- id:boundary -->
- The Archdiocese of Seattle is on this map for two reasons. First, it directly runs Catholic parishes and schools in Pierce County. These include Holy Rosary, St. Ann, St. Rita, and Visitation in Tacoma, plus Bellarmine Preparatory and several grade schools. Second, it sponsors Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (a major hospital chain in Pierce County). That gives it a voice in Pierce County's health-care market. Its 2020 to 2022 "Pierce Deanery" plan merged four Tacoma parishes into one. That was a big land-use and institutional change.
- **Adjacent groups not profiled.** The Vatican and the global Catholic Church are too remote. Catholic Community Services of Western Washington is a separate nonprofit. CommonSpirit Health (the parent of VMFH) has its own profile. Independent Catholic schools that are not archdiocesan (like Annie Wright, which is Episcopal) are not included.

## 1. Who they are
<!-- id:identity tier:1 -->
- **Legal name:** Archdiocese of Seattle (in Latin: Archidiœcesis Seattlensis).
- **Entity type:** A Roman Catholic archdiocese (Latin Rite means the standard Western form of the Catholic Church). The civil corporate side is the **Corporation of the Catholic Archbishop of Seattle**, a nonprofit under Washington state law (RCW 24.03). This corporation holds title to parish property, schools, and investments. *Inferred — UNVERIFIED in this round of research, but standard for US Latin-rite dioceses.*
- **History:** 1850 as the Diocese of Nesqually. Renamed in 1907. Became a metropolitan archdiocese (the head of a church region) in 1951.
- **Territory:** 24,814 square miles — all of Western Washington, including all of Pierce County.
- **Stats (2022):** 143 parishes, 72 schools, 6.1 million people in territory, about 899,000 Catholics (14.7%).
- **Mother church:** St. James Cathedral, Seattle (804 9th Avenue).
- **Current archbishop:** Paul D. Etienne (DD, installed 2019).
- **Governing law:** Canon law (the Catholic Church's own legal system) and Washington state law (RCW 24.03 for nonprofits, RCW 84.36 for religious-property tax breaks).

## 3. Where their power comes from
<!-- id:power-basis -->
- The Archdiocese holds three types of power. It owns and runs Catholic parish, school, and cemetery real estate in Pierce County. It sponsors CHI Franciscan / Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (a hospital chain). That gives it three power levers:
 1. **Land-use decisions.** It can consolidate, sell, or redevelop property. In 2022 it sold four First Hill Seattle properties to Westbank. In 2020 to 2022 its Pierce Deanery plan merged Holy Rosary, St. Ann, Visitation, and St. Rita into one parish.
 2. **Cultural and community reach.** About 900,000 Catholics live in Western Washington. That makes the Archdiocese the largest single organized religious group in Pierce County. Its parishes can mobilize people on school-board, charter, and immigrant-services issues.
 3. **Health-care influence.** The Archdiocese sponsors CommonSpirit, the parent of VMFH. The archbishop's office has a say in mission and ethics at Pierce County's largest hospital chain. That includes St. Joseph Medical Center in Tacoma; St. Anthony in Gig Harbor; St. Clare in Lakewood; St. Elizabeth in Enumclaw; and St. Francis in Federal Way.
- **Key facts:**
 - **Tax status:** Houses of worship and their integrated groups are tax-exempt under IRC §501(c)(3) (a federal tax code for charities). Parishes and schools pay no federal income tax. They also get a property-tax break under RCW 84.36.020.
 - **Board overlaps:** The archbishop sits on Catholic Health Ministries and the Archdiocesan Finance Council. Pastors sit on parish councils. Lay trustees sit on parish finance councils.
 - **Government funding:** Schools get state K–12 funding (under RCW 28A.150) from the Common Schools fund. Parishes rely on Sunday collections and the Annual Catholic Appeal. Downstream, VMFH brings in large Medicaid and Medicare payments.

## 3. Where their power comes from
<!-- id:power-indicators -->

| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Parishioners get religious and educational services. The Archdiocese collects a yearly tithe (a set share of income, here called the Annual Catholic Appeal) and capital gifts. VMFH patients get faith-based health care. | 1, 2, 4 |
| Who sits | Archbishop Etienne governs Pierce County parishes and sits on CHI/CommonSpirit sponsorship bodies. Pastors sit on parish pastoral councils. Lay trustees sit on parish finance councils. | 1, 2 |
| Who governs | The Archdiocese directly governs parish real estate (the Holy Rosary building fate was decided 2020 to 2022 at the archdiocesan level). It indirectly governs VMFH mission through CHI/CommonSpirit sponsorship. | 2, 3, 4 |
| Who wins | The Archdiocese wins on property control and consolidation. Tacoma congregations of the merged Pierce Deanery parish face structural change, including school mergers and building sales. | 3, 4 |

## 9. Who they are connected to

| Connected entity | Relationship | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| CommonSpirit Health (`commonspirit`) | religious_affiliation | 2 |
| VMFH/CHI (`vmfh`) | religious_sponsor | 3 |
