Etienne; mother church St. James Cathedral; territory 24,814 sq mi; metropolitan status since 1951. | Wikipedia, "Archdiocese of Seattle" (compiling archdiocesan statistical data) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archdiocese_of_Seattle | secondary (Wikipedia, sourced from archdiocesan statistical directory) | 0.85 |
| 2 | Pierce Deanery strategic-planning committee, led by Auxiliary Bishop Daniel Mueggenborg, is consolidating parishes; "Partners in the Gospel" is the archdiocesan pastoral-renewal framework. | Archdiocese of Seattle news release (Mar 10, 2021) and homepage | https://archseattle.org/news-and-events/news-releases ; https://archseattle.org | primary (archdiocesan communications) | 0.95 |
| 3 | Holy Rosary Tacoma is the anchor parish for the new merged Tacoma parish (Holy Rosary + St. Ann + Visitation + St. Rita); founded 1891 as the second parish in Tacoma; pastorate and deanery-leadership committees named. | Archdiocese of Seattle — Pierce Deanery page | https://archseattle.org/about-the-archdiocese-of-seattle/archbishop-etienne/archdiocesan-strategic-planning/pierce-deanery | primary | 0.95 |
| 4 | Bellarmine Preparatory School, Tacoma; Holy Rosary Bilingual Academy, Fife; St. Charles Borromeo, Tacoma; St. Frances Cabrini, Tacoma; St. Patrick, Tacoma; St. Nicholas, Gig Harbor — all listed as Archdiocese of Seattle Catholic schools serving Pierce County. | My Catholic School — Archdiocese of Seattle Catholic Schools List | https://mycatholicschool.org/2018/07/25/archdiocese-of-seattle-catholic-schools-list | secondary (archdiocese-affiliated directory) | 0.80 |

## 1. Who they are
<!-- id:assessment -->
- **Verdict:** The Archdiocese is a stable, long-lasting institution in Pierce County. Its power comes from parish real-estate decisions (the 2020 to 2022 Pierce Deanery merger is a clear example), sponsorship of the dominant Catholic hospital chain (CHI Franciscan → VMFH), and a parish-school network that reaches thousands of families each week. Its composite power score (0.012) is too low, because the framework under-weights canonical and religious power.
- **Conflict flags:** Sponsorship of VMFH gives the Archdiocese a voice in a major Pierce County employer with a large land footprint. Canonical authority over a hospital chain creates a parallel accountability channel outside public meetings. The property-tax break for parish and school land is a recurring public-finance question. The defense: religious property-tax breaks are constitutional (Walz v. Taxpayers, 1970) and predate the modern hospital chain. The Archdiocese's Pierce County footprint is small compared to public-school or secular nonprofit landholdings.
- **Counter-reading:** The Archdiocese is in steep national demographic decline. Western Washington's Catholic population is still growing (Hispanic and immigrant inflows). VMFH is one of the largest private employers in Pierce County. The Archdiocese is not vestigial, but it is constrained by sexual-abuse bankruptcy filings that have drained reserves in other dioceses. Confidence in this profile: **Medium**.
- **Confidence:** Medium — territorial, demographic, parish, school, and Pierce-Deanery data are all primary-sourced; the corporate-veil detail (Corporation of the Catholic Archbishop of Seattle) is INFERRED from standard US Latin-rite practice.

fields.graph_description: Central Pierce Fire & Rescue (Pierce County Fire District 6); merged with Graham Fire & Rescue and Orting Valley Fire & Rescue effective Jan 1, 2026; governed by elected Board of Fire Commissioners under Title 52 RCW
fields.profile:
## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Inclusion rule — power and decision-making.** Central Pierce Fire & Rescue is a special-purpose fire district. It is governed by an elected Board of Fire Commissioners under Title 52 of the Revised Code of Washington (RCW), the state law that covers fire districts.
- It levies taxes on property owners in its service area. It controls a budget of more than $100 million. It runs fire and emergency medical services.
- On January 1, 2026, the district merged with Graham Fire & Rescue and Orting Valley Fire & Rescue. That made it one of the largest fire districts in Pierce County.
- **Adjacent but excluded:** East Pierce Fire & Rescue and West Pierce Fire & Rescue are peer districts mapped separately. South Pierce Fire & Rescue is adjacent and mapped separately. Pierce County Fire Training Consortium is a shared service entity and not a power node.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Central Pierce Fire & Rescue. Also known as Pierce County Fire District 6.
- **Entity type:** Government — a special-purpose fire protection district under Title 52 RCW. Set up as a municipal corporation with taxing authority.
- **Governing law:** Title 52 RCW. The Board of Fire Commissioners is "the legislative body of Central Pierce Fire & Rescue."
- **Merger history:** On April 22, 2025, voters approved merging Graham Fire & Rescue and Orting Valley Fire & Rescue into Central Pierce. The Graham vote was 7,483 yes to 1,130 no. The merger took effect January 1, 2026. The three legacy districts are now one.
- **Board:** After the merger, the board has 14 commissioners from the three legacy districts. Commissioners are elected at-large by voters. They serve six-year terms.
- **Executive leadership:** Fire Chief Dustin Morrow.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Statutory authority.** Under RCW 52, Central Pierce can levy voter-approved property taxes (Regular Fire Levy, EMS Levy), charge a Fire Benefit Charge (FBC), issue general obligation bonds with voter approval, and provide fire and emergency medical services within its borders.
- **Taxing authority:** Three voter-approved funding sources:
  - Regular Fire Levy — about 40% of the budget. Rate was $0.50 per $1,000 of assessed value (AV) in each legacy district. A levy lid lift from $0.73 to $1.00 per $1,000 AV went on the April 2024 ballot (Resolution 24-01). A "levy lid lift" is a vote to raise the property-tax rate above the state cap.
  - EMS Levy — about 16% of the budget. 20.1% of Central Pierce funding in 2024.
  - Fire Benefit Charge (FBC) — about 36% of the budget. Based on property use and square footage, not assessed value. Must be reauthorized by voters every six years.
- **Budget control:** The 2021 appropriated budget totaled $105,386,885 across six funds. General Fund: $64.9 million. EMS Fund: $16.6 million. GEMT (Ground Emergency Medical Transport) Fund: $12.2 million. Debt Fund: $2.5 million. Capital Projects Fund: $9.08 million. HRA/Flex: $50,000. Actual 2021 spending was $88.4 million. Post-merger 2026 totals are not verified.
- **Domain overlaps:**
  - **Government ↔ Economic:** Taxing authority over property in the district; contracts for equipment and services.
  - **Government ↔ Institutional:** Interlocal agreements (formal cooperation contracts between governments) with peer fire districts; member of Pierce County Fire Training Consortium.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Residents and property owners in the district get fire and EMS service paid for by levies and the FBC. The merger with Graham and Orting Valley extends that base. | Sources 1, 5, 7 |
| Who sits | The 14-member Board of Fire Commissioners governs the district. The 2025–2026 merger with Graham and Orting Valley Fire & Rescue significantly expanded its territorial and fiscal footprint, making it one of the largest fire districts in Pierce County. Its Board of 14 elected commissioners exercises budgetary and operational governance. Its budget exceeded $105M (2021 appropriated) and has likely grown post-merger.

Commissioner races are partisan-adjacent elections with low voter engagement, which could allow incumbent entrenchment.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- The Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce runs the county's top business group. It shapes local politics in three main ways.
- First, it runs the Candidate Academy. This program trains people who want to run for office. The Chamber does not say who the graduates are.
- Second, it issues voter guides. These tell members which candidates and ballot measures to back.
- Third, its board seats are filled by leaders of the county's biggest employers. They include MultiCare, the Port of Tacoma, Boeing, Puget Sound Energy (PSE), and Banner Bank. These board ties give the Chamber a direct line into policy fights.
- The Chamber is a 501(c)(6) business league. The IRS gives this tax status to groups that work to improve business conditions. Its address is 950 Pacific Ave, Suite 300, Tacoma, WA 98402. Its phone number is (253) 627-2175. Its EIN (Employer Identification Number, the IRS tax ID) is 91-0434830.
- **Related but separate groups (not part of the Chamber):** The Economic Development Board for Tacoma-Pierce County (EDB) is a separate partner. The Manufacturing Industrial Council for the South Sound is a Chamber program, not its own group. The Chamber Foundation (EIN 20-4962532, revenue $76K) is a separate nonprofit that supports the Chamber.

## 1. Who they are
- **Official name:** Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce
- **Type:** 501(c)(6) business league
- **EIN:** 91-0434830

## 2. Their career and offices
- **CEO/President:** Andrea Reay. She was paid $196,300 in fiscal year 2024, per the IRS 990 form (the annual tax return nonprofits file). She took over from Tom Pierson. Pierson was CEO from 2011 to 2021. He came back as interim CEO before Reay's appointment.

- **Voter guides:** The Chamber publishes voter guides. These guide members' views on candidates and ballot measures.
- **Board overlaps:** The 25+ member board includes top leaders from the county's biggest employers and most powerful institutions. They come from MultiCare, the Port of Tacoma, Boeing, PSE, and Banner Bank. These ties create a steady channel for business influence on local policy.
- **Advocacy and lobbying:** The Chamber's stated programs include "Advocacy." This means direct lobbying of Pierce County Council, Tacoma City Council, and the state legislature on business-friendly policy.
- **501(c)(6) tax-exempt status:** The Chamber is tax-exempt under federal law as a business league. The Pierce County Council has indirect power over local tax rules that affect Chamber members.

 - *Revenue:* about $3.08 million in fiscal year 2024 (per IRS 990)
 - *Ownership:* nonprofit, no owners; run by an elected board

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** The Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce holds power in three ways. First, the Candidate Academy trains and may pick future candidates who back business. Second, board ties link the county's biggest employers (MultiCare, Port, PSE, Boeing) and growth-machine developers (Rush, Miles, Southport, Tucci, Lincoln Park, Nall) into one advocacy network. Third, the Chamber lobbies directly and issues voter guides. Its $3.08 million in revenue is small next to the billions run by its board members' groups. The Chamber's value is as a coordinator, not as a money mover. Falling revenue (down 22% over two years) and four straight years of audit findings (FY2022–FY2025, including two "material noncompliance" findings) point to stress that could weaken it.

 - *Developer board ties:* Developers sit on the board (Rush, Miles, Southport, Tucci, Lincoln Park, Nall). They have land-use cases before the County Council. That creates a direct conflict between the Chamber's advocacy role and its members' money interests.
 - *Audit findings:* Four straight fiscal years (FY2022–FY2025) carry audit findings — "material noncompliance" in FY2022 and FY2024; internal-control deficiencies in FY2023 and FY2025. The audits' presence suggests the Chamber handled $750K+ in federal grant money in those years (inference from the single-audit requirement; confirm from the audit reports). This raises money-oversight questions if the Chamber handles any public funds.
 - *501(c)(6) versus political activity:* As a business league, the Chamber can do some political work but cannot give money to candidates directly. The line between "civic education" (voter guides, candidate forums) and election work is thin.
- **Analysis of alternatives:** The other reading is that the Chamber is in decline and its power is overstated. Revenue is falling. Reserves are dropping. The CEO has changed twice in three years. Audit findings point to governance problems. The "Chamber candidate" label may be a relic of past power, not a sign of current power. Under this view, real economic power sits with the corporations on the board (MultiCare, the Port, PSE, Boeing), not with the Chamber as a coordinator. The Candidate Academy may produce few real elected officials. The voter guide may barely move votes. The Chamber's rank of 2 out of 163 in the graph may come from its dense connections, not from real power to make decisions.
- **Confidence:** Medium — IRS 990 data is primary-source and highly reliable, but the Chamber's political influence channels (Candidate Academy, lobbying) are opaque. The audit findings are concerning but not yet fully investigated. The decline in revenue and net assets is factual but its political implications are inferred.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
<!-- id:boundary -->
- **Why Chatham is on the map.** Chatham Asset Management owns The McClatchy Company. McClatchy publishes The News Tribune in Tacoma — the main daily paper for Pierce County. Chatham is based in New Jersey. But its decisions about money, layoffs, and use of AI directly shape what Pierce County residents read about their local government.
- **What that gives Chatham.** Two kinds of power. One is ownership of a regional newspaper monopoly. The other is the impact of newsroom cuts on accountability reporting at the local-government level.
- **Who is NOT on the map.** McClatchy itself has its own profile. Postmedia is a Canadian chain owned by Chatham but is outside the case area. A360media (also called American Media) merged into McClatchy in December 2024 and is now part of the McClatchy operation.

## 1. Who they are
<!-- id:identity tier:1 -->
- **Legal name:** Chatham Asset Management, LLC.
- **Type of business:** A private hedge-fund manager set up as a New Jersey LLC.
- **Headquarters:** 26 Main Street, Chatham Borough, NJ 07928.
- **Founded:** 2000 (about 26 years ago, per Wikipedia).
- **Founder and owner:** Anthony Melchiorre. He owns about 70% of the firm. He was born around 1968 (per 2023 reports). He grew up near Chicago and now lives in Short Hills, NJ.
- **Other key principal:** Larry Buchalter.
- **Regulatory history:** In April 2023, the SEC charged Chatham and Melchiorre with improper trading in fixed-income securities tied to American Media / AMI stock. They paid a $19.3 million civil penalty to settle (per NJ Globe and Reuters, April 2023).
- **Major companies Chatham owns:**
 - **The McClatchy Company, LLC.** Private; bought September 4, 2020, out of Chapter 11 bankruptcy for $312 million. Headquartered in Sacramento, California. Runs 30 daily papers across 14 states. Merged with A360media in December 2024 and is now called **McClatchy Media**.
 - **Postmedia Network Canada Corp.** About 66% control since October 2016. It is Canada's largest newspaper chain.
 - **A360media, LLC.** Formerly American Media, Inc. Merged into McClatchy in December 2024.
 - **RR Donnelley.** Printing and distribution company.
- **Governing law:** Delaware and New Jersey LLC rules. SEC-registered investment adviser. Where required, it files reports under Section 13 of the Securities Exchange Act (Postmedia is publicly listed in Canada).

## 3. Where their power comes from
<!-- id:power-basis -->
- **What power does this company hold?**
 1. **Control of media markets.** Through McClatchy, Chatham owns Washington's second-largest newspaper (The News Tribune in Tacoma) plus The Olympian, The Bellingham Herald, and the Tri-City Herald. The four biggest McClatchy papers in Washington cover the I-5 corridor from Bellingham down through Pierce County (per NW Labor Press and the Seattle Times).
 2. **Power over the newsroom.** Since buying McClatchy in 2020, Chatham has pushed repeated newsroom cuts. The Miami Herald had layoffs (per WFLA). In 2025, The News Tribune, The Olympian, and the Bellingham Herald all had layoffs (per Seattle Times). This affects what gets reported on Pierce County government, schools, Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM), and the Port of Tacoma.
 3. **Capital and political economy.** A hedge fund owning regional newspapers plays into the broader decline of local news in America (covered by PEN America and the Notre Dame Local News Index). In 2025 and 2026, Northwest journalists went on strike against McClatchy over the use of AI in place of reporters and over starting pay of about $45,000.
- **Key facts about the media side:**
 - **Ownership chain:** Chatham (NJ) → McClatchy Co. LLC (Sacramento, post-Chapter 11 since September 4, 2020) → The News Tribune (Tacoma).
 - **Reach:** The News Tribune is "the second-largest newspaper in Washington, covering the local news market of Pierce County in print and online" (per McClatchy's own markets page). It also covers JBLM (one of the largest U.S. military bases) and the Port of Tacoma.
 - **Editorial direction:** Local, not partisan-national. Investigative capacity has dropped (per Seattle Times reporting on 2025 layoffs and the 2026 strike, which note reporters covering Pierce County government have been cut).

## 3. Where their power comes from
<!-- id:power-indicators -->

| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|---|-------|---|
| Who benefits | Chatham and McClatchy shareholders gain from cost cuts. Remaining newsroom staff face lower pay and AI substitution. Pierce County readers lose accountability reporting. | 1, 3, 4 |
| Who sits | Chatham's principals (Melchiorre, Buchalter) do not sit in Pierce County government. McClatchy CEO Tony Hunter has run the company since 2020. Chairman Kevin McClatchy is a name left over from the founding family, but Chatham controls the company. | 2 |
| Who governs | Chatham controls how McClatchy spends its money, decides on layoffs, and ultimately decides whether Pierce County still has a daily paper of record five years from now. | 1, 3 |
| Who wins | Pierce County officials who want less scrutiny win through attrition. Chatham wins by pulling out cash. Readers and accountability journalism lose. | 3, 4 |

## 1. Who they are
<!-- id:assessment -->
- **The bottom line.** Chatham is based out of the region but still matters a lot for Pierce County. Their ownership of The News Tribune is the single biggest private factor in whether Pierce County has strong local-government reporting. The 2025 layoffs at The News Tribune (which cut the Tacoma City Hall and Pierce County government beat) and the 2026 strike over AI substitution are direct, documented Chatham-era decisions. The composite power score (0.010) understates that real-world influence.
- **Conflicts to watch.** First, the 2023 SEC settlement for improper trading shows Chatham had governance problems. Second, hedge-fund ownership of a regional newspaper of record is a structural mismatch with the civic-journalism mission. Third, the December 2024 merger of McClatchy and A360media (a tabloid publisher) further cut into hard-news capacity. The defense reading: Chatham bought McClatchy out of bankruptcy and saved jobs that would have been lost otherwise. That is partly true. It does not erase the structural critique.
- **The counter-argument.** McClatchy might have failed anyway given the long decline of the newspaper industry. Chatham's money stopped an immediate collapse. But the Seattle Times reporting and the 2026 strike suggest that Chatham-era cuts went deeper than the industry-wide decline would predict.
- **Confidence:** Medium — corporate ownership, SEC settlement, McClatchy acquisition price, and 2025 layoffs / 2026 strike are primary-sourced; the *counterfactual* (what would have happened absent Chatham) is necessarily INFERENCE.

The Cheney Foundation is one of the largest private family foundations in Pierce County. It gives grants across youth, education, community development, and human services. These areas overlap with many public agencies and nonprofits in the network.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- Chris Gildon is on the map because he holds office and makes decisions. He is the sitting State Senator for the 25th Legislative District. That district covers Puyallup, South Hill, Summit, and Waller in Pierce County. As Senate Republican lead on the Ways and Means Committee (the operating budget committee), he plays a big role in shaping the state's operating budget. That budget directly affects Pierce County funding. He also co-chairs the bipartisan Pierce County legislative delegation. That delegation includes members from both parties and both chambers.
- **Adjacent figures not profiled here.** Cyndy Jacobsen (R-25) is the current House member who succeeded Gildon. She is not at this tier. Joyce McDonald (R-25) was the House member Gildon succeeded. She is a former officeholder.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Christopher Don Gildon (Source 1, 2).
- **Aliases:** Chris Gildon (common usage).
- **Date of birth / birthplace:** August 14, 1971, Odessa, Texas (Source 1).
- **Current residence:** Puyallup, Washington (Source 2, 5).
- **Family / spouse:** Wife Autumn Gildon. They were married 31 years. She passed away in April 2025. He has two adult children (Source 2, 5).
- **Education:** B.A. in Political Science from the University of Texas. M.P.A. (Master of Public Administration) from Webster University. M.A. in Strategic Security Studies from National Defense University (Source 2, 5).
- **Military service:** 23-year U.S. Army veteran. He did five overseas deployments. He earned two Bronze Star medals (Source 5).
- **Occupation:** Commercial real estate broker and property manager (Source 2). Also a politician.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power held — elected office:** Washington State Senator for the 25th Legislative District. He has served since January 11, 2021. His current term ends January 8, 2029. Before that, he served in the Washington House of Representatives. He represented the 25th District, Position 2, from January 14, 2019 to January 11, 2021 (Source 1, 2).
- **Committee authority:** He is the Senate Republican Leader on the Ways and Means Committee. That makes him the lead Republican voice on the state's operating budget. It is one of the most powerful committee assignments in the Senate (Source 2, 5). He also sits on the Housing Committee.
- **Additional roles:** Member, Economic and Revenue Forecast Council. Member, Legislative Ethics Board. Co-chair of the Washington State Institute for Public Policy (WSIPP) Board of Directors. Co-chair of the bipartisan Pierce County legislative delegation. Member, Joint Committee on Veterans' and Military Affairs. Member, Legislative Committee on Economic Development and International Relations. Member, Washington State Criminal Sentencing Task Force. Member, Legislative-Executive WorkFirst Poverty Reduction Oversight Task Force (Source 2, 5).
- **Budget controlled:** As Senate Republican Operating Budget Leader, he shapes Republican budget proposals. He negotiates with the Democratic majority on the state operating budget, which is about $70 billion for two years.
- **Jurisdiction governed:** 25th Legislative District — Puyallup, South Hill, Summit, Waller (Pierce County).

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Pierce County residents get budget attention through his co-chair role on the Pierce County delegation. Republican-aligned donors and groups like T-Mobile, WA Food Industry, and Washbankpac get access to the budget leader (Source 6). | 6 |
| Who sits | Gildon sits on the WSIPP Board (co-chair), the Economic and Revenue Forecast Council, the Legislative Ethics Board, the Pierce County delegation (co-chair), and Senate Ways and Means (Republican lead). | 2, 5 |
| Who governs | As operating budget leader for the Senate Republican Caucus, he governs the minority party's budget strategy. He has floor influence over spending bills. | 2, 5 |
| Who wins | He won re-election in 2024 with 57.7% of the vote. He defeated Kenneth King. He won the 2020 Senate race with 53.8%. He won the 2018 House race with 51.2%. His steady wins point to a structural Republican edge in the 25th District. | 2 |

## 5. How they touch government
- **Campaign finance (WA PDC):** He reported a total of $585,389 in campaign contributions across the 2018 to 2024 cycles. The 2018 House race brought in $165,899. The 2020 Senate race brought in $419,491. The 2024 Senate race brought in $0 reported. Recent contributors in 2025 included T-Mobile USA Inc ($1,200), Washbankpac ($1,200), and Washington Food Industry ($1,200) (Source 6).
- **PDC complaint (2020):** A complaint was filed. It said Gildon broke state law (RCW 42.17A.405) by taking an over-limit contribution from an affiliated group (Washington Forward, $1,000). PDC staff found it did not warrant further investigation. The money had not been spent. It was a one-time over-limit acceptance. Staff sent a reminder about contribution limits (Source 7).
- **Election results (certified by WA Secretary of State):**
 - 2024 General (Senate D25): Gildon (R) 57.7% / 41,862 votes. He defeated Kenneth King (D) at 42.2%.
 - 2020 General (Senate D25): Gildon (R) 53.8% / 41,440. He defeated Julie Door (D) at 46.0%.
 - 2018 General (House D25-Pos 2): Gildon (R) 51.2% / 27,701. He defeated Brian Duthie (D) at 48.8% (Source 2).
- **Lobbying:** No registered lobbying activity was found. UNVERIFIED.
- **Contracts and grants:** No personal government contracts were found. UNVERIFIED.

## 6. Other seats they hold
- **Senate Republican Caucus:** He is one of the 19 Republican minority caucus members. He is listed alongside John Braun (Minority Leader), Phil Fortunato (D31), and other SRC senators (Source 5).
- **Washington State Institute for Public Policy (WSIPP):** He is co-chair of the Board of Directors. WSIPP does nonpartisan research to inform public policy (Source 5).
- **Pierce County legislative delegation:** He is co-chair. The delegation is bipartisan and bicameral. It coordinates Pierce County legislators from both chambers (Source 5).
- **SRCC (Senate Republican Campaign Committee):** He is listed as a supported senator on the SRCC website (Source 5).
- **Economic and Revenue Forecast Council:** A state body that forecasts economic conditions and revenue for budget planning.
- **Legislative Ethics Board:** A body that interprets and enforces ethics rules for legislators.

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** Gildon's power comes from his role as Senate Republican Operating Budget Leader. It is the top budget job for the minority party in the Washington Senate. The Republican caucus is in the minority, with 19 of 49 seats. Even so, his budget role, his co-chair role on the Pierce County delegation, and his many board seats (WSIPP, Economic and Revenue Forecast Council, Legislative Ethics Board) give him real influence over state spending that affects Pierce County. His military record and real-estate work add weight on veterans' affairs and housing policy.
- **Conflict flags:** As a commercial real-estate broker on the Senate Housing Committee, his private work could overlap with his legislative role on housing. The 2020 PDC complaint (over-limit contribution) was cleared without a violation finding, but it shows campaign-finance issues. Recent corporate PAC gifts (T-Mobile, WA Food Industry) while serving as budget leader raise standard access-influence questions.
- **Counter-reading:** Gildon's real power is limited by the Republican minority. The Democratic majority controls the budget process. His role is advisory and oppositional rather than final. His committee leadership is "Republican Leader," not chair. The Pierce County delegation co-chair role is mostly coordinative.
- **Confidence:** High. Multiple primary sources confirm all key claims. These include the WA Legislature, the Senate Republican Caucus, PDC, and WA Secretary of State certified results. Electoral, financial, and biographical data are well-documented.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- Chyna Willman is the Board Chair of the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce for the 2025–2026 year. The Chamber is the main business-advocacy group in Pierce County. She speaks for the business community while the Chamber looks for a new CEO.
- She runs the Chamber board at a time when it still holds seats on the Tacoma-Pierce County Economic Development Board (EDB), runs the Candidate Academy that trains people who want to run for office, and talks with the County Council and Tacoma City Council on business rules.
- This seat gives her a public role and a clear line to county leaders. The actual CEO job is currently held by an interim leader after Andrea Reay left in 2024.
- **Adjacent but excluded:** Kierra Phifer (DoorDash) was the 2024–2025 Chair. Past Chairs and the interim CEO are not on the map. Co-founders and staff at her gym are also not separate nodes.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why it is on the map.** Clover Park School District (CPSD) is one of Pierce County's largest K-12 public school districts. It serves about 12,395 students across 33 schools. Its schools sit in Lakewood, Tillicum, Woodbrook, and parts of unincorporated Pierce County (a county not part of any city). It also borders Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM). The district runs on a $262 million budget for the 2024-25 school year (FY2024-25). It has the legal power to levy property taxes. It is a Purple Star Award District, which means it serves many military-connected students whose families move with JBLM's deployment cycle. It has won statewide awards for its board and its superintendent.
- **Who is left out.** Tacoma Public Schools, Bethel, Puyallup, University Place, Sumner-Bonney Lake, and Peninsula are separate districts and are mapped on their own pages. JBLM itself is mapped separately. The city of Lakewood is mapped on its own. Madigan Army Medical Center is part of JBLM and is mapped under military and defense.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Clover Park School District (CPSD).
- **Type:** A public K-12 school district under Washington State law. It is a government body, not a nonprofit. The IRS does not treat it as a 501(c)(3) (federal tax-exempt charity).
- **Governing law:** RCW 28A (Washington's Revised Code of Washington for common schools) and the Pierce County Charter.
- **EIN (tax ID number):** Not verified. School districts are government bodies and do not file IRS Form 990.
- **Location:** Head office in Lakewood, Washington. Schools spread across Lakewood, Tillicum, Woodbrook, parts of unincorporated Pierce County, and a small part of Tacoma near JBLM.
- **Schools:** 33 schools (2023-24).
- **Students:** 12,395 (2023-24).
- **How it is run:** A 5-member elected Board of Directors governs it. No single person owns it.
- **Subsidiaries:** None found.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power held:**
  - **Legal power (RCW 28A):** CPSD enforces compulsory school attendance, sets curriculum, manages buildings, and bargains with employee unions.
  - **Tax power:** The Board can put property-tax levies on the ballot. Pierce County collects the money through the Assessor-Treasurer's office.
  - **Workforce:** About 1,100 staff (a third-party estimate from August 2026). That includes teachers, support staff, and 19 district leaders plus 54.5 school leaders (2023-24 NCES, the National Center for Education Statistics).
  - **Buildings budget:** $6.38 million in capital spending (FY2021-22). Bond measures need voter approval.
  - **Buying power:** CPSD signs contracts for buses, food, technology, curriculum, and building upkeep.
  - **Community role:** It partners with the Lakewood Multicultural Coalition and runs a youth council. It gives community leadership awards.
- **Where its power crosses over:** CPSD sits at the meeting point of schools, government, the local economy, and military-civilian life.
- **Key facts:**
  - **Tax status:** Government body, not a 501(c)(3).
  - **Money mix (FY2021-22 NCES):** Federal $49.588M (20%); State $161.046M (66%); Local $33.565M (14%). Total: $244.199M.
  - **Current money (FY2024-25):** Revenue $262,088,238. Expenses $274,886,723. The district spent more than it took in. The Board approved a $12.6 million cut for FY2026-27 to fix the gap.
  - **Board (2025-26):** Darrin Lowry (District 4, until 2029); Dana Kelleher (District 3, until 2029); Janet Caldwell (District 5, until 2027); Krissy Kim (District 1, until 2027); Bryan Thomas (District 2, until 2027).
  - **Government share:** About 86% of revenue came from federal and state sources combined (FY2021-22).
- **Money trouble:** A $12.6 million cut for FY2026-27 was approved in February 2026 to keep the district solvent.

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** CPSD holds tier-3 institutional power. It is the public K-12 monopoly for about 12,400 students across 33 schools. It runs a $262 million budget (FY2024-25). It has the legal power to levy property taxes. It must enforce compulsory school laws. It is a Purple Star Award District, which is a formal state award for helping military-connected students. That links it to JBLM. In FY2024-25 expenses ($274.9M) topped revenue ($262.1M). The Board approved a $12.6 million cut for FY2026-27. That is a real financial gap that limits future programs. Superintendent Ron Banner won the 2025 WASA Superintendent of the Year award and the 2026 AWSP President's Award. The Board won WSSDA 2024 Board of Distinction and 2019 Board of the Year for large districts. The 5-member Board is elected by district on a nonpartisan ballot. The tier-3 composite power score of 0.006 matches a large but resource-strapped public agency. Its power comes mostly from being well-connected to JBLM families and civic groups. It depends on outside money: about 86% of revenue comes from federal and state sources.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags:** The defense view is that school-board work is open. Board meetings are public. Levies and bonds go to voters. Collective bargaining is required by law. Campaign money for Board races is filed with the state's campaign-finance agency (PDC). The financial gap is public. The WASA, AWSP, and WSSDA awards come from outside groups, not from insiders.
- **Analysis of alternatives (ICD-203):** The opposing view is that CPSD's power is small. The $12.6 million cut shows real money pressure. About 66% of revenue comes from the state, which can change. Voters may tire of levies. JBLM deployments can shake up enrollment. A composite power of 0.006 fits a tier-3 institutional actor with broad scope (compulsory education for about 12,400 students) but limited decision-making power. State law, levy and bond votes, and OSPI oversight all constrain it.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- Inclusion rule: **well-connected + reputational**. Columbia Bank (now operating as Umpqua Bank after the Feb-2023 merger) is on the map because (a) **William Weyerhaeuser** was Chairman of the Board of Columbia Banking System — a direct tie to the Weyerhaeuser entity already on the map — and (b) Columbia is the holding company for what was once Tacoma's regional bank, with ties to the Greater Tacoma Community Foundation (GTCF) board and the Tacoma Chamber.
- Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates: Umpqua Bank (now the operating brand, a separate Oregon-chartered bank); Bank of America Private Bank; routed to open questions.

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** Columbia Banking System, Inc. (the holding company). Columbia Bank was the bank before the merger. Umpqua Bank is the bank brand after March 2023.
- **Type of business:** A Washington-state bank holding company. Its bank is insured by the FDIC (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation). It is registered with the the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), ticker COLB. The holding company is a Washington corporation. The bank was a Washington state-chartered bank.
- **History:** Founded in Longview WA in 1973. Headquarters moved to Tacoma (1301 "A" Street) in 1993. In October 2021, Columbia announced a merger of equals with Portland-based Umpqua Holdings. The deal closed Feb 28, 2023. Columbia was the named survivor, but Umpqua was the accounting acquirer. The combined bank took the Umpqua Bank brand. The holding company kept the name Columbia Banking System, Inc. and kept Tacoma as the holding-company home.
- **Leadership:** Clint Stein is President, CEO, and Chairman (since the 2023 merger). Christopher Merrywell and Torran Nixon are Co-Presidents. Ivan Seda is the CFO. William Weyerhaeuser was the former Chairman. He stepped down after the merger.
- **Locations:** 376 branches (2026) across 8 states. The bank's headquarters moved to Portland, OR in 2023. The holding company's headquarters is still in Tacoma, WA.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Market power:** Columbia Banking System is the holding company for a top-30 U.S. bank after the Umpqua merger. It has about 376 branches. It controls business lending, deposits, and treasury services across the Pacific Northwest and Mountain West.
- **Civic ties:** William Weyerhaeuser's chairmanship connected Columbia's lending to one of America's oldest timber families (Weyerhaeuser Co.). Weyerhaeuser also served on the Greater Tacoma Community Foundation board. This is the main way Columbia enters the power map.
- **Establishment ties:** As a Tacoma Chamber member and long-time Tacoma bank, Columbia is tied to the local establishment: GTCF, the Chamber, Weyerhaeuser Co., and MultiCare's supply-chain financing.
- **Why it scores:** GTCF board tie (weight 2), Weyerhaeuser chairman tie (weight 3), Chamber of Commerce membership (weight 3).

| Who sits | William Weyerhaeuser (Chairman, before the merger). Clint Stein (Chairman/CEO after the merger). Tacoma Chamber leaders. GTCF board observers. | #1, #2, #3 |
| Who governs | The Washington Department of Financial Institutions (DFI) regulates the bank. The Federal Reserve regulates the holding company. The FDIC insures deposits. The SEC regulates public-company disclosures. The Board of Directors is the fiduciary authority. | #1, #2 |
| Who wins | The Tacoma establishment kept a "Tacoma-headquartered" holding company even after the operating bank moved to Portland. That is a reputational and tax win for Tacoma. The Weyerhaeuser family's influence carried through the merger. | INFERENCE from #1, #2 |

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Inclusion rule:** From holding office + decision-making. CommonSpirit Health is included as the parent company that controls Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (VMFH). VMFH runs many hospitals and clinics in Pierce County. These include St. Joseph in Tacoma, St. Clare in Lakewood, and St. Anthony in Gig Harbor.
- CommonSpirit is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit health system. It is Catholic-affiliated. As a large health system, it shapes hospital pricing, charity-care policy, capital decisions, and labor relations across the Puget Sound region. The graph records it as the parent of VMFH (weight 6) and as affiliated with the Catholic Archdiocese (weight 2).
- **Excluded but related:** MultiCare Health System is the main Pierce County rival. It is profiled separately as `multicare`. PeaceHealth, Swedish Health (Providence), and UW Medicine are nearby regional systems. They have a small Pierce County presence. The Catholic Archdiocese of Seattle is profiled separately. It connects to CommonSpirit through VMFH's Catholic affiliation and the Ethical and Religious Directives for Catholic Health Care Services (ERDs).

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** CommonSpirit Health.
- **Entity type:** 501(c)(3) nonprofit, Catholic-affiliated health system. National office in Chicago, IL.
- **How it was formed:** Created in February 2019. It was a merger of Catholic Health Initiatives (CHI, headquartered in Englewood, CO) and Dignity Health (headquartered in San Francisco, CA). Both were large Catholic-affiliated systems before the merger.
- **Scale:** About 150,000 employees. About 25,000 physicians and advanced practice clinicians. It runs 137 hospitals and more than 1,000 care sites across 21 states. Fiscal Year 2019 revenue was about $29 billion.
- **Pierce County subsidiary:** Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (VMFH). VMFH was formed January 5, 2021. It merged CHI Franciscan (Tacoma) with Virginia Mason (Seattle). Ketul J. Patel was the CEO of VMFH. He was also president of the Pacific Northwest Division of CommonSpirit Health.
- **Governing law:** Washington State nonprofit corporation statutes (state law (RCW) 24.03A). Catholic-affiliated governance through board oversight and the Ethical and Religious Directives (ERDs). The ERDs are issued by the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Market position in Pierce County:** Through VMFH and CHI Franciscan, CommonSpirit runs several hospitals in or near Pierce County. These include St. Joseph Medical Center (Tacoma), St. Clare Hospital (Lakewood), St. Anthony Hospital (Gig Harbor), St. Elizabeth Hospital (Enumclaw), and St. Francis Hospital (Federal Way). The system also runs Franciscan Medical Group clinics and CHI Franciscan urgent-care sites. Tacoma-Pierce County Health Department and Chamber listings show CHI Franciscan and VMFH sites as major regional providers.
- **Tax status:** 501(c)(3) nonprofit, Catholic-affiliated. Tax-exempt status gives an indirect subsidy. CommonSpirit pays no federal income tax. It pays no state B&O tax on most activities. It also has property-tax exemptions on many sites. This is a structural edge over for-profit hospital operators.
- **Decision-making authority:** Capital projects, mergers, EHR systems, staffing, charity care, and reproductive-health rules are all set at the CommonSpirit corporate level. They are not set at the VMFH local-board level. Ketul Patel was VMFH and Pacific Northwest Division President until 2024. He led Pacific Northwest ops for CommonSpirit.
- **Domain overlap:**
 - **inst ↔ gov:** Hospital licensing, certificate-of-need (CON) for capital projects, Medicare and Medicaid — heavy work with the WA Department of Health and CMS.
 - **inst ↔ econ:** One of the largest private employers in the region. Big purchasing power. Big real-estate holdings.
 - **inst ↔ social:** Charity-care and community-benefit duties tied to tax-exempt status. Reproductive health and end-of-life rules under the ERDs.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Inclusion rule — from holding office + decision-making:** The Pierce County Council is the county's legislative branch. It is the "policy-determining body" under the Home Rule Charter (Charter Section 2.20). It has "all powers of the County not otherwise reserved to the people, the Executive, or general law." Its powers include: approving the budget, controlling zoning and land use, approving contracts, and setting taxes. The Council's 70+ graph edges make it the most connected node. Anyone who wants county money, zoning changes, or policy changes has to come to the Council.
- **Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates:** The Pierce County Charter Review Commission (21 members, elected 2025) is a separate temporary body that reviews the charter. It is excluded because it only meets from time to time. The Board of Health (which includes Council members) is mapped separately as `tpchd`. The Performance Audits Committee is a Council committee, not a separate entity.

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** Pierce County Council
- **Entity type:** Government — legislative branch of Pierce County, a home-rule charter county
- **Governing law:** Pierce County Home Rule Charter (adopted 1981); state law (RCW) 36 (county government)
- **Parent/subsidiaries:** Part of Pierce County government; not a separate legal entity
- **Address:** 1501 Market Street, Suite 530, Tacoma, WA 98402
- **Council Chambers:** 1501 Market Street, Suite 140, Tacoma, WA 98402

## 2. Their career and offices
- **Chair:** Jani Hitchen, District 6 (D) — represents the Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM) and Lakewood district. She sets the legislative agenda and runs Council meetings.
- **Vice Chair:** Dave Morell, District 1 (R) — Bonney Lake, Buckley, Lake Tapps. He handles land use.
- **Executive Pro Tempore:** Robyn Denson, District 7 (D) — Gig Harbor, Key Peninsula.
- **Full roster (2025–2026):**

- **Composition:** 4D–3R. The Democratic majority holds the chair and controls the agenda. It takes 5 votes to override an Executive veto. With 4 Democrats, they can sustain a Democratic Executive's vetoes. But they cannot override a veto without at least 1 Republican vote.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Statutory authority (Charter Section 2.20):** "The Council has all powers of the County not otherwise reserved to the people, the Executive, or general law." This is the broadest possible grant of legislative authority. Specific powers include:
 - **Budget appropriation (Charter Section 2.20(1)(a)):** "To levy taxes, appropriate revenue, and adopt budgets for the County." The Council adopts the biennial budget by Dec. 1 of each odd-numbered year.
 - **Zoning and land use:** Controls county zoning, the comprehensive plan, and land-use rules. This is the most direct power over the growth-machine developers in the graph.
 - **Contract approval:** Approves major county contracts.
 - **Ordinance enactment:** Adopts all county ordinances and resolutions.
 - **Appointment confirmation:** Confirms certain Executive appointments.
- **Budget authority:** The 2026–2027 biennial budget is $3.5 billion (adopted Nov 25, 2025, ordinance O2025-562s3). The General Fund is $967.4M (up 2.2%). The Council can amend the Executive's proposed budget. The budget passed 4–3 on a party-line vote.
- **Veto override (Charter Section 2.50):** Override requires 5 affirmative votes. That is a supermajority of 7. With a 4D–3R split, party-line vetoes by a Democratic Executive cannot be overridden. This limits the Council's power compared to the Executive.
- **key facts:**
 - *Budget controlled:* $3.5B biennial ($1.75B each year)
 - *Appointment/veto powers:* Confirms certain Executive appointments; 5-vote supermajority to override Executive veto
 - *Jurisdictions governed:* All of unincorporated Pierce County (about 920K people); some county-wide functions affect incorporated cities too

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** The Pierce County Council holds the county's legislative power. It approves the $3.5B biennial budget. It controls zoning and land use. It approves contracts and sets taxes. Its 70+ graph edges make it the most connected node. But this high connectivity is partly a structural artifact. Every group that wants county money, zoning changes, or policy changes has to come to the Council. The 4D–3R makeup, combined with the 5-vote veto override threshold, means the Council is subordinate to a same-party Executive on vetoed items. Its real power lies in (1) the budget amendment process, (2) land-use decisions that affect the growth-machine developers, and (3) confirmation of Executive appointments.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense view anticipated):**
 - *Developer-lobbyist pipeline:* Six growth-machine developers (Rush, Miles, Southport, Tucci, Lincoln Park, Nall) have land_use edges to the Council. If Council members get donations from these same developers, there is a direct conflict between their zoning votes and their campaign funding.
 - *Puyallup Tribe lobbying + donations:* The Tribe both lobbies the Council (weight 5) and donates to individual Council members (Ayala, Hitchen, Cruver). This dual channel creates the appearance of a trade.
 - *Party-line budgeting:* The 4–3 party-line budget vote suggests the Council's budget process is driven by partisan priorities rather than technical analysis.
 - *Candidate Academy pipeline:* If Council members are Candidate Academy alumni, their votes on Chamber priority issues (tax policy, land use, business regulation) create a structural conflict.
- **Analysis of alternatives:** The other reading is that the Council is not a power center but a procedural bottleneck. The Executive proposes the budget. The Council amends at the margins. The real decisions are made by the Executive and the groups that lobby the Council (Tribe, MultiCare, Chamber, developers). The Council's high graph centrality is an artifact of being the place where decisions are ratified, not where they are made. The 4–3 partisan split means the Democratic majority is a rubber stamp for a Democratic Executive. The Republican minority cannot block party-line votes. ## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why included:** decision-making + well-connected + holds office. Division II of the Washington Court of Appeals is on the map because (a) it is the appeals court of last resort for most civil and criminal cases that start in Pierce County Superior Court (a court that handles major felonies, civil suits, and family cases); (b) Pierce County is one of the 13 counties it covers; (c) its rulings bind Pierce County Superior Court judges under stare decisis (the rule that courts must follow prior decisions); (d) it sits one step above Pierce County Superior Court in the Washington court system. (Sources 1, 2, 3, 4)
- **Who was left out and why:** The Washington Supreme Court is state-level and has its own profile. Division I (Seattle) covers King, Snohomish, Skagit, Island, San Juan, and Whatcom counties. Division III is in Spokane. Pierce County Superior Court has its own profile. The Federal District Court for Western Washington has its own profile and only handles federal cases. The U.S. Ninth Circuit appeals court handles federal appeals. None of these are Division II.

## 1. Who they are
- **Full legal name:** Washington Court of Appeals, Division II.
- **Type:** State appeals court (intermediate). It is part of the unified Washington State Court System under Article IV of the Washington State Constitution.
- **Governing law:** Washington Constitution Article IV (Judiciary); Washington Court of Appeals set up by constitutional amendment; state law RCW (Revised Code of Washington) 2.06.
- **Headquarters:** 950 Broadway Plaza, Tacoma, WA 98402-4454. (Source 3)
- **Phone:** (253) 593-2970. (Source 3)
- **Parent:** Washington State Court System. The state Office of the Administrator for the Courts is the central office.
- **Subsidiaries:** None. Division II is a single court with rotating 3-judge panels.
- **Court roster (from the current WA Courts Directory):**
 - **Judges (7):** Chief Judge Bernard F. Veljacic; Acting Chief Judge Erik D. Price; Judge Meng Li Che; Judge Anne Cruser; Judge Rebecca Glasgow; Judge Linda Lee; Judge Bradley A. Maxa.
 - **Commissioners (2):** Aurora R. Bearse; Karl Triebel.
 - (Source 4)
- **Constitutional basis:** Article IV § 30 of the Washington State Constitution lets the Legislature create intermediate appeals courts. Division II was created by statute in 1969-70 and seated in 1970.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power held:**
 - **Mandatory appellate jurisdiction:** Per WA Courts, "It is a non-discretionary appellate court — it must accept all appeals filed with it." (Source 2)
 - **Disposition authority:** "The Court of Appeals has authority to reverse (overrule), remand (send back to the lower court), modify, or affirm the decision of the lower court." (Source 2)
 - **Binding precedent on Pierce County:** Published opinions by Division II bind Pierce County Superior Court judges and Pierce County lower tribunals. Pierce County is in Division II's territory.
 - **No en banc review available.** (Source 1)
- **Counties covered (Division II, 13 counties):** Pierce, Thurston, Mason, Kitsap, Jefferson, Grays Harbor, Clallam, Clark, Cowlitz, Lewis, Pacific, Skamania, and Wahkiakum. (Source 2)
- **Selection / retention:** Nonpartisan election. Judges serve 6-year staggered terms. (Sources 1, 2)
- **Panel structure:** "Panels of three judges hear each appeal," per the Washington Court of Appeals. (Source 1)
- **Caseload discretion:** None. The court must accept all properly filed appeals. (Source 2)
- **Key facts:**
 - **Tax status:** Government entity (not 501(c)(3), a federal tax-exempt charity).
 - **Roster (per WA Courts Directory):** Chief Judge Bernard F. Veljacic; Acting Chief Judge Erik D. Price; Judge Meng Li Che; Judge Anne Cruser; Judge Rebecca Glasgow; Judge Linda Lee; Judge Bradley A. Maxa. Commissioners: Aurora R. Bearse; Karl Triebel. (Source 4)
 - **Government funding:** State-funded through the state Office of the Administrator for the Courts.
 - **Caseload volume:** UNVERIFIED exact figure for FY2024-25. The statewide Court of Appeals caseload is in the low thousands per year.
 - **Discretion vs. obligation:** Mandatory jurisdiction — no certiorari screening (certiorari is the discretion to pick which appeals to hear, like the U.S. Supreme Court does).

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Source # |
|-----------|---------|----------|
| Who benefits | People who file appeals in 13 Washington counties (Pierce, Thurston, Mason, Kitsap, Jefferson, Grays Harbor, Clallam, Clark, Cowlitz, Lewis, Pacific, Skamania, Wahkiakum). Pierce County is the largest single county. | 2 |
| Who sits | 7 judges (Chief Veljacic, Acting Chief Price, Che, Cruser, Glasgow, Lee, Maxa) + 2 commissioners (Bearse, Triebel). Each judge is elected in a nonpartisan election. | 1, 4 |
| Who governs | Division II binds Pierce County Superior Court through its published opinions. It also binds lower Pierce County courts (Tacoma Municipal Court, Pierce County District Court) on state-law questions. It coordinates with Division I/III through chief judges. | 1, 2 |
| Who wins | Plaintiffs and appellants who get reversals or remands; Pierce County trial lawyers whose arguments win at the appeals level; statewide legal-doctrine growth in WA. | 2 |

 - Washington Court of Appeals Division I (Seattle; peer division; Division II judges may serve as visiting judges there).
 - Washington Court of Appeals Division III (Spokane; peer division).

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** Washington Court of Appeals Division II holds tier-3 legal power as the mandatory appeals court for Pierce County (and 12 other Washington counties). Its published opinions bind Pierce County Superior Court and Pierce County lower courts on state-law questions. FACT: It must accept all properly filed appeals (non-discretionary). FACT: It is based in Tacoma (950 Broadway Plaza) and has 7 judges + 2 commissioners per the current WA Courts Directory. FACT: It can reverse, remand, modify, or affirm lower court rulings. FACT: Judges are elected in nonpartisan elections to 6-year staggered terms. FACT: 3-judge panels hear each appeal — no en banc review. REASONING: Division II's tier-3 composite power (0.006) reflects a regional appeals court whose individual rulings bind Pierce County practice. But its weight statewide is moderate (7 of 22 judges). Its judges do not typically sit on cross-domain community boards. Its main power is doctrinal (shaping the law through written opinions). Pierce County is its largest single county, so the Pierce County bar has outsized influence on its docket.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags (counter-argument):** A defense would say Division II is a constitutionally independent court. Its judges are publicly elected on nonpartisan ballots. Decisions are publicly published. The recusal process is set by statute. Panels are randomly assigned (which limits any single judge's ability to set the agenda). Mandatory jurisdiction means the court cannot pick and choose which cases to hear.
- **Analysis of alternatives:** The opposing view is that Division II's power is limited by (a) mandatory jurisdiction (no certiorari screening); (b) random panel assignment; (c) 3-judge panels that require a supermajority for any single ruling; (d) discretionary Supreme Court review that can override its rulings; and (e) lack of enforcement power (rulings bind but must be sent back to Superior Court for execution). Its power is doctrinal, not financial or coercive. It shapes legal practice through precedent, not budgets or hiring. The 0.006 composite score reflects a regional appeals court with binding reach over a set territory, bounded by higher review.
- **Confidence:** Medium — court structure, jurisdiction, judge roster, and procedure have primary sources (state Administrative Office of the Courts + state Bios page). History dates and caseload numbers are backed by Wikipedia/Ballotpedia. Exact FY caseload volumes are not in the sources reviewed and remain UNVERIFIED.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why Sowell is on the map.** Dale Sowell has sat on the MultiCare Health System board since 2001. MultiCare runs nine hospitals in Washington, including MultiCare Good Samaritan Hospital in Puyallup and Mary Bridge Children's Hospital. It is the largest private employer in Pierce County. Sowell joined the board the same year he became CFO of Green Diamond Resource Company. He has financial oversight over Pierce County's biggest private employer and a regional hospital network. His Green Diamond career ties Pierce County's forest-products capital to Pierce County healthcare governance.
- **Who is NOT on the map.** John Wiborg (MultiCare board chair), Sally Leighton (Tacoma-based MultiCare director), and other MultiCare board members are not separate entries. Green Diamond's parent company, the Reed Family or Hancock Natural Resource Group, sits at the parent level, not at MultiCare.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Dale L. Sowell (the federal tax agency (IRS) Form 990 filing for MultiCare Health System lists "Dale L Sowell, Director").

It has $5 billion in revenue and about 84,000 admissions a year.
- **Bridge between two worlds:** Sowell's career spans Green Diamond (a forest-products company based in Seattle) and MultiCare (a healthcare system). As Green Diamond's CFO, he learned audit-grade financial discipline. That maps onto MultiCare's Finance and Audit committee work.

- **Legal name:** Deborah Krishnadasan.

- **Current residence:** Gig Harbor, WA (since 2008).
- **Family:** Husband Baiya Krishnadasan — a Sri Lankan-born heart-and-lung surgeon. Three children: Alexander, Audrey, Gabriel.
- **Education:** Bachelor of Arts in Communications, Western Washington University.
- **Prior jobs:** Communications and human resources roles at Burlington Resources (oil and gas), Visio Corporation (a tech firm bought by Microsoft in 2000), and Microsoft.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power held.**
  - **Washington State Senator, 26th Legislative District (Democrat):** Sworn in December 11, 2024. Current term ends January 11, 2027. She is running for re-election on November 3, 2026 against Republican Gary Parker (per Ballotpedia).

    - Vice Chair, State Government, Tribal Affairs & Elections.
    - Vice Chair, Agriculture & Natural Resources.
    - Member, Early Learning & K-12 Education.
    - Member, Transportation.
  - **Legislative actions.** In March 2025, she was one of two Democrats who voted with Republicans against the state budget because of tax increases. She also sponsored a constitutional amendment to lower the school-bond voter-approval threshold from 60% to 55%.
  - **Former Peninsula School Board President.** Two-year term as board president (2019–2021). Elected District 2 in a 2015 special election and re-elected unopposed in 2017.
- **Why this gives her cross-domain power:** She is a state senator who also has a school-board background. That ties the government domain to the institutional and education-policy domains. Her seat on the Tribal Affairs committee also links her to the Puyallup Tribe's relationship with the state.
- **Key facts:**
  - **Office:** Washington State Senate. 4-year term. 26th LD, which partly covers Pierce County.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- The Pierce County District Court handles most criminal and civil cases in the county. It is the county's only "limited jurisdiction" court. That means it handles smaller cases, not big felonies.
- The Pierce County Council sets its budget. The graph shows this as an edge where the Council gives the court its funding.
- It is the front door for most state-court cases. Skipping parking tickets, about seven out of every eight cases filed in all state courts land at this level.

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** Pierce County District Court.
- **Entity type:** A Washington state court of limited jurisdiction. It is a government body, not a private company. It is created and governed under state law, Title 3 of the Revised Code of Washington (RCW).
- **Governing law:** state law (RCW) 3.50 covers district courts in large counties. RCW 3.62 covers judges. RCW 3.66 covers civil cases. Pierce County is a "class A" county, meaning its population tops 500,000.
- **Parent or subsidiaries:** It runs inside Pierce County government. It has no separate corporate status. The court administrator is Misty Butler Robison. Location: County-City Building, 2nd floor, 930 Tacoma Ave S, Room 239, Tacoma, WA 98402. Phone: (253) 798-7487.
- **Officers:** Court Administrator Misty Butler Robison. The presiding judge rotates among the elected judges.
- **Departments and functions:** Criminal cases (misdemeanors, gross misdemeanors, DUIs, reckless driving, and some assaults). Civil cases up to $100,000. Small claims up to $5,000, or $10,000 for a person. Traffic tickets. Domestic-violence and no-contact orders. Name changes. Some lien foreclosures. First hearings in felony cases. It also runs a probation department, therapeutic courts, a court resource center, and court services.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Its caseload.** It handles the large majority of state-court cases in Pierce County. Every misdemeanor, traffic ticket, and most civil disputes up to $100,000 flow through it.
- **Its power to punish.** It can order up to 90 days in jail and a $1,000 fine for a misdemeanor. For a gross misdemeanor, up to one year and a $5,000 fine. It decides pretrial detention and supervises probation.
- **Protection orders.** It issues domestic-violence, antiharassment, and no-contact orders. These carry real limits on personal freedom.
- **Felony gatekeeping.** First hearings in felony cases happen here. Judges decide if there is enough evidence to send a case up to Superior Court.
- **Trials.** Six-person juries hear criminal cases. Small claims have no lawyers unless the court allows one. Traffic tickets have no jury.
- **How it is scored.** Its legal power overlaps with government (the County Council funds it) and law enforcement (prosecutors and defense lawyers work in it). Small claims is where everyday residents meet the court for consumer, landlord, and neighbor disputes.
- **Key questions answered:**
 - **Area of authority:** All of Pierce County.
 - **Judges' discretion:** Judges have wide sentencing discretion within the legal caps.
 - **How judges are picked:** Elected in nonpartisan races for 4-year terms. The top two from the primary advance to the general.
 - **Caseload:** Statewide, more than two million cases are filed each year. About seven of every eight state-court cases (not counting parking tickets) are district-court level.
 - **Judge pay:** Not confirmed. The County Council sets the budget.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Who benefits | Pierce County residents who use small claims, civil, and traffic courts. People seeking protection orders. Misdemeanor defendants who have a right to a lawyer and a jury. |
| Who sits | Eight elected judges (Lineberry, McCann, Padula, Buttorff, Oaks, Williams, Christopher, Sussman) plus administrator Misty Butler Robison. The Pierce County Council funds it. |
| Who governs | State law (RCW Title 3) sets the framework. The County Council holds the budget. The court administrator runs daily operations. |
| Who wins | Prosecutors and police get an efficient forum. Debt collectors and businesses use small claims. People without lawyers use small claims and protection orders. |

## 1. Who they are
- **The bottom line.** This court's power is broad and routine, not concentrated. It is the front door for most state-court cases in Pierce County. Its eight elected judges hold real power to jail people, fine them, and issue protection orders. It depends on the County Council for its budget. That limits its independence on money and staff, but not on its rulings.
- **The defense view.** The court is an independent branch of government. Judges are elected by voters, not appointed by the Council or the Executive. The Council cannot cut a sitting judge's salary (state law, RCW 3.58). Eight judges and nonpartisan races limit any one seat from being captured. Small claims and protection orders are built to help people without lawyers and victims.
- **The other way to read it.** It is a routine service-delivery body. Its judges are professional, its docket predictable, and its budget is a small slice of county spending. Its power is capped by law. People can appeal to Superior Court. Its composite power score of 0.023 reflects this: it is on the map, but its influence on the big power structures is low.
- **Confidence:** Medium — jurisdiction, structure, judge roster, and how judges are picked are all primary-sourced. The caseload figures are statewide, and the Pierce-specific caseload is not confirmed.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why he's on the map.** Drew Stokesbary is the state House Representative for Washington's 31st Legislative District, Position 1. That district covers parts of King and Pierce Counties, including Auburn, Bonney Lake, Buckley, Edgewood, and Sumner. More importantly, he has been the House Minority Leader since April 2023. That makes him the top Republican in the Washington House. His district includes a lot of Pierce County territory.
- **Who is NOT on the map.** Josh Penner (R-31, House Position 2) is a district-mate but is not on the map at this tier. Phil Fortunato (R-31, Senate) is on the map separately.

## 1. Who they are
- **Full name:** Andrew R. Stokesbary (Source 6). He goes by Drew Stokesbary.
- **Nickname:** Drew Stokesbary (common usage); Andrew R. Stokesbary (legal/formal name on state campaign-finance agency (PDC) filings).
- **Born:** UNVERIFIED — public sources do not list a date. He is described as a "lifelong Washingtonian" (Source 5).
- **Home:** Auburn, Washington (Source 2, 5).
- **Family:** Wife Ashley Stokesbary; four sons; a border collie named Scout (Source 2, 5).
- **Education:** B.S. in Economics and Mathematics from Duke University (he also studied History there); J.D. *cum laude* from the University of Notre Dame Law School (Source 2, 5, 7).
- **Bar admissions:** Washington, Arkansas, and Texas. He is also admitted to practice before the U.S. Supreme Court, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas, and the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington (Source 7).
- **Day job:** Attorney. He is a partner at Chalmers, Adams, Backer & Kaufman LLC (sometimes called "Chalmers & Adams"), a small law firm. He handles corporate and securities work for startups, emerging companies, and private investment funds. Before that, he was a policy aide for a King County Councilmember (Source 2, 5, 7).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Elected office.** He has served in the Washington House of Representatives, 31st District, Position 1, since January 12, 2015. He is in his 6th term. His current term ends January 11, 2027. He is running for re-election in November 2026. He won the August 4, 2026 primary with 57.9% to Stephen Szczurko-Walton's 42.0% (Source 2).
- **Leadership role.** He has been House Minority Leader since April 2023 — the top Republican job in the House. That makes him the chief strategist and spokesperson for the House Republican Caucus. He decides committee assignments for his members and runs the floor strategy (Source 2, 5).
- **Past leadership jobs.** He was the Ranking Member of the House Appropriations Committee. He was Minority Floor Leader. He chaired the Select Committee on Pension Policy. He was assistant ranking Republican on House Appropriations (Source 5, 8).
- **Current committee (2025–2026):** Rules Committee (Source 5).
- **Budget.** As former Appropriations Ranking Member and current Minority Leader, Stokesbary has real influence over Republican budget strategy. The actual budget is controlled by the Democratic majority.
- **Where his power reaches:** 31st Legislative District — Auburn, Bonney Lake, Buckley, Carbonado, Edgewood, Milton, South Prairie, Sumner, Wilkeson.

| Who wins | He won 2014 (~60%+ as a first-time candidate). He won 2016 unopposed in the primary. He won 2018 (58.9%). He won 2020 unopposed. He won 2022. He won 2024 (63.6% / 51,651 vs. Sutterfield's 36.3%). He won the 2026 primary (57.9%). His seat is very safe. | 2, 5 |

## 5. How they touch government
- **Campaign money (state campaign-finance agency, PDC).** He is registered as Andrew R. Stokesbary, with the committee "Friends of Drew Stokesbary." He files PDC reports for 2024 (Source 6). TransparencyUSA shows he got $1,000 from DAA Northwest in 2021 and 2022, and DaVita HealthCare Partners listed him as a recipient of $1,200 to "Friends of Drew Stokesbary WA" (Source 8).
- **Election results (certified by the WA Secretary of State):**
 - 2026 Primary (House D31, Position 1): Stokesbary (R) 57.9% / 12,019 — beat Szczurko-Walton (D) 42.0%.
 - 2024 General (House D31, Position 1): Stokesbary (R) 63.6% / 51,651 — beat Sara Sutterfield (D) 36.3%.
 - 2018 General (House D31, Position 1): Stokesbary (R) 58.9% / 36,844 — beat Victoria Mena (D) 41.1%.
 - 2016 Primary: Unopposed (advanced with John Frostad, Libertarian) (Source 2).
- **Lobbying.** He has no registered lobbying activity. However, he co-founded the Citizen Action Defense Fund (CADF), a nonprofit that sends demand letters to legislative leaders on constitutional and initiative-related matters (Source 7, 8).
- **Contracts or grants.** No personal government contracts identified. UNVERIFIED.

## 6. Other seats they hold
- **House Republican Caucus.** Leader since April 2023. The caucus has about 40 Republican members. Stokesbary sets strategy and works with the Senate Republican Caucus (Source 5).
- **Chalmers, Adams, Backer & Kaufman LLC.** Partner at this small law firm. The firm gives corporate and securities legal advice to startups and emerging companies in the Puget Sound region and around the world (Source 7).
- **Citizen Action Defense Fund (CADF).** Co-founded during the pandemic. CADF is a nonprofit that says it is dedicated to "protecting the constitutional rights of all Washingtonians." It has sent demand letters to legislative leaders, including the Governor, Speaker Jinkins, the Senate Majority Leader, the Senate Minority Leader, and Stokesbary himself as House Minority Leader, about how initiatives are processed (Source 8).

fields.graph_description: Pierce County Fire Protection District No. 22 (East Pierce Fire & Rescue / EPFR) — career fire district formed 1999/2000 via merger of Bonney Lake Fire, Fire District 22 (Lake Tapps), and Fire District 24. Serves 115,000+ residents across 153 sq mi.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why included:** Holds office + makes decisions + well-connected — East Pierce Fire & Rescue (EPFR / Pierce County Fire Protection District No. 22) is one of the two largest career fire districts in Pierce County (the other is Central Pierce Fire & Rescue). It has legal power over firefighting, emergency medical services, marine rescue on Lake Tapps, and fire code enforcement for 115,000+ residents across 153 square miles. It is run by an elected Board of Fire Commissioners. It collects voter-approved property tax levies ($1.50 per $1,000 fire levy approved by voters in 2024 + $0.41 per $1,000 EMS levy). (Sources 1, 2, 3, 6)
- **Adjacent but NOT included:** Central Pierce Fire & Rescue (peer district serving the urban core). Tacoma Fire Department (city fire dept). West Pierce Fire & Rescue (a separate district covering west county). Buckley Fire Department (Wilkeson left East Pierce in 2014 to contract with Buckley).

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Pierce County Fire Protection District No. 22, doing business as "East Pierce Fire & Rescue" (EPFR). (Sources 1, 2)
- **Type:** Washington fire protection district. This is a special-purpose district set up under state law RCW Title 52. RCW 52.04 covers fire districts. RCW 52.33 covers Standards of Cover. An elected Board of Fire Commissioners runs it. (Sources 1, 2, 5)
- **When it formed:** Merged in 2000 (effective Jan 1, 2000) from City of Bonney Lake Fire Department + Pierce County Fire District 22 (Lake Tapps) + Pierce County Fire District 24. On Nov 2, 1999, voters approved the merger (7,636 yes to 1,332 no). The three agencies had already been consolidated under the name "East Pierce Fire & Rescue" since 1995. (Sources 1, 2)
- **Later annexations:**
  - 2006: Pierce County Fire District 12 (South Prairie/Fire District 20)
  - 2008: Sumner/Fire District 1
  - 2010: Edgewood/Fire District 8
  - 2013: Milton Fire Department
  - 2014: Wilkeson ended its contract (now with Buckley FD) (Sources 1, 2)
- **HQ address:** 8601 Main Street East, Bonney Lake, WA 98391. (Sources 2, 3)
- **Operating budget (2024):** $59,865,333 budgeted. $58,022,515 in actual revenues. $51,991,391 in actual expenditures (and $52,109,920 in a second count — slight underrun per the 2024 Annual Report). (Source 4)
- **Funding model:** EPFR stays within the state-law maximum levy rate of $2.00 per $1,000 of assessed property value (Fire Levy $1.50 + EMS Levy $0.50 max). As of 2024, EPFR is the only major Pierce County fire district operating WITHOUT a Maintenance & Operations (M&O) levy or a Benefit Charge that would push rates above $2.00. Most career fire districts in WA collect over $3.00 per $1,000. (Sources 4, 6)
- **Fire levy history:** 2024 — voters approved restoring the fire levy to $1.50 per $1,000 of assessed value after several years of compression below the state maximum. EMS levy $0.41 per $1,000 of assessed value, renewed in 2021 for 10 years. (Source 6)

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **State law power (government side):** Provides firefighting, EMS, marine rescue on Lake Tapps, fire code enforcement, and hazardous materials response for 115,000+ residents across 153 sq mi. Run by an elected Board of Fire Commissioners (RCW 52.14). (Sources 1, 2)
- **Budget power:** About $59 million in annual operating budget (2024). Most of it comes from two voter-approved property tax levies (Fire + EMS). (Sources 4, 6)
- **Levy power (taxing):** Voters approved the fire levy restoration to $1.50 per $1,000 in 2024. This is state-law power given by Pierce County voters to the District. It does not come from the County Council — it is direct voter power. (Source 6)
- **Workforce size:** EPFR cross-trains all full-time firefighters as either EMTs (emergency medical technicians) or paramedics. There are 9 fire stations (8 staffed + 1 marine rescue). The exact uniformed staff count is UNVERIFIED. (Source 2)

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** East Pierce Fire & Rescue has state-law power as Pierce County Fire Protection District No. 22. It provides firefighting, EMS, marine rescue on Lake Tapps, and code enforcement for 115,000+ residents across 153 sq mi. It runs 9 fire stations and a $59 million annual budget. The District stays within the state-law combined levy cap of $2.00 per $1,000 — making it the only major Pierce County fire district without a third revenue stream (M&O levy or Benefit Charge). Voters approved restoring the fire levy to $1.50 per $1,000 in 2024. They renewed the EMS levy in 2021 for 10 years.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags:** The map edge between EPFR and the Pierce County Council labeled "taxing" is INACCURATE in the strict state-law sense. EPFR's taxing power comes directly from district voters under RCW 52, not from the County Council. The Council's role is limited to interlocal agreements and boundary matters. An opposing reading might note that the Council can still affect District operations through budget cycles, regional coordination, and boundary annexation review — but the direct taxing power is voter-controlled. (FACT — Source 6)
- **Analysis of alternatives:** A defense reading: EPFR is a high-service, low-cost district. A restrained levy rate plus full staffing delivers services below the cost of peer districts. An opposing reading: running at the legal minimum levy cap with no M&O revenue makes EPFR always vulnerable to revenue compression. State law caps levy growth at 1% per year unless voters approve a higher rate. That pushes the district into periodic ballot-measure battles when costs outstrip revenue. The 2024 fire-levy restoration is exactly this dynamic.
- **Population discrepancy (Source 2 lists ~100,500; Sources 1 and 3 list "over 115,000"):** The 100,500 figure appears on the Contact page. The 115,000 figure appears on About and Fire Stations pages. This likely reflects recent expansion or methodology (residents vs. service population). UNVERIFIED — flag for follow-up.
- **Confidence:** High — primary-source confirmation from EPFR official website (About, Contact, Fire Stations, Funding, Annual Report) and Washington State Council of Fire Fighters.

- **The bottom line.** The Economic Development Board for Tacoma-Pierce County runs a convening platform. It brings together 40+ institutional leaders from Pierce County's economic, government, health, education, and labor sectors. EDB does not hold statutory authority, taxing power, or regulatory power. Its power is well-connected and convening — it brokers ties between businesses, government, and institutions to create jobs and capital ($1.6B and 25,000 jobs claimed over 20+ years, source #2). The board roster is EDB's strongest asset. It includes the two biggest health systems (MultiCare, VMFH), the Port of Tacoma, TPU, PSE, two banks, the Chamber, the labor council, UW Tacoma, and elected officials. That makes EDB a structural hub of Pierce County's power network, even though its formal authority is small. The 2024 leadership change from Bruce Kendall (25-year CEO) to Michael Catsi (source #8) is a generational shift.

Their shared board seat could lead to quiet coordination on markets. (2) Elected officials (Dave Morell, Ryan Mello, Anders Ibsen) sit on the EDB board while EDB pushes for economic development policies — a revolving door between government and advocacy.
