## §0 why this entity is on the map
Museum of Glass is on this map because it is the lasting project of the Russell family. George F. Russell Jr. (1932–2025) co-founded and bankrolled the museum. He built it as an anchor for the Thea Foss Waterway redevelopment. The museum is now a flagship of Tacoma's "Museum Row" cultural cluster.

Its 501(c)(3) tax status, its annual revenue of about $5 million, its capital expansion project, and its broad board ties make it a network node. It links Tacoma arts donors to waterfront redevelopment.

## §1 who they are legally
**FACT** Museum of Glass is a registered 501(c)(3) charitable organization. Its federal tax ID number (EIN) is 91-1669422. Its tax exemption began in January 1996.
**Source:** https://www.museumofglass.org/press-release-archive (primary; reliability 0.95); https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/911669422 (primary; reliability 0.95); https://www.charitynavigator.org/ein/911669422 (primary; reliability 0.9)

**FACT** The museum sits at 1801 Dock Street, Tacoma, WA 98402. It opened in 2002 on a former Superfund site. Building the museum kicked off the Thea Foss Waterway cleanup and the surrounding museum district. Six museums now sit within walking distance.
**Source:** https://www.linkedin.com/company/museum-of-glass (secondary; reliability 0.85); https://www.museumofglass.org/george-russell (primary; reliability 0.95).

**FACT** The most recent IRS Form 990 (per ProPublica and Charity Navigator) shows the following. Contributions ranged from about $1.6 million to about $3.1 million in recent years. Program services brought in $1.3 million to $1.6 million. Investment income ranged from $17,000 to $296,000. Total annual revenue sits in the $3 million to $6 million range.
**Source:** https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/911669422 (primary; reliability 0.9).

**FACT** The Board of Trustees is chaired by Kenneth Farmer, Jr., M.D. He is the Principal of Ken Farmer Advisors, LLC and a retired U.S. Army Major General. The Vice Chair is Walt Riehl. The Secretary is Todd Gilman. He is SVP, Deputy General Counsel, and Secretary of TrueBlue, Inc. Other trustees include Barry Anton, Rex Bates, Jonah Bergman, Joanna Carey Cleveland (UPS), Mary Carstensen, Clemencia Castro-Woolery, Curtis Cox, Calvin Gasaway, Brent Heilesen, Ian MacNeil, Marc Mangel, Megan Mead, Altaf Merchant (Milgard Endowed Dean, UW Tacoma), Katelyn Smith, and others.
**Source:** https://museumofglass.org/board (primary; reliability 0.9).

## §2 Power basis
**FACT** The museum runs a working Hot Shop. It is one of the largest and most active museum glass studios on the West Coast. That gives it cultural power. The museum curates national traveling shows, runs artist residencies, and shapes Tacoma's identity as a glass-arts city. Tacoma is the birthplace of Dale Chihuly.
**Source:** https://www.linkedin.com/company/museum-of-glass (secondary; reliability 0.85); https://museumofglass.org/board (primary; reliability 0.9)

**FACT** The museum receives Tacoma Creates funding. Tacoma Creates is a voter-approved city fund for arts, culture, and science. The museum also runs a 2026 capital campaign for expansion. Its mix of donations and program-service revenue shows blended public and private support.
**Source:** https://www.museumofglass.org (primary; reliability 0.9); https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/911669422 (primary; reliability 0.9).

**FACT** George F. Russell Jr. (1933–2025) co-founded the museum with Phil Phibbs. He co-chaired the founding Board of Trustees with Jane Russell. The museum's Hot Shop is named the "Jane Russell Hot Shop" in her memory after her early death.
**Source:** https://www.museumofglass.org/george-russell (primary; reliability 0.95).

## §3a what they influence 
| Indicator | Evidence |
|---|---|
| **Who benefits** | The Tacoma museum district, arts patrons, the glass-art community, the Chihuly tourism economy, and Foss Waterway businesses. |
| **Who sits** | Trustees include Kenneth Farmer (chair, retired US Army general), Todd Gilman (TrueBlue), Joanna Carey Cleveland (UPS), and Altaf Merchant (UW Tacoma Milgard Dean), plus community volunteers. The board cuts across many sectors. |
| **Who governs** | The Board of Trustees governs the museum. The executive leadership runs daily operations. Derek Klein is listed as staff on LinkedIn. |
| **Who wins** | The Russell family legacy is permanently anchored in Tacoma's waterfront. Tacoma's cultural tourism brand wins. |

## §7 who they are connected to
Museum of Glass is a cultural-anchor node. It bridges three things. First, the Russell family's giving legacy (graph edge: russell-family → museum-of-glass, weight=4). Second, higher education. Altaf Merchant, the Milgard Dean at UW Tacoma, sits on the board. Joanna Carey Cleveland of the University of Puget Sound also sits on the board. Third, downtown Tacoma's museum cluster, with six museums within walking distance. The museum sits on a cleaned-up Superfund site, making it a waterfront-redevelopment success story.

It is not a decision-making power node in the regulatory sense. But its board ties (UW Tacoma, UPS, TrueBlue, retired military) place it at a small-network crossroads. Its power is bounded by 501(c)(3) limits and by the visitor market for the museum district.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- NASH Cascadia Verde, LLC (NCV) is on the map for three reasons. First, it owns and entitles the 4,756-acre Tehaleh planned community in the Pierce County Urban Growth Area. That is the largest single private landholding on the county's eastern plateau. Second, NCV gives money to both Democrats and Republicans in Pierce County Council, Tacoma city, and state legislature races. Its donor list includes Fey, Dammeier, Gildon, Stokesbary, Mello, Jinkins, O'Ban, and Chambers. That gives NCV standing across the political map.
- **Excluded but related:**
 - Newland Communities — NASH's co-developer / joint venture (JV) partner at Tehaleh (per Panattoni and NASH releases). NCV is the legal fee-simple owner and the named party to the Pierce County Development Agreement. So NCV is the profile, not Newland.
 - Brookfield Properties (Brookfield Residential Washington) — listed as the JV partner on NASH's own marketing site. But Brookfield does not sign the County DA.
 - Panattoni Development — only entered via a separate Frederickson industrial parcel, not Tehaleh.
- All three are routed to open questions and leads.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** NASH CASCADIA VERDE, LLC (a Washington profit LLC; UBI 603-091-079 on Washington Secretary of State records).
- **Type:** Washington Limited Liability Company. Status is "Active" per Washington Company Directory. Registered agent is Corporation Service Company, 300 Deschutes Way SW STE 208 MC-CSC1, Tumwater WA.
- **Date/place of formation:** February 25, 2011 in Washington.
- **Tehaleh acquisition date:** March 23, 2011, by direct purchase from the bankruptcy estate of Cascadia Development Corporation.
- **Registered office:** 19001 Cascadia Blvd E, Bonney Lake WA 98391-9613 (MapQuest listing).
- **JV partner of record:** Brookfield Properties (Brookfield Residential).
- **Trademark "TEHALEH"** (Registration No. 4318141, Serial 85490794) registered December 2011 to NASH CASCADIA VERDE, LLC. It covers homeowner-association and online information services.
- **Brand:** Tehaleh is a master-planned community. The name is Salish-derived. It means "the land above" or "highlands." Grand opening was in 2012. NASH bills it as the best-selling single-family community in the Puget Sound region since opening.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Land-use veto power (decision-making):** NCV owns 4,756 acres in fee-simple title. The land is zoned Employment-Based Planned Community (EBPC). The 2018 Phase 2 Development Agreement (Ordinance 2018-90s) vests development rights under state law (RCW) 36.70B.170–.210. The Pierce County Council must approve NCV's Project Master Plan (under PCC 18A.75.080) to allow more than 6,400 entitled residential units plus a 419-acre employment center. NCV sets the pace, mix, and order of growth on the Bonney Lake plateau.
- **Market concentration (economic):** NCV is the sole developer of record for Tehaleh. Its 2024 amendment (per the News Tribune) raised the Phase 2 dwelling-unit cap to 2,490 units (60% above the 2018 cap) before the new arterial road is finished. That means NCV can pull forward permit revenue and home-builder commitments on its own schedule.
- **Political influence (well-connected):** NCV gave $85,050 in Washington state political contributions from 2017 to 2022 (Transparency USA). The donor roster is unusual. NCV gave to both parties. Pierce County Council members (Dammeier, Mello). Tacoma-area Democrats (Jinkins, Fey). Suburban Republicans (Gildon, Stokesbary, Chambers, O'Ban, Barkis). NCV also gave $25,000 in one donation to the Sumner-Bonney Lake Citizens for Schools committee (a school bond vehicle).
- **Brand/IP control:** NCV owns the trademarked TEHALEH mark. That gives it exclusive rights to the community identity, signage, and HOA-services language tied to the brand.
- **Scoring overlap basis:** graph edges (donated to Ryan Mello weight 4; donated to Amy Cruver weight 4 — Cruver is the graph's state-legislative recipient; this matches transparencyusa.org data). Plus decision-making weight from the Development Agreement.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | NCV benefits directly: vested zoning for 6,400+ entitled units, ability to accelerate Phase 2 build-out under the 2024 amendment, and privileged access to the County Council through donations and EBPC brand halo. The community benefits are secondary: the Tehaleh brand promise is sustainability ("Three-Star Built Green Community") and Donald Eisman Elementary (opened 2010, pre-acquisition). | #1, #2, #3 |
| Who sits | NCV is the legal counter-party to Pierce County under the 2018 Phase 2 DA; Council members Dan Roach and Pam Roach appear in the 2018 ordinance context. Pierce County Hearing Examiner retains approval authority on Project Master Plan. | #1, #2 |
| Who governs | **Pierce County Council** governs through Development Agreement amendments and PCC Chapter 18A.100; **Pierce County Hearing Examiner** governs through Project Master Plan approval under PCC 18A.75.080. NCV itself is private but its contractual position gives it de facto co-governance over the build-out schedule. | #1, #2 |
| Who wins | Short-term: NCV (vested rights, accelerated Phase 2). Medium-term: homebuilders participating in Tehaleh (DR Horton, Lennar, Richmond American — typical master-planned roster, UNVERIFIED specific roster); Sumner-Bonney Lake schools (the $25,000 NCV contribution implies a bond-campaign alignment). Long-term: depends on whether the 419-acre employment center is built out — INFERENCE that NCV's marketed job-creation target (~tens of thousands per EBPC plan) remains aspirational. | INFERENCE from #1, #2, #3 |

## 9. Who they are connected to

Ryan Mello's 2024 cycle includes $3,400 from Nash Cascadia Verde LLC. | Transparency USA, "Nash Cascadia Verde LLC" contributor page; "Ryan Mello" candidate page | https://www.transparencyusa.org/wa/contributor/nash-cascadia-verde-llc?cycle=2017-to-now; https://www.transparencyusa.org/wa/candidate/ryan-mello?cycle=2024-election-cycle | secondary (aggregator of the state campaign-finance agency (PDC) filings) | 0.90 |

Grand opening 2012. Three-Star Built Green Community designation. | NASH Communities official project page, "Tehaleh" | https://www.nashcommunities.com/projects/tehaleh | primary (developer corporate site) | 0.90 |
| 4 | Pierce County Council approved amendment in 2024 allowing 60% more dwelling units (2,490) to be built in Tehaleh Phase 2 prior to completion of a new road, after a traffic analysis conducted by NASH Cascadia Verde LLC found generated traffic was lower than 2018 projections. | The News Tribune, "Development of massive Tehaleh development to accelerate" | https://www.thenewstribune.com/news/local/article286553440.html | secondary (mainstream regional press) | 0.85 |

## 1. Who they are
- Verdict: NASH Cascadia Verde, LLC is a tier-3 economic-and-decision-making node. Its power is concentrated in land-use vesting, not raw cash. The 2018 Phase 2 Development Agreement and the 2024 amendment give NCV de facto co-governance over the timing of thousands of dwelling units on Pierce County's largest single private landholding. Politically, NCV hedges both parties. It gave to Dammeier and Mello alike. It bankrolled the Sumner-Bonney Lake schools political action committee (PAC). That shows NCV's lobbying posture is issue-driven (school capacity, transportation vesting) rather than party-driven.
- Conflicts-of-interest flags: (a) The 2024 amendment lets Phase 2 dwelling permits speed up before the planned new arterial is built. That pushes the cost of road capacity onto Pierce County taxpayers via concurrency requirements. NCV produced the very traffic study used to justify the cap raise. That is the classic self-dealing pattern. (b) NCV's $25,000 to the school-bond vehicle in Sumner-Bonney Lake — the same district serving Tehaleh residents — creates a clear quid-pro-quo risk on school capacity and impact-fee decisions. (c) Brookfield Residential is named JV partner on NASH's marketing site but does NOT sign the Pierce County DA. So it is worth asking if Brookfield holds economic interest without regulatory disclosure (UNVERIFIED).
- Analysis of alternatives (investigative control document (ICD)-203 opposing view): NASH could be read as a national master-planned-community developer that competes on placemaking and sustainability branding. Its political donations could be read as normal development-industry engagement rather than capture. That reading is defensible only if donation patterns track industry peers (e.g., master-planned community competitors) and if the 2024 traffic-study amendment survives an independent peer review.
- **Confidence:** **Medium** — four independent sources confirm who they are legally, donation patterns, and the Development Agreement; Brookfield JV interest is asserted by NASH's own site but not corroborated by an independent Pierce County filing. The exact NASH ownership chain (parent LLC, members/managers) is not publicly disclosed in the records reviewed.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- Nathe Lawver is on the map for two reasons: he holds office, and he is well-connected. He sits on boards in three worlds at once — labor, nonprofit, and economic development.
- He is Secretary-Treasurer of the Pierce County Central Labor Council (PCCLC). That is the top job for a labor council. PCCLC speaks for 96 unions and 45,000 workers.
- He is Board Chair of United Way of Pierce County (UWPC). UWPC is the county's biggest health and human services nonprofit, with $7.8M in revenue.
- He also sits on the boards of the Greater Tacoma Community Foundation (GTCF) and the Economic Development Board for Tacoma-Pierce County (EDB).
- The graph puts him in the institutional domain with three strong ties (weight 5).
- People near him who are not on the map: Alice Phillips (PCCLC President — she has her own page `alice-phillips`). Patty Rose held the PCCLC Secretary-Treasurer job for 20 years before Lawver. She is not mapped. Former PCCLC President Vance Lelli is not mapped.

- **Aliases:** Nathe Lawver (the name he uses in public)

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- The News Tribune is on the map because it is the main daily newspaper in Pierce County. It covers the county government, city politics, and the Port of Tacoma.
- The paper can shape what people read and talk about. It can also endorse candidates in local elections. Those endorsements carry weight.
- Not included: Tacoma Weekly (a smaller weekly paper), KNKX (public radio, listed separately), and The Olympian (covers Thurston County). They have fewer readers or a different focus.

## 1. Who they are
- **Name:** The News Tribune. It is published by The McClatchy Company.
- **Type of business:** A privately held newspaper. McClatchy is a Delaware corporation.
- **Who owns it:** The News Tribune → McClatchy Media Company → Chatham Asset Management (a hedge fund in New Jersey). McClatchy went bankrupt on Feb 13, 2020. Chatham bought the company in a court-approved sale that closed Sep 4, 2020, for $312 million.
- **Old owners:** McClatchy bought the News Tribune from the Baker family in 1986 for about $112 million. The Bakers had owned it since 1912.
- **Tax status:** A private company. It pays taxes. It is not a nonprofit.
- **Where it is:** 1950 South State Street, Tacoma, WA 98405.
- **When it started:** 1880 (as The Tacoma Ledger). The current name came from a 1918 merger.

## 2. Their career and offices
- **Editor:** Stephanie Pedersen.
- **CEO of McClatchy:** Tony W. Hunter became CEO when Chatham bought the company in 2020. The current CEO is not confirmed.
- **Publisher:** Not publicly listed.
- **Board:** As a private company, McClatchy's full board is not public. Two independent members were named at the 2020 sale.
- **Who shows up in our map:** Stephanie Pedersen is the only News Tribune figure in our power map.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power:** The News Tribune holds cultural power. It is the main local news source.
- **What it controls:** The paper picks which stories get top billing. It covers county government, city politics, and the Port of Tacoma. Its endorsements carry weight in local races.
- **Reach:** Second-largest daily newspaper in Washington state (as of 2020).
- **Declining:** Daily print copies fell from 130,000 in 2001 to about 30,945 in 2020. In March 2024, the paper cut back to three print days a week. Even with cuts, it is still the main paper of record.
- **Who owns it now:** McClatchy → Chatham Asset Management (a hedge fund) since 2020.
- **Editorial line:** Mainstream and centrist. It makes endorsements in local races.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Chatham Asset Management (the hedge fund owner) benefits financially. Local readers benefit from continued local coverage. | #3, #5 |
| Who sits | Stephanie Pedersen as editor. McClatchy's corporate office sets editorial direction and staffing. | #2, #7 |
| Who governs | McClatchy Media / Chatham Asset Management. Local editors make daily choices. Corporate owners decide on layoffs and print schedule. | #3, #5 |
| Who wins | Local candidates who get News Tribune endorsements. Incumbents benefit from name recognition. | #9 |

## 4. Their money
- **Revenue:** Not confirmed. McClatchy is private and does not share financials.
- **Where the money comes from:** Print and digital ads. Print and digital subscriptions. No government grants.
- **Tax status:** A for-profit company. Not tax-exempt.
- **Property:** Headquarters at 1950 South State Street, Tacoma. Printing moved to Vancouver, WA in February 2019.

## 5. How they touch government
- **Lobbying:** No direct lobbying found at the state or federal level.
- **Government contracts:** None found.
- **Campaign donations:** No corporate political donations found.
- **Rules that apply to it:** Standard rules for media companies. No special issues.
- **Land use:** None. The Tacoma printing plant closed in 2019.

## 6. Other seats they hold
- **Board seats:** No News Tribune board members sit on other mapped boards.
- **McClatchy family:** McClatchy owns 29 daily newspapers in 14 states. The News Tribune is one of four in Washington (with The Olympian, The Bellingham Herald, Tri-City Herald).
- **Peer newsroom:** KNKX (public radio) is a peer in our graph.
- **Union:** The News Tribune newsroom is part of the Pacific Northwest Newspaper Guild. McClatchy laid off 7 unionized workers at the paper (and sister papers) in 2024. That was about a third of union staff in Washington and Idaho. Layoffs took effect Oct 11, 2024.

- **The bottom line.** The News Tribune shapes the local news story in Pierce County. But its power is fading. Daily print circulation dropped from 130,000 in 2001 to about 31,000 in 2020. Print dropped to 3 days a week. McClatchy has cut staff again and again (most recently a third of unionized workers in 2024). The paper can still set the agenda. It is still the only daily paper covering Pierce County government. But its ability to do deep investigative work has been gutted by hedge-fund ownership. FACT: The News Tribune is the newspaper of record for Pierce County. INFERENCE: With fewer reporters, the paper leans more on press releases and less on original reporting. That gap can help incumbents stay in power with less public scrutiny.

Editorial endorsements go through a transparent process. Layoffs are an industry-wide response to digital change, not a plan to weaken watchdog reporting. The paper still does significant local reporting on Tacoma City Hall, Pierce County government, and the Port of Tacoma.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Inclusion rule:** decision-making + economic. The Northwest Seaport Alliance (NWSA) is the only bi-county port-operating joint authority in the U.S. It runs the marine cargo terminals that drive Pierce County's biggest private-sector employer cluster (logistics, longshore, drayage). It is also a Federal Maritime Commission–regulated body. Its actions affect every trade-dependent employer in the South Sound.
- **Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates:** Port of Seattle (parent). Port of Tacoma (parent, kept as a separate node `port-tacoma`). SSA Marine and Northwest Container Services, which lease terminals from NWSA. Individual shipping lines (Maersk, MSC, ONE, etc.).

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** The Northwest Seaport Alliance (NWSA).
- **Entity type:** Port development authority under state law (RCW) 53.57 (Wash. Rev. Code, "Joint Port Authorities"). Federal Maritime Commission–approved operating agreement (FMC Agreement No. 201228).
- **Formation date:** August 4, 2015, via an Interlocal Agreement between the Port of Seattle and the Port of Tacoma.
- **Governing law:** Washington RCW 53.57; FMC oversight. Interlocal agreement effective 8/4/2015. Current Alliance Agreement effective 9/18/2023.
- **HQ:** P.O. Box 2985, Tacoma, WA 98401-2985. Office space is also in Tacoma.
- **Parents:** Jointly owned by Port of Seattle and Port of Tacoma as equal members. Each port keeps ownership of its own real estate and assets.
- **CEO:** John Wolfe. He is also Port of Tacoma CEO. He was the first CEO when NWSA formed.
- **Charter/Bylaws:** Third Amended PDA Charter (effective 9/18/2023). Sixth Amended Bylaws (signed 1/7/2025).
- **Governance body:** "Managing Members" = the two 5-member port commissions acting together. The president of each home-port commission serves as co-chair of the NWSA Managing Members. They meet monthly, in public, on the first Tuesday. Meetings are streamed live.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Statutory authority:** RCW 53.57 lets two ports form a port development authority. NWSA has joint operating power over marine cargo terminals. It can bind both ports on terminal leases, capital projects, and labor rules.
- **Market position:** The combined gateway is the 6th-busiest U.S. container port by volume. It handles about $68 billion of waterborne trade with 175 trading partners (NWSA 2025 stats). 2024 international container volume: 3,340,733 TEUs (up 12.3% YoY). 2025: down 5.5% to 3.2M TEUs.
- **Economic leverage:** NWSA operations support about 52,000 jobs statewide and about $14 billion in business output (2025 Community Attributes study).
- **Federal nexus:** Subject to Federal Maritime Commission oversight (FMC Agreement No. 201228). It competes for federal INFRA and MEGA grants (e.g., Puget Sound Gateway Program Executive Committee — Marzano sits there).
- **Veto power:** Each port commission (5 elected members) can block alliance actions through the Managing Members structure. It acts like a two-house check.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Trade-dependent employers. International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) labor (longshore jurisdiction). Pierce County property-tax base via Port of Tacoma lease revenue. | 1, 4 |
| Who sits | Managing Members = 10 elected port commissioners (5 Seattle / 5 Tacoma). Pierce Co. reps in 2026: Marzano, McCarthy, Keller, Wilcox, Ang. | 1, 2 |
| Who governs | Tacoma-side commissioners co-chair with Seattle-side. Pierce Co. effectively holds 50% of Managing Members votes, even though Port of Tacoma carries a smaller cargo share in some segments. | 1, 2 |
| Who wins | Cargo volumes, lease rent to ports, ILWU hours, Pierce Co. property-tax base from Port of Tacoma industrial district. Trade-offs: noise and environmental hits concentrated near Tacoma Tideflats. | 1, 3 |

That is the inverse of the real parent/child relationship. NWSA is *operated* by the two ports together. See "New relationships discovered" below.

| 2 | Port of Tacoma commissioners for 2025: McCarthy (president), Marzano (vice president), Don Meyer (secretary), Keller (1st asst.), Ang (2nd asst.); McCarthy as commission president also serves as co-chair of the NWSA | Port of Tacoma news release, 12/17/2024 | https://www.portoftacoma.com/news/port-tacoma-designates-commission-officer-positions-2025 | primary | 0.95 |
| 3 | 2024 international container volume 3,340,733 TEUs (up 12.3% YoY); 2025 down 5.5% to 3.2M TEUs; supports about 52,000 jobs; about $68B waterborne trade with 175 partners (2025) | NWSA cargo statistics page & Port of Seattle maritime cargo post | https://www.nwseaportalliance.com/about-us/cargo-statistics ; https://www.portseattle.org/blog/2025-maritime-cargo-comings-and-goings | primary | 0.90 |
| 4 | Wikipedia summary (good-article rated): CEO John Wolfe (also Port of Tacoma CEO); parent organizations Port of Seattle and Port of Tacoma; revenue $195M (2017); formed 8/4/2015 | Wikipedia: Northwest Seaport Alliance | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Seaport_Alliance | secondary | 0.80 |

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** The NWSA is a new kind of legal tool. It is the first North American inter-port operating authority. It pulls cargo-terminal decisions for two big U.S. ports into one 10-member Board. For Pierce County the effect is clear. 5 of 10 votes on every lease, capital project, and labor rule sit with Pierce County voters through their port commissioners. That makes the Port of Tacoma commission — especially its president, who co-chairs the NWSA — a structural lever on regional trade policy.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags:** Commissioner Dick Marzano (Port of Tacoma, Position #2) served six years as ILWU Local 23 president before his 1995 election. He sits on the Tacoma-Pierce County Economic Development Board and the WSDOT Puget Sound Gateway Program Executive Committee. Those overlap with NWSA interests.
- **Analysis of alternatives:** The defense reading: NWSA is a transparent public body with audited financials and a two-house check. The critical reading: Pierce County holds 50% of votes on a body that drives billions in trade-dependent activity. The environmental and labor costs land in Tacoma Tideflats neighborhoods.
- **Confidence:** High. Primary-source governance docs, NWSA newsroom, Port of Tacoma newsroom, and FMC filings all agree on formation, structure, and 2025 leadership.

fields.summary: Pierce County Prosecuting Attorney's Office — institutional legal power center
facts: Prosecutes all state felony cases in Pierce County
Civil division advises all county departments
fields.known_facts: Led by elected Prosecuting Attorney Mary Robnett (since 2019). Three divisions: Criminal, Civil, Family Support. 263 total positions (197 in Criminal Division, 65%). RCW 36.27 governs.
fields.graph_description: Elected county prosecutor's office with criminal, civil, and family support divisions; ~263 FTE positions, $88.6M proposed budget.
fields.profile:
## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why included:** The Pierce County Prosecuting Attorney's Office is on this map because it holds a key legal office and makes major charging decisions. It is the only office that can bring felony charges anywhere in Pierce County. It also prosecutes misdemeanors outside city limits. And it represents every county office in civil lawsuits. State law (RCW 36.27.020) gives it this power. The office has about 263 full-time positions and an $88.6 million proposed budget for two years. The elected prosecutor has independent power under state law. She is not under the County Executive or Council. (sources #1, #2)
- **Adjacent but NOT included:** Pierce County Public Defender's Office (separate office, not on the map). Washington State Attorney General's Office (state-level, helps on some cases under RCW 43.10). Tacoma City Attorney's Office (handles city-only misdemeanors). These are nearby but not in the map at this level.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Pierce County Prosecuting Attorney's Office
- **What kind of office:** County government office led by an elected prosecutor. Created under state law RCW Chapter 36.27.
- **Governing law:** RCW Chapter 36.27 covers the prosecutor. It sets who can serve (RCW 36.27.010: must be a lawyer in Washington and a U.S. citizen). It lists the duties (RCW 36.27.020). It lets the prosecutor hire deputies (RCW 36.27.040). It says the office must be at the county seat (RCW 36.27.070).
- **Location:** 930 Tacoma Ave S, Rm 946, Tacoma, WA 98402 (source #3)
- **Federal tax ID (EIN):** Not applicable — it is part of Pierce County, not a separate legal body.
- **Parent:** Pierce County government
- **Current head:** Mary Robnett, elected Prosecuting Attorney. Took office January 2019 (source #1).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **State law power:** RCW 36.27.020 sets the duties. The office must prosecute every criminal case in the county. It must represent the county in civil lawsuits. It must advise county officials. This gives the office a monopoly on felony prosecution in Pierce County.
- **Charging power:** The office chooses which cases to charge. This lets it control what enters the criminal justice system. In 2024, it received 7,155 case referrals. About 54% of those were violent crimes (source #5).
- **Three divisions:**
  1. **Criminal Division** — handles all felony cases in Pierce County and all misdemeanors outside city limits. It has 197 full-time positions (65% of the total 263). It also runs therapeutic court programs (sources #4, #5).
  2. **Civil Division** — represents county officials and departments in lawsuits. It supports civil commitment-forcing involuntary treatment under state law (source #4).
  3. **Family Support Division** — protects children, establishes who the parents are, and enforces child support (source #4).
- **Budget:** The proposed budget for 2024–2025 was $88.6 million (source #4). The office also faces $3.35 million in cuts. Twelve positions paid with federal COVID aid will end by 2026 (source #5).
- **Where the office reaches:** All of Pierce County (about 920,000 people). Felonies county-wide. Misdemeanors only outside city limits (cities have their own prosecutors).
- **How the head is chosen:** Prosecuting Attorney is an elected office. Terms are four years. Elections are non-partisan (no party listed on the ballot). Mary Robnett won in 2018 and took office in January 2019 (sources #1, #6).

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Crime victims get prosecution. County officials and departments get civil legal help. Children and parents get child support help. Some go to therapeutic courts instead of prison. | #4 |
| Who sits | Mary Robnett is the elected prosecutor. She hires deputies under RCW 36.27.040. The office has 263 full-time positions, with 197 in the Criminal Division. | #1, #5 |
| Who governs | Mary Robnett runs the office day-to-day. The Pierce County Council approves her budget. | #1, #4 |
| Who wins | The cases the office chooses to charge shape criminal justice outcomes. In 2024, 54% of 7,155 referrals were violent crimes. The felony backlog dropped from about 2,500 cases (early 2022) to about 1,800 cases (2025). | #5 |

## 5. How they touch government
- **County Council funding:** The Pierce County Council approves the prosecutor's budget. The Council approved the $88.6 million proposed budget for 2024–2025 (source #4).

She secured more than $121 million in CDS for WA projects in FY2026 alone. She also brought in more than $5 billion in direct state funding (source #1, #2).

- **Career before Senate:** Preschool teacher at Shoreline Community College. Citizen lobbyist for environmental and education issues. Shoreline School Board (1985–1989). Washington State Senate, 1st District (1989–1993). She served as whip from 1990 to 1992 (source #2, #4).

## 3. Where their power comes from

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- The PCCLC is the Pierce County Central Labor Council, AFL-CIO. It is the main political body for organized labor in Pierce County. It represents 114 affiliated unions and more than 44,000 workers.
- PCCLC is on the map for three reasons. (1) It exercises political power through endorsements and PAC (political action committee) spending. (2) Its officers sit on other boards: Nathe Lawver on the Greater Tacoma Community Foundation (GTCF) board, Alice Phillips on the Clover Park Board of Trustees. (3) Its endorsement process is driven by delegates, so it can pull labor votes behind a single candidate.
- Not on the map separately: the Washington State Labor Council (state parent body), Pierce County Labor Community Services Agency (the nonprofit arm), and each individual member union.

## 1. Who they are
- **Full name:** Pierce County Central Labor Council, AFL-CIO (PCCLC).
- **Type:** A 501(c)(5) labor organization. It is a chartered local labor council of the AFL-CIO.
- **Parent:** The AFL-CIO (national federation) and the Washington State Labor Council (state body).
- **Founded:** 1890 as the Tacoma Trades Council. The AFL chartered it as the Tacoma Central Labor Council. It later became the Pierce County Central Labor Council.
- **Address:** 3049 South 36th St., Suite 201, Tacoma, WA 98409.
- **Governing law:** The National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) and the AFL-CIO constitution.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Endorsement power:** PCCLC endorsements come from "union delegates representing more than 44,000 working people across Pierce County after a democratic process." Endorsements bring volunteer capacity, get-out-the-vote (GOTV) work, and PAC support. In 2025, PCCLC endorsed candidates for State Senate District 26 (Deborah Krishnadasan), Tacoma Mayor (Anders Ibsen), Tacoma City Council (Latasha Palmer, Silong Chhun, Joe Bushnell), Puyallup City Council, and multiple school board races.
- **PAC spending:** PCCLC has a political action committee that files with the state PDC (Public Disclosure Commission). Older records show $24,650 in 2014, $45,550 in 2016, and $32,150 in 2018. Current cycle spending is not confirmed.
- **Candidate training:** PCCLC recruits and trains labor-aligned candidates for local office. Its endorsement pipeline feeds into the Pierce County Democratic Party.
- **Solidarity work:** PCCLC calls itself "a democratic hub where unions come together to organize, advocate, educate, and build solidarity across industries and communities."

## 4. Power in numbers
|| Indicator | Finding | Source # |
||-----------|---------|----------|
|| Who benefits | Endorsed candidates get volunteers, GOTV, and PAC support. The 44,000+ union members get labor movement coordination. Member unions get political leverage through collective action. | #1, #3, #5 |
|| Who sits | President Alice Phillips (IBEW Local 483). Secretary-Treasurer Nathe Lawver (Building Trades). Vice President Christina Hall. Ten or more Executive Board members and Trustees. | #1, #2 |
|| Who governs | Delegate-driven governance. Monthly delegate meetings at 7 to 9 PM. Endorsements and resolutions are voted on by delegates. The executive board runs things between meetings. | #1, #5 |
|| Who wins | Endorsed candidates gain labor vote share. PCCLC backed the Pierce Transit ballot measure to expand transit. It named May 2026 Hispanic Heritage Month by resolution. | #3, #5 |

## 5. How they touch government
- **Campaign finance and PAC:** PCCLC files political expenditure reports with the state PDC. Older totals were $24,650 (2014), $45,550 (2016), and $32,150 (2018). Current cycle totals are not yet confirmed.
- **Endorsements:** PCCLC endorses candidates for local, county, and state races. 2025 endorsements include State Senate District 26, Tacoma Mayor, Tacoma City Council, Puyallup City Council, Gig Harbor City Council, Steilacoom Mayor, and several school board races.
- **Ballot measures:** PCCLC endorsed the Pierce Transit ballot measure to expand transit service.
- **Lobbying:** As a 501(c)(5), PCCLC can do political activity and lobbying beyond what a 501(c)(3) can do. Specific lobbying registrations are not confirmed.
- **Government contracts:** None identified. Not confirmed.

## 6. Other seats they hold
- **Alice Phillips** — President. IBEW Local 483 member (retired Business Manager, longest-serving, 30 years). Sits on the Clover Park Board of Trustees. 40 years of labor movement experience. First woman in several IBEW Local 483 leadership roles.
- **Nathe Lawver** — Secretary-Treasurer. Also Executive Secretary of the Pierce County Building and Construction Trades Council AFL-CIO. Sits on the GTCF board At-Large. Connects PCCLC to philanthropy and the building trades.
- **Christina Hall** — Vice President.
- **Executive Board:** Rick Hertzog, Jade Monroe, Brenda Wiest, Brent Wagar, Amber Roulst, Jared Ross, Cindy Richardson, Floyd David Dugan, Patti Dailey-Shives.
- **Patti Dailey-Shives** — Executive Board member. Also sits on the Pierce County Labor Community Services Agency board.
- **Member unions:** ILWU Local 23, Teamsters, plus 112 other affiliated unions.
- **Pierce County Democrats:** Aligned. PCCLC endorsements usually match Democratic Party candidates.
- **Ryan Mello:** Endorsed. Now the Pierce County Executive.

She has 40 years of labor experience and was the longest-serving Business Manager of IBEW Local 483 (30 years). She sits on the Clover Park Board of Trustees. | PCCLC website bio | https://unionhall.aflcio.org/pcclc/about-us/alice-phillips | primary | 0.97 |
| 3 | PCCLC 2025 endorsements: Deborah Krishnadasan (State Senate D26), Anders Ibsen (Tacoma Mayor), Latasha Palmer, Silong Chhun, Joe Bushnell (Tacoma Council), and other local races. | Blue Voter Guide | https://bluevoterguide.org/endorser-org/Pierce_County_(WA)_Labor_Council,_AFL-CIO/WA/4490 | secondary | 0.85 |

| 6 | PCCLC political expenditures per PDC records: $24,650 (2014), $45,550 (2016), $32,150 (2018). | Freedom Foundation | https://www.freedomfoundation.com/washington/freedom-foundation-sues-pdc-again-for-ignoring-union-violations-of-campaign-finance-laws | secondary | 0.70 |
| 7 | Patti Dailey-Shives sits on the PCCLC Executive Board and on the Pierce County Labor Community Services Agency Board. | Pierce County Labor Community Services Agency | https://www.pclaborcares.org/aboutus | primary | 0.90 |

## 12. Bottom line
- **The bottom line.** PCCLC is the central voice of organized labor in Pierce County. It has 114 affiliated unions and more than 44,000 members. It can move labor votes through endorsements and PAC spending.
- **Why it matters.** Endorsements bring volunteers and money. The PCCLC pipeline feeds into the Pierce County Democratic Party. It endorsed Ryan Mello, who is now County Executive. Its leaders also sit on the GTCF board and the Clover Park school board.
- **The counter-view.** Union density has dropped nationally. The PAC totals of $24,000 to $46,000 (2014 to 2018) are small compared to independent-expenditure campaigns. The 44,000-member number may overstate how many members are politically active.
- **Why PCCLC still matters.** The delegate-driven endorsement process and the dense board overlaps give PCCLC real structural influence. Its leaders connect labor, philanthropy (GTCF), and education (Clover Park).
- **Confidence:** Medium. The AFL-CIO website provides strong primary sourcing for the council's structure and leaders. PAC totals come from a secondary source (the Freedom Foundation). Current-cycle PDC data was not pulled.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why we added Phil Fortunato:** He holds office. He is the sitting State Senator for Washington's 31st Legislative District. The district covers southeast King County and northeast Pierce County. It includes Auburn, Bonney Lake, Buckley, Carbonado, Edgewood, Milton, South Prairie, Sumner, and Wilkeson. The district covers a large slice of Pierce County. He sits on four Senate committees: Law and Justice, Transportation, State Government/Tribal Affairs/Elections, and Business/Trade/Economic Development. His district overlaps with many Pierce County cities and towns.
- **Other people we did not add:** Drew Stokesbary (R-31, House Position 1) and Josh Penner (R-31, House Position 2) are his district-mates. They are added in this investigation separately. Pam Roach, a former D31 Senator who came before Fortunato, is excluded because she no longer holds office.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Philip D. Fortunato (Source 1).
- **Common name:** Phil Fortunato.
- **Birth:** Born 1953 or 1954 (Source 1). Birthplace not verified.
- **Home:** Auburn, Washington (Source 1, 2, 5).
- **Family:** Wife Suzanne Fortunato (married 42 or more years per Source 5). Five children. Three of the children served in the U.S. Marine Corps (Source 1, 5).
- **Education:** Rutgers University, New Brunswick (Source 1).
- **Job:** Owner and founder of Eco-3. Eco-3 is an erosion and stormwater management company based in Kent, WA. He has been a contractor for 30 or more years. He started his first business at age 18 (Source 2, 4, 5). He is a recognized expert on the federal Clean Water Act, which controls water pollution. He was the first person in Washington certified as a CESCL instructor. CESCL stands for Certified Erosion and Sediment Control Lead. The Washington State Department of Ecology certifies them (Source 4).
- **Group memberships:** Knights of Columbus, Buckley Eagles, Sons of Italy, Washington Arms Collectors, the National Rifle Association (NRA), Renton Fish and Game Club, and Black Diamond Gun Club (Source 5). He is a past president and founding director of the Pacific Northwest chapter of the International Erosion Control Association, or IECA (Source 4).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Elected office:** Washington State Senator, 31st Legislative District, since January 7, 2017. Current term ends January 11, 2027. He is running for re-election in the November 2026 general election. He advanced from the August 4, 2026 primary with 53.9% of the vote against Tamara Stramel (D), who got 46.0% (Source 2). Before that, he served in the Washington House of Representatives, 47th District, from January 11, 1999 to January 8, 2001 (Source 1).

- **Past statewide campaigns:** He ran for Governor of Washington in 2020. He finished 6th in the primary with 4.0% (99,265 votes) (Source 1, 2). He ran for Insurance Commissioner in 2024. He lost the general election to Patricia Kuderer (D), 43.3% to 56.6% (Source 2).
- **Budget power:** Fortunato is in the minority party. He does not control a budget on his own. He takes part in budget talks through his committee seats.
- **Jurisdiction:** 31st Legislative District — Auburn, Bonney Lake, Buckley, Carbonado, Edgewood, Milton, South Prairie, Sumner, Wilkeson (Source 5).

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** Fortunato's power comes from his long tenure as State Senator for the 31st District and his wide committee portfolio (Law and Justice, Transportation, State Government/Elections, Business/Economic Development). He does well at the district level (consistently 55 to 60% in his district) but does not win statewide races. He lost the Insurance Commissioner race by 13 points and placed 6th in the gubernatorial primary. His business, Eco-3, sits at the meeting point of his private commercial work and his legislative role overseeing construction, environmental rules, and economic development.

His seats on the Business, Trade and Economic Development committee and the Transportation committee overlap with his business in construction-related environmental compliance. His CESCL training certification from the Washington State Department of Ecology is a state-recognized business relationship. His NRA and gun club memberships signal an ideological match that may shape his work on the Law and Justice committee.

His repeated statewide runs (Governor, Insurance Commissioner) have failed. His influence is confined to his conservative district. His wide committee list may reflect a lack of seniority-based specialization rather than strong influence. His company is a small enterprise, not a major contractor.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why it's on the map:** Pierce County Library System is included as a junior taxing library district under state law (RCW) 27.12. It raises property taxes over a defined service area. That area covers unincorporated Pierce County plus 15 annexed cities and towns. It runs a multi-million-dollar annual budget. It serves about 680,000 residents through 20 branches. The graph edge `pierce-county-library → county-council, taxing, weight=3` shows its tie to the County Council.
- **Neighbors NOT added to the map:** Tacoma Public Library is a separate system inside the City of Tacoma. Puyallup Public Library serves the City of Puyallup. Both are separate and excluded. The Washington State Library coordinates statewide but is outside this profile's scope.

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** Pierce County Library System (PCLS). Formally the Pierce County Rural Library District.
- **Entity type:** Washington junior taxing library district. A government entity under RCW 27.12 (Library Districts). It is separate from municipal libraries (Tacoma Public Library, Puyallup Public Library) and from the Pierce County government's general-purpose departments.
- **Formed:** Established by ballot measure passed by voters in unincorporated Pierce County on November 7, 1944. Began operating January 2, 1946. Opened seven station branches in its first year.
- **Service area:** Unincorporated Pierce County plus 15 cities and towns that have annexed for library service. Excludes the City of Tacoma (which has its own library system) and the City of Puyallup (which has its own library system).
- **Branches:** 20 library locations. They include:
 - Administrative Center and Library, 3005 112th St. E., Tacoma / Summit-Waller area.
 - Anderson Island.
 - Bonney Lake.
 - Buckley.
 - DuPont.
 - Eatonville.
 - Fife.
 - Gig Harbor / Peninsula.
 - Graham.
 - Key Center.
 - Lakewood.
 - Milton / Edgewood.
 - Orting.
 - Parkland / Spanaway.
 - South Hill.
 - Steilacoom.
 - Summit (Tacoma).
 - Sumner.
 - Tillicum (Lakewood).
 - University Place.
Busiest: Gig Harbor, South Hill, Lakewood, University Place, Parkland / Spanaway.
- **Board of Trustees:** Five members. They are appointed by the Pierce County Executive (current executive: Ryan Mello). Five-year terms, with the option of up to two consecutive terms. Meetings are the second Wednesday of each month at 3:30 pm at the Administrative Center.
- **Executive leadership:** Executive Director Gretchen Caserotti (one of five directors in PCLS history; predecessors: Marion Cromwell, Carolyn Else, Neel Parikh, Georgia Lomax).
- **Collection:** About 1.2 million items. Circulation about 6.9 to 7.4 million items a year. 334,362 members (2016). About 2.2 million in-person visits a year (2016). Website had about 3.5 million visitors (2016).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power from the law:** As a library district under RCW 27.12, PCLS can levy property taxes (subject to Washington's 1% cap, also called the levy lid). It can issue bonds with voter approval. It can sign contracts, hire staff, buy property, and provide library services inside its boundaries.
- **Taxing power:** Property taxes are the main funding source per PCLS's own statement: "Property taxes are the primary source of funding for the Library System." The 2018 levy (Levy Sustainability Fund) was approved by voters. It builds savings for long-term stability. Per the 2026 Budget Book, Washington's 1% property tax cap limits annual revenue growth. In 2025, General Fund expenses exceeded revenues. The budget had to be balanced carefully.
- **Budget control (2026 figures):** Total budget about $31.9M (2016 reference figure from Wikipedia, citing Washington Public Library Statistical Report 2016). The 2026 budget summaries show several separate funds:
 - General Fund operating budget.
 - Capital Improvement Fund.
 - Election Fund.
 - Debt Service Fund.
 - Levy Sustainability Fund.
 - Property and Facility Fund.
The specific 2026 total is UNVERIFIED — budget summary PDFs show fund-level detail but the total was not added up in this pass.
- **How it touches government:**
 - **Board picks:** The Pierce County Executive (Ryan Mello since Jan 2025) appoints all five trustees. They are subject to County Council confirmation (UNVERIFIED — confirmation rules vary by RCW).
 - **Annual budget approval:** The Board adopts the annual budget. It is subject to public hearings and final public-hearing rules per RCW 27.12.
 - **State Auditor oversight:** Subject to SAO accountability audits (UNVERIFIED — specific 2024 / 2025 SAO report not pulled).
 - **Levy lid:** Subject to Washington's 1% annual property-tax revenue growth cap (RCW 84.55). Lifting the lid requires voter approval.
- **Where the domains overlap:**
 - **gov ↔ social:** Library services to about 680,000 residents. Summer reading programs. Children's programs. Community events.
 - **gov ↔ econ:** Big spending on books, databases, technology. Capital projects for branch upkeep. Recent or upcoming: Gig Harbor closure for maintenance Sept 14 to 26; Steilacoom closure Sept 28 to Oct 13.
 - **gov ↔ inst:** Interlocal partnerships with schools, community colleges, museums. Shared catalog systems.

## 3. Where their power comes from

| Who benefits | About 680,000 Pierce County residents outside Tacoma and Puyallup benefit from library services. That includes physical lending, digital resources, children's programs, summer reading, and community meeting space. Cardholders (334,362 as of 2016) benefit directly. Non-cardholders benefit from public programs and community space. | Sources 1, 2, 3 |
| Who sits | A five-member Board of Trustees governs PCLS. Current roster (as of 2026): Neesha Patel (Chair, Edgewood resident, tenured math professor at SPSCC, term ends Aug 11, 2030); Ryan Wheaton (Vice-Chair, Puyallup, Chief Planning Officer at Pierce Transit, term ends Aug 13, 2029); Pam Duncan (Lakewood, CEO of Tierra Sólida Enterprises, term ends Feb 14, 2029); Pat Jenkins (Puyallup, program coordinator at Lutheran Community Services NW, term ends Mar 31, 2027); Tono Sablan (Parkland, Executive Director of LeMay Family Foundation, term ends Aug 5, 2031). Executive Director Gretchen Caserotti runs operations. | Sources 2, 3 |
| Who governs | The Board of Trustees sets policy direction, approves budgets, adopts policies, and advocates for library services. The Pierce County Executive appoints trustees. That creates an indirect accountability link to the county executive. | Sources 2, 3 |
| Who wins | Voters in the PCLS service area keep library services funded by their property taxes. The Pierce County Executive gains influence over library governance through trustee picks. Specific contractors (book vendors, IT providers, capital construction) win public-sector contracts. | Sources 2, 3 |

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** PCLS runs a multi-million-dollar public library district. It delivers lending, programming, and community-space services to about 680,000 Pierce County residents across 20 branches. Its power is mostly fiscal and service-delivery. It levies property taxes (subject to the 1% cap). It adopts annual budgets. It runs a regional library system. The five-member Board of Trustees — appointed by the Pierce County Executive — sets policy direction. PCLS is limited by Washington's property-tax cap (RCW 84.55). It is also limited by voter approval rules for levy lid lifts and bonds. In 2025, General Fund expenses exceeded revenues, creating fiscal pressure. The 2018 Levy Sustainability Fund was set up to manage that constraint.
- **Conflicts of interest:** Several Board members have direct professional ties to Pierce County or its affiliated groups. Ryan Wheaton is the Chief Planning Officer at Pierce Transit (a separate Pierce County agency). Pam Duncan chairs the Tacoma-Pierce County Affordable Housing Consortium. She chairs the Washington State Community Action Partnership. She also sits on the Washington Low-Income Housing Alliance. Tono Sablan sits on the Greater Tacoma Community Foundation Board. These cross-board memberships create alignment of interests in funding and policy choices. No specific conflict has been alleged. Trustee picks by the County Executive (Ryan Mello since Jan 2025) create political accountability but no formal confirmation gate is documented — UNVERIFIED.
- **The other reading:** An opposing reading: PCLS is a service-delivery group with limited political power. Its choices affect library patrons but not the broader political economy of Pierce County. It is one of several library systems in the county (Tacoma Public Library, Puyallup Public Library). It competes for patron attention. The 2025 General Fund shortfall suggests fiscal pressure. That pressure may force service cuts or a levy lid lift (which would need voter approval). The trustee-appointment setup by the County Executive makes PCLS open to political capture. It also brings democratic accountability through executive elections. The board's makeup (multiple members with nonprofit and social-service backgrounds rather than business or government) tilts its policy stance toward equity, literacy, and community services.
- **Confidence:** High. The official PCLS website, primary board packets, and Wikipedia confirm formation history, governance setup, financial scale, and current board makeup. The 2016 budget figure ($31.9M) is from the 2016 Washington Public Library Statistical Report referenced in Wikipedia. The current 2026 budget total is UNVERIFIED at the aggregate level. Fund-level detail is available in the 2026 Budget Summaries PDF.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Inclusion rule — power and decision-making.** The Pierce County Democratic Central Committee (PCDCC) is on this map as the county Democratic Party. It backs candidates with endorsements, trains campaigns, fills empty elected offices, and runs the Precinct Committee Officer (PCO) network.
- The PCDCC is a statutory party organization under Washington law. It has formal powers to endorse candidates and to fill vacancies in partisan offices.
- **Important caveat:** Party nodes are an artifact of how the graph works. They collect all the "member" edges from legislators who share that party label. That makes them look more connected than they really are. The PCDCC's 17 graph edges mostly come from Democratic officials — that is party affiliation, not a chain of command. The composite score is capped at 0.12 to correct for this.
- **Adjacent but excluded:** The Washington State Democratic Central Committee (WSDCC) is the parent. King County Democrats is a peer. Pierce County Republicans is the counterpart. LD-level Democratic groups (2nd, 25th, 26th, 27th, 28th, 29th, 31st) are sub-units, not separate map nodes.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Pierce County Democratic Central Committee (PCDCC).
- **Common name:** Pierce County Democrats / Pierce Dems.
- **Entity type:** Political committee registered with the Washington State Public Disclosure Commission (PDC). Not a 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(6). Governed by state law (RCW 42.17A) and the WSDCC charter.
- **EIN or PDC registration:** Not verified. Political committees usually file with the PDC, not the IRS.
- **Parent and sub-units:** Under the Washington State Democratic Central Committee. Legislative District (LD) Democratic groups (2nd, 25th, 26th, 27th, 28th, 29th, 31st) work under the PCDCC.
- **Ownership chain:** Democratic National Committee → Washington State Democratic Central Committee → Pierce County Democratic Central Committee → LD Democratic organizations.
- **Governing law:** RCW 42.17A (Public Disclosure Commission); WSDCC charter; PCDCC bylaws.
- **Address:** PO Box (per the official site). Office: 3049 S 36th St, Tacoma, WA 98409 — same building as PCCLC.

## 2. Their career and offices

| Chair | Marianna Hyke |
| Vice Chair | Jared Richardson |

- **Previous Chair:** Kathy Orlando. The move from Orlando to Hyke is not verified in detail.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power held.** The PCDCC has statutory party power under Washington law. It endorses candidates, fills vacancies in partisan Democratic offices, organizes the PCO network, and coordinates campaigns across Pierce County.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- The Pierce County Republican Party (PCRP) is on this map as a key hub in the power graph. The investigation framework caps its composite power at 0.12. It earned its place because it is well-connected and has strong name recognition. The party endorses candidates, channels donor money, trains campaigns, and links elected Republicans to each other and to the state party.
- Its endorsement process and donor network make it a hub, even though the party itself does not hold direct government power.
- The Washington State Republican Party (WAGOP) is the parent. It is not a separate graph node. The Pierce County Democrats are a parallel node. Individual Republican officials are separate person nodes.

## 1. Who they are
- **Full legal name:** Pierce County Republican Party (PCRP). Also known as "Pierce County Republican Central Committee."
- **Type:** Political party organization. It is registered with the state campaign-finance agency (PDC) as two committees:
  - **Pierce County Republican Party Exempt** (PDC committee ID: 15410) — federal/exempt funds.
  - **Pierce County Republican Party Non-Exempt** (PDC committee ID: 15541) — state/non-exempt funds.
- **Governing law:** State law (RCW) 29A.80 for political parties. WA PDC rules. WAGOP bylaws. PCRP bylaws.
- **Federal tax ID (EIN):** Not publicly listed. Address: 10209 Bridgeport Way SW, #C-1, Lakewood, WA 98499.
- **Parent group:** Part of the Washington State Republican Party (WAGOP). WAGOP Chair: Jim Walsh (State Rep, 19th LD). PCRP is in WAGOP Region 7 with Thurston County.
- **Website:** piercegop.org

## 2. Their career and offices
- **Chair:** Dave McMullan (re-elected). He also sits on the WAGOP Executive Board as Region 7 Chairman for Pierce County.
- **Vice President:** Connie Coleman-Lacadie
- **Treasurer:** David Patrick

- **Endorsement power:** The PCRP endorsement is a formal process. Candidates fill out questionnaires. The Endorsements Committee interviews them. The central committee votes. - **Party machinery:** Chair McMullan controls strategy, fundraising, and the endorsement calendar. He also sits on the WAGOP Executive Board (Region 7), linking the county party to the state party.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Inclusion rule:** Pierce Transit is on this map on the grounds of "from holding office," "decision-making," and "well-connected." It is the main public transit operator in Pierce County. It controls a $367 million annual budget. It runs the county's bus and paratransit service.

Its Board of Commissioners is made up of elected officials from Tacoma, Pierce County, Lakewood, Puyallup, and other cities. That creates direct board overlaps with municipal governments. Pierce Transit has its own sales tax. The current rate is 0.6 percent. A proposal would raise it to 0.9 percent. That is direct taxing power over all purchases in the Public Transportation Benefit Area (PTBA).
- **Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates:** Sound Transit is a separate regional transit agency (mapped as `sound-transit`). Community Transit is in Snohomish County, outside the boundary. King County Metro is also outside the boundary. The Pierce Transit Workers' Union, ATU Local 758, has a non-voting seat on the board. It is not on the map as a separate node.

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** Pierce County Public Transportation Benefit Area Corporation (also called "Pierce Transit")
- **Entity type:** Government — municipal corporation (Public Transportation Benefit Area, PTBA)
- **Governing law:** state law RCW 36.57A (Public Transportation Benefit Areas). Pierce Transit was formed under Chapter 36.57A of the Revised Code of Washington.
- **tax ID number (EIN) and registration:** UNVERIFIED. Pierce Transit is a government municipal corporation. Its EIN is not publicly listed in easily accessible sources.
- **Parent and subsidiaries:** None. It is an independent municipal corporation.
- **Founded:** November 6, 1979. Voters approved a 0.3 percent sales tax to fund the PTBA. Service began January 1, 1980. The agency adopted the name "Pierce Transit" in June 1980.
- **Headquarters:** 3701 96th Street Southwest, Lakewood, WA 98498.

## 2. Their career and offices
- **CEO:** Mike Griffus (Chief Executive).
- **Board of Commissioners (10 members — 9 voting, 1 non-voting):**

| Commissioner | Role | Represents |
|-------------|------|-----------|
| Kristina Walker | Chair | Tacoma City Council (Position 8) |
| Rosie Ayala | Vice Chair | Pierce County Council |
| Lauren Adler | Commissioner | Puyallup City Council |
| Paul Bocchi | Commissioner | Mayor of Lakewood |
| Olgy Diaz | Commissioner | Tacoma City Council (Position 7) |
| Doug Fagundes | Commissioner | Cities of Auburn, Edgewood, Fife, Milton, Pacific, Ruston, and Steilacoom |
| John Hines | Commissioner | Tacoma City Council (Position 1) |
| John Hoheusle | Non-voting | Labor Representative (ATU Local 758 President) |
| Ryan Mello | Commissioner | Pierce County Executive |
| Shannon Reynolds | Commissioner | Mayor of Fircrest (represents Fircrest, Gig Harbor, and University Place) |

- **Board composition over time:** Tacoma holds three seats. Pierce County holds two. Lakewood holds one. Puyallup and Edgewood share one. Smaller cities rotate the rest. The board has approved a reallocation recommendation to adjust seats based on population changes.
- **Board overlaps flagged:**
  - **Kristina Walker** (`kristina-walker`): Board Chair and Tacoma City Council Position 8. Graph node (weight 5, chair).
  - **Rosie Ayala** (`rosie-ayala`): Vice Chair and Pierce County Council. Graph node (weight 4, board).
  - **Ryan Mello** (`ryan-mello`): Commissioner and Pierce County Executive. Graph node (weight 5, board).
  - **Mike Griffus** (`mike-griffus`): CEO. Graph node (weight 4, ceo).
  - **Olgy Diaz** and **John Hines**: Both Tacoma City Council members on the Pierce Transit Board. This creates a board overlap with `tacoma-city-council`.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Statutory authority:** RCW 36.57A lets PTBAs levy sales tax (with voter approval), run transit service, contract with other agencies, and own and operate property. Pierce Transit runs fixed-route bus, dial-a-ride (SHUTTLE paratransit), vanpool, and rideshare services.
- **Taxing authority:** Pierce Transit currently levies a 0.6 percent local sales tax within the PTBA. The last increase, from 0.3 to 0.6 percent, was approved by voters in 2002. A November 3, 2026 ballot measure (Resolution 2026-006) would raise the rate to 0.9 percent. That is a 0.3 percentage-point increase (3 cents on a $10 purchase). If approved, it would fund a 47 percent boost in service and bring in about $64 million a year.
- **Market share:** Pierce Transit is the main (near-monopoly) public transit provider in Pierce County. It runs 29 routes and 174 buses. Weekday ridership averages about 29,700 (Q2 2026). Annual ridership was 7,833,600 in 2025.
- **Regulatory capture:** Limited. Pierce Transit must follow FTA rules and WSDOT oversight. It needs voter approval for tax increases.
- **Domain overlaps:** Government (transit authority and taxing power), economic (transportation infrastructure that supports commerce), and political (board members are elected officials who campaign on transit positions).

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Transit riders (about 7.8 million per year). Seniors and disabled riders who use paratransit. Students (more than 1,051,775 free youth rides in 2025). Employers who use transit to reach workers. Cities that get transit infrastructure investment. | #7, #10 |
| Who sits | 10-member Board of Commissioners. Elected officials from Tacoma (3), Pierce County (2), Lakewood (1), Puyallup (1), smaller cities (2), plus a non-voting ATU 758 labor rep. CEO Mike Griffus runs operations. | #5, #8 |
| Who governs | The Board of Commissioners sets policy, approves budgets, and places tax measures on the ballot. CEO Griffus runs operations. The Executive Finance Committee, ended in March 2026 (Resolution 2026-004), used to approve contracts up to $1 million. | #5, #8, #9 |
| Who wins | Communities that get new or expanded service. The proposed 2026 ballot measure would fund a 47 percent service increase. Labor (ATU 758) holds a non-voting board seat. Transit-dependent riders benefit most when service is kept. | #6, #10 |

## 4. Their money
- **2025 budget:** $367,362,470 total across all parts. Operating budget is $206.8 million. Capital budget is $166.1 million.
- **Revenue breakdown:**
  - Sales tax: $113,220,060. That is 81.1 percent of operating revenues, excluding the Sound Transit contract.
  - Regional Transit Service (Sound Transit contract): $60,919,470.
  - Passenger fares: $7,030,520.
  - Advertising: $605,000.
  - Miscellaneous: $823,280.
- **Sales tax rate:** 0.6 percent. This is the lowest rate among similar-sized transit agencies. The last voter-approved increase was in 2002.
- **Financial health:** Pierce Transit has healthy reserves. It carries no debt. The budget is balanced. Expenses are expected to outpace revenue as early as 2027 due to inflation.
- **Tax status:** Pierce Transit is a government municipal corporation. It is not a tax-exempt nonprofit. It is a taxing authority.
- **Property holdings:** The headquarters is at 3701 96th St SW, Lakewood. Pierce Transit also owns transit centers, park-and-ride lots, and bus bases. Specific assessed values are UNVERIFIED.
- **Levy and bond history:** Pierce Transit has no property-tax levy authority. Revenue comes from a sales tax approved by voters. Voters approved a 0.3 percent rate in 1979. They raised it to 0.6 percent in 2002. A 2026 ballot measure would raise it to 0.9 percent.

## 5. How they touch government
- **Pierce County Council** (`county-council`): Board member Rosie Ayala (County Council) creates a direct link. The Council does not appropriate Pierce Transit's budget (the PTBA is independent). But council members serve on the board (weight 4, ballot_measure in the graph, meaning the board can place tax measures on the ballot).
- **Tacoma City Council** (`tacoma-city-council`): Three board members (Walker, Diaz, Hines) are Tacoma council members. The City of Tacoma holds 3 of the 9 voting board seats. That is the largest single-city share.
- **Sound Transit** (`sound-transit`): Pierce Transit contracts with Sound Transit to operate regional bus service. That contract is worth $60.9 million a year. Pierce Transit also operates the Hilltop light rail extension for Sound Transit under FTA requirements.
- **Jake Fey** (`jake-fey`): Washington State Representative. He appears in the graph as transit_funding (weight 5). State legislative appropriations for transit move through WSDOT grants.
- **FTA (Federal Transit Administration):** The FTA funds capital projects like bus purchases and facility upgrades. Pierce Transit must follow FTA requirements for the Hilltop extension.
- **Campaign donations:** Pierce Transit does not make campaign donations. It is a government entity. Board members may donate in their personal capacity. See their individual profiles.
- **Lobbying:** Pierce Transit lobbies the state legislature for transit funding. Specific lobbying spending was UNVERIFIED from the state's campaign-finance agency (PDC) in this pass.

## 6. Other seats they hold
- **Kristina Walker** (`kristina-walker`): Board Chair. Tacoma City Council. Graph node (weight 5, chair).

- **Jake Fey** (`jake-fey`): WA State Rep. Transit_funding. Graph node (weight 5).
- **Tacoma City Council** (`tacoma-city-council`): Three board members (Walker, Diaz, Hines) serve on both. Not directly in graph edges for Pierce Transit, but creates a strong institutional board overlap.
- **ATU Local 758:** Non-voting board seat held by John Hoheusle, ATU 758 President. This is a labor board overlap.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- Why PLU is on the map: Pacific Lutheran University (PLU) is on the map for three reasons. First, its president, Allan Belton, is a board-overlap node in the graph. Second, PLU co-signed the February 2024 Partnership for Health Innovation with MultiCare and WSU. Third, PLU controls land use and workforce training in central Pierce County (Parkland). It now hosts a WSU medical-school satellite on campus.
- Who is NOT on the map: The WSU Elson S. Floyd College of Medicine is excluded as the parent of record. PLU is the host partner. Pacific Lutheran Theological Seminary in Berkeley, California is excluded. It is a separate campus. Concordia University Wisconsin is excluded. It is a different ELCA school. Open questions and leads are listed below.

## 1. Who they are
- Legal name: **Pacific Lutheran University, Inc.** (a Washington nonprofit corporation).
- Entity type: **501(c)(3) private university**. A 501(c)(3) is a tax-exempt nonprofit under U.S. tax law. It is affiliated with the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (ELCA). It is a tax-exempt nonprofit. It is governed under state law RCW 24.03 (Washington Nonprofit Corporation Act) and Title 28B RCW (Higher Education).
- Parent and subsidiaries: No parent company. PLU Foundation, Inc. is a separate fundraising arm. PLU Tacoma is the main campus. It is in Parkland, an unincorporated part of Pierce County. The mailing address is Tacoma, WA 98447.
- Founding: Started in 1890 by Rev. Bjug Harstad. The 14th president, **L. Allan Belton**, was picked by the Board of Regents. He started April 3, 2019. He had been acting president since 2017.
- Provost: Joanna Gregson. Faculty: 340. Students: 2,754 (2,366 undergraduate and 388 postgraduate). Campus: 156 acres in suburban Parkland, WA.
- Endowment: **$123.1 million** (Wikipedia infobox, FY24 figure).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Decision-making power (institutional):** PLU's Board of Regents sets tuition. It approves the academic-medical partnership. It governs the on-campus MultiCare Medical Center that opens in 2025–26. That gives the Board veto and approval power over any clinical site on its 156-acre campus.
- **Cultural influence (symbolic):** PLU is the largest ELCA university on the West Coast. It is the only private four-year school in central Pierce County. That makes it a key name for Lutheran employers, regional hospital systems, and Tacoma-area civic boards.
- **Workforce-pipeline power:** Through the Partnership for Health Innovation, PLU channels MultiCare hiring, WSU medical-school rotations, and NIH and HRSA grant applications. HRSA is the Health Resources and Services Administration, a federal agency. NIH is the National Institutes of Health. In short, PLU sits at a key point for the Pierce County healthcare workforce.
- How the score covers different domains: board overlap (Belton graph weight 5), partnership (MultiCare graph weight 5), and reputational role as the only private university in unincorporated Pierce County.

## 3. Where their power comes from

| Who sits | Allan Belton (PLU president) sits at the top of the partnership. The PLU Board of Regents holds final approval. MultiCare CEO Bill Robertson co-signed the partnership letter. | #1, #2, #3 |
| Who governs | The PLU Board of Regents governs the university. Board members are ELCA lay and clergy trustees. The on-campus MultiCare Medical Center will be run by MultiCare under a ground-lease and operating agreement. PLU will not run it. | #2, #3 |
| Who wins | Short-term: PLU wins through enrollment and endowment growth. MultiCare wins through a geographic monopoly extension into Parkland and Spanaway. Long-term: mostly the same. The ELCA loses some control as the medical-center arm drifts toward MultiCare's operational culture. | INFERENCE from #1, #3 |

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- Port of Tacoma is on the map because it holds power through office, makes big decisions, and drives the local economy. It is a public port district under state law (RCW) Title 53. It works as an independent city-like government with elected commissioners. It runs container terminals, industrial property, and rail-truck interchanges. Through the Northwest Seaport Alliance (NWSA), it shares control of one of the largest container ports in North America. Its commissioners are elected county-wide, which gives it direct democratic legitimacy. Its board members also sit on the Chamber of Commerce and the Economic Development Board (EDB). It hires ILWU Local 23 longshore workers.
- **Groups not profiled here.** Port of Seattle — separate port in King County, but connected through NWSA. NWSA is profiled as its own node (`nwsa`) — it is a Port Development Authority (PDA), not a port district. The Washington Public Ports Association is a trade group, not a power node. Foss Waterway Development Authority is a subsidiary.

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** Port of Tacoma [Source #1, #2]
- **Entity type:** Independent city-like government and special purpose district [Source #1]
- **Governing law:** Title 53 of the Revised Code of Washington (RCW 53) — including:
 - RCW 53.08: Powers of port districts
 - RCW 53.12: Commissioner elections
 - RCW 53.35: Budgets (legal budget rules)
 - RCW 53.36: Finances (general-obligation debt)
 - RCW 53.40: Revenue bonds and warrants
 - RCW 53.57: Port development authority (the basis for NWSA)
 [Source #1, #3]
- **Tax ID (EIN) or registration:** UNVERIFIED — port districts are government bodies, not IRS 501(c)(3) filers.
- **Parent and subsidiaries:** No parent company. Port of Tacoma is one of two equal members of the Northwest Seaport Alliance (NWSA), a Port Development Authority formed under an RCW 53 change in 2015. [Source #4, #5]
- **Ownership chain:** Public body — owned by Pierce County citizens through elected commissioners.
- **Designation:** Special purpose district under Washington law [Source #1]

## 2. Their career and offices
- **Executive Director:** Eric Johnson — joined Port of Tacoma as executive director in 2019. He runs the port. Before that, he was Executive Director of Washington Public Ports Association. He is from Pierce County. He earned a BA in Biology and Political Science from Pacific Lutheran University. He also earned an MPA (Master of Public Administration) from the University of Washington. It focused on environmental policy and natural resources. He sits on the boards of the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce. He also sits on the Economic Development Board for Tacoma-Pierce County (EDB). That includes the EDB Executive Committee. [Source #6]
- **Chief Financial and Administrative Officer:** Erin Galeno — runs finance, accounting, contracts, purchasing, and security. She joined the Port in 2009. Before that, she spent 23 years at Weyerhaeuser. Her last role was Director of Internal Audit. She is a licensed CPA. She has a BA from the University of Puget Sound. She also has an Executive Leadership certificate from Seattle University. She sits on the Advisory Board at UW Tacoma. [Source #6]
- **Chief External Strategy Officer:** Alisa Praskovich — runs Real Estate and Economic Development, Government Affairs, and Communications. Before this, she was Vice President of Sustainability at Crowley. She was also a White House Ocean Policy Advisor. She is a retired Coast Guard Commander. She has a BA in Biology from Eckerd College. She also has an MS in Marine Affairs from UW. [Source #6]
- **Chief Human Resources Officer:** Vanessa Audett — joined in 2025. She came from the City of Federal Way, where she was HR Director. Before that, she worked for the City of SeaTac and UtilX Corporation. She holds SHRM-SCP and SPHR certifications. These are human-resources credentials. [Source #6]
- **Chief Information Officer:** Martyn Adamson — named the first CIO in 2025. He has been at the Port since 2003. He has a BS in Computing from Edinburgh Napier University. [Source #6]
- **Commission (5 members, elected at-large, 4-year terms):** [Source #1, #7, #8, #9, #10]
 - **John McCarthy** — Position #1, current term Jan 2026-Dec 2029; elected four times (1983-1989, 1989-1992, 2018-2021, 2022-2026+); Second Assistant Secretary; sits on the Freight Mobility Strategic Investment Board and the PSRC Executive Board [Source #7]
 - **Dick Marzano** — Position #2, current term Jan 2026-Dec 2029; first elected 1995; Commission President; former ILWU Local 23 longshore worker (52 years) and 6-year Local 23 president; past president of the Washington Public Ports Association; sits on the Tacoma-Pierce County EDB and the Puget Sound Gateway Program Executive Committee [Source #8]
 - **Deanna Keller** — Position #3, current term Jan 2024-Dec 2027; first elected 2019; Commission Vice President [Source #9]
 - **JT Wilcox** — Position #4 (graph node `jt-wilcox`); UNVERIFIED current term dates from the Port website; formerly WA State House Representative (R-2nd District), House Minority Leader [graph]
 - **Kristin Ang** — Position #5, current term Jan 2024-Dec 2027; first elected 2019; Commission Secretary; Filipino-American attorney; first person of color elected to the Port of Tacoma commission; NWSA Managing Member; endorsed by the Puyallup Tribe; sits on the Central Puget Sound Economic Development District executive board, the Washington Council on International Trade, and the UW-Tacoma Urban Waters Advisory Board [Source #10]
- **Board overlaps flagged:**
 - John McCarthy (`john-mccarthy`) — commissioner and node in graph [Source #7]
 - JT Wilcox (`jt-wilcox`) — commissioner and node in graph [Source #1]
 - Dick Marzano (`dick-marzano`) — commissioner and node in graph [Source #8]
