## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Inclusion rule:** Reputational and media reach. South Sound Business is the only monthly magazine in the South Sound that covers only business topics. It serves Pierce, South King, Kitsap, and Thurston counties, plus Bainbridge Island. It is the main chronicler of the Pierce County business community. It covers the port, MultiCare (a hospital system), and Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM) contractors. It also covers regional banks and the local Chamber. The magazine calls itself the "#1 business communication media in the South Sound since 1985." Its editorial choices shape which businesses get steady regional attention.
- **Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates:** The News Tribune, the main daily paper, is owned separately. Seattle Business Magazine and 425 Business are run by Premier Media Group. KNKX is public radio. Tacoma Weekly is another local outlet. KING5 runs a South Sound bureau.

## 1. Who they are
- **Publication title:** South Sound Business (current brand). Earlier called *South Sound Biz* from 1985 to 2021 under Business Examiner Media.
- **Publisher:** Premier Media Group (PMG), based in Tacoma, WA. Mailing address: P.O. Box 1362, Tacoma, WA 98401-1362. Phone: (253) 588-5340. Web: https://www.southsoundbiz.com/.
- **Acquisition history:** Launched in 1985 by Business Examiner Media, founded by Jeff and Jill Rounce. Acquired by Premier Media Group, founded by Josh and Michelle Dunn, around August 19, 2021. Rebranded from "South Sound Biz" to "South Sound Business" after the sale.
- **Editorial staff (current, per About page):** Jeff Burlingame is Editor in Chief. He worked at Seattle University and the Gates Foundation. He won a Sigma Delta Chi award from the Society of Professional Journalists (SPJ). Joanna Kresge is Managing Editor.
- **Recognition:** 2023 Silver Best of Show Excellence Award for Best Website. The award came from the Alliance of Area Business Publishers at its summer conference in Detroit.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Niche dominance:** The magazine calls itself the "only local media dedicated exclusively to business topics in the South Sound." No other outlet fills that niche since PMG bought Business Examiner Media.
- **Geographic reach:** It covers 24 cities across Pierce, South King, Kitsap, and Thurston counties. It also covers Bainbridge Island. It is produced in Tacoma. It reaches leaders at CHI Franciscan, JBLM, MultiCare, Dillanos, Heritage Bank, and Umpqua.
- **Award-winning:** 2023 Alliance of Area Business Publishers (AABP) Silver Best of Show for Best Website.
- **Format:** Monthly print and digital, plus "Hallmark Events" like Women to Watch. These events are both marketing tools and access points for the region's business elite.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Premier Media Group (parent) and its advertisers gain the most. Featured businesses earn profile-raising "thought leader" coverage. | 1, 2, 4 |
| Who sits | Editor in Chief Jeff Burlingame worked at Seattle U and the Gates Foundation. Managing Editor Joanna Kresge runs daily news. Director of Sales Lander Martinson has been with PMG since 2003. | 1 |

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- Southport Financial Services is on the map because it makes decisions and has strong ties. It is a national affordable housing developer with a Tacoma office. It works with Pierce County government on big subsidized housing projects. One example is Cedar Flats (276 units, with $7 million from the county).
- The company focuses on Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) properties. LIHTC is a federal program that gives tax credits to developers who build affordable housing. That focus gives it special know-how in federal, state, and local affordable housing finance. It sits on the board of the Affordable Housing Consortium of Pierce County. That gives it a direct line into the local affordable housing policy network.

This needs to be checked. Macdonald Ladd is not on the map unless it turns out to be a partner or subsidiary. The Maureen Howard Affordable Housing Fund (a county program) is not an entity. Southport's Tampa HQ is outside Pierce County, so it is not in this map.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Southport Financial Services, Inc.
- **Type:** For-profit corporation. It does real estate development, construction, and property management.

- **Ownership:** J. David Page is named as Southport's leader or founder in Housing Finance magazine. Specific ownership is unverified. VP of Finance: Stephane Varenne (per VisualVisitor).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Market power:** Southport has developed over 120 LIHTC properties. It holds about 12,000 units in 18 states. It has "built or acquired a substantial number of market rental housing projects." It has "a demonstrated ability to secure LIHTC allocations, as well as volume cap tax-exempt bond allocations in multiple states." That multi-state LIHTC know-how gives it special power in affordable housing finance.
- **Pierce County presence:** Southport has a Tacoma office at 1911 65th Ave W. That makes it one of the few national affordable housing developers with a physical office in Pierce County. Its VP, Zac Baker, sits on the board of the Affordable Housing Consortium of Pierce County. That gives the company a direct line into the local affordable housing policy network.
- **Government partnerships:** Pierce County named Southport as a partner in the Cedar Flats groundbreaking. Cedar Flats is a 276-unit affordable housing complex in the Puyallup / South Hill / Frederickson area. The county put $7 million from the Maureen Howard Affordable Housing Fund into the project. NOTE: The Urbanist names "Macdonald Ladd Development, LLC" as the Cedar Flats lead. The relationship between Southport and Macdonald Ladd is unverified. They may be co-developers. Or Southport may be the LIHTC partner while Macdonald Ladd leads development.
- **Revenue:** Unverified from public sources (private company). The scale (12,000 units, 120+ LIHTC properties, 18 states) suggests large revenue from development fees, property management, and LIHTC syndication (selling tax credits to investors).
- **Jobs:** 11-50 employees across three offices. More jobs come from construction projects and property management.
- **Land and buildings:** About 12,000 units in 18 states. Specific Pierce County holdings beyond Cedar Flats are unverified. The company also runs regular apartment complexes in central Florida and the southeastern U.S.

The project serves households earning less than 60% of Area Median Income (AMI) — the local middle income set by the federal government. The max income is $72,480 for a family of four. It includes larger units for families and reserves a portion for people with disabilities. The County Council approved $12.2 million for four housing projects (including Cedar Flats) at its September 2, 2025 meeting. The total Cedar Flats cost is nearly $109 million.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why it is here:** South Sound Military and Communities Partnership is a formal intergovernmental group. It works between Joint Base Lewis-McChord and 50+ nearby cities, counties, tribes, and groups. JBLM is the largest employer in Pierce County. The Elected Officials Council brings together top leaders from the county, the city of Lakewood, and JBLM command. It is a clear exercise of cross-jurisdictional power.
- **Who is left out:** The Office of Local Defense Community Cooperation is a federal funder of SSMCP. It is not a local power node. JBLM has its own profile. Member cities like Lakewood, Lacey, and DuPont may get their own profiles too.

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** South Sound Military & Communities Partnership (SSMCP).
- **Entity type:** Intergovernmental partnership — not a separate legal body. The memorandum of agreement (MOA) says SSMCP is a regional partnership. It can fund staff but does not directly employ anyone. The City of Lakewood acts as the fiduciary agent. It provides legal advice and administrative services.
- **Formed:** 2011, by memorandum of agreement. The current MOA is dated 2018.
- **Governing law:** The MOA among member jurisdictions. The Elected Officials Council (EOC) follows Washington's Open Public Meetings Act (Revised Code of Washington (RCW) 42.30).
- **Staff:** Two full-time paid staff with military backgrounds, funded by SSMCP. Program Manager: Maria Tobin (253-983-7804, mtobin@cityoflakewood.us). Past Program Director: Bill Adamson (retired Colonel).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **What power does SSMCP hold?** SSMCP works on land use, housing, transport, childcare, and economic development across Pierce and Thurston Counties. It has no legal authority. It shapes policy through the MOA, the Elected Officials Council, working groups, and studies. Its influence grows with JBLM's huge economic footprint.
- **Budget it controls:** SSMCP is funded by member dues and grants. Grants come from OLDCC. OLDCC is the federal Office of Local Defense Community Cooperation. That office used to be called the Office of Economic Adjustment. Exact budget numbers are not verified.
- **Appointment or veto powers:** None. The EOC makes policy suggestions and coordinates legislative strategies.
- **Area covered:** Pierce and Thurston Counties. This includes Lakewood, Lacey, Tacoma, DuPont, University Place, Yelm, Olympia, and nearby areas.

## 3. Where their power comes from

Steering Committee: Tacoma, Thurston County, University Place, Puget Sound Energy, Yelm. Working Group Chairs: Bates Technical College, Olympia, Clover Park School District, Pierce Transit, Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber. | 2, 3 |
| Who governs | Elected Officials Council. Co-chaired by the Lakewood Mayor, the Pierce County Executive, and the Thurston County Commission Chair. Meets twice a year. One vote per government body. | 2, 7 |
| Who wins | JBLM's interests get advanced through coordinated land-use plans. SSMCP-backed projects get regional priority. Former Pierce County Executive Bruce Dammeier praised SSMCP's "wide, deep" impact. | 7, 8 |

## 5. How they touch government
- **Pierce County:** Executive Leadership member. The Pierce County Executive serves as an EOC co-chair. Ryan Mello is the current Pierce County Executive. He sits on the EOC.
- **City of Lakewood:** Fiduciary agent and Executive Leadership member. It provides legal and administrative services. SSMCP staff are Lakewood city employees.
- **JBLM:** Ex officio Executive Leadership member. JBLM commanders take part in EOC meetings. These commanders include Col. Phil Lamb, Col. Dave Fazenbaker, and Lt. Gen. Xavier Brunson.
- **Office of Local Defense Community Cooperation:** Federal grant funder. Known as OLDCC.
- **Legislative advocacy:** SSMCP runs a Legislative Agenda. It pushes for state and federal funding for JBLM-community projects. Key efforts include the Defense Community Compatibility Account. They also include the North Clear Zone. They include the I-5 Nisqually River Delta Project.
- **Requests for Proposals:** SSMCP puts out RFPs for professional services. In 2025 it asked for bids on the JBLM Growth Implementation II plan. That plan covers three things: a Transportation Corridor Readiness Study, a Communications Interoperability Plan, and an Energy Grid Readiness Plan.

## 6. Other seats they hold

- **Amazon:** Sponsored an EOC event in May 2026.

## 1. Who they are
- Verdict: SSMCP is the main coordinating body between JBLM and 50+ nearby civilian jurisdictions. JBLM is Pierce County's largest employer. Its statewide impact is $9 billion. SSMCP's power comes from its structure, not from law. The Elected Officials Council meets twice a year. It is the region's formal forum for military-community policy coordination. It is co-chaired by the Pierce County Executive, the Lakewood Mayor, and the Thurston County Commission Chair. SSMCP shapes regional land-use strategy. It also shapes infrastructure planning, housing policy, and legislative advocacy. Lakewood is the fiduciary agent. That means SSMCP staff are effectively Lakewood employees. Amazon's sponsorship of EOC events shows corporate interest in SSMCP's work.
- Conflicts-of-interest flags: SSMCP has a dual mission. It supports both JBLM military readiness and community interests. These can clash. Military land-use needs like the North Clear Zone and noise zones may conflict with civilian development. The EOC's one-vote-per-government structure may favor larger places. Corporate sponsorship by Amazon of EOC events raises questions about influence. SSMCP-commissioned economic impact studies may inflate JBLM's perceived importance.
- Analysis of alternatives : The opposing reading is that SSMCP is a voluntary coordination body. It has no binding authority. It cannot force member jurisdictions to adopt any policy. Its suggestions are advisory. Members keep local control. The "$9 billion economic impact" figure comes from an economic model. That model, called input-output analysis, may overstate JBLM's real marginal impact. SSMCP's actual policy outputs beyond studies and forums may be modest.
- **Confidence:** High — SSMCP's structure, membership, economic impact data, and how they touch government are extensively documented in primary sources including its own MOA, official website, U.S. Army publications, and Pierce County government records. The organization's coordinating role is well-established and verifiable.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why she's on the map:** Stephanie Pedersen is President and Editor of The News Tribune in Tacoma. That is the only daily newspaper in Pierce County. She is also Regional Editor for McClatchy's Washington state papers. Those are the Bellingham Herald, the Tri-City Herald, The Olympian, and The News Tribune. She is the editorial decision-maker at the main print outlet covering Pierce County politics, business, and courts. The graph places her as a media node. She ties to News Tribune, and through it to McClatchy and Chatham Asset Management.
- **Neighbors NOT added to the map:** Josh Dunn runs South Sound Biz / Premier Media. Suzanne Schotzko and other editors work at Tacoma Weekly or South Sound Talk. KIRO and MyNorthwest.com cover the area digitally. All are nearby media figures, but they are not the same node.

## 1. Who they are
- **Full legal name:** Stephanie Pedersen.
- **Born / birthplace:** Not located in public sources (UNVERIFIED).
- **Lives in:** Tacoma, WA (RocketReach location field matches her employer).
- **Family / spouse:** Not in public sources (UNVERIFIED).
- **Schooling:** BA in Public Relations and Communications from Auburn University, 2003 to 2007 (per RocketReach).
- **Career path:**
 - 2007 to 2011: Copy Desk Chief, then Metro Editor, then Senior Editor for Digital at the Columbus Ledger-Enquirer in Georgia.
 - 2012: Metro Editor at the Ledger-Enquirer.
 - 2016 to 2020: Executive Editor at The Sun News in Myrtle Beach, SC.
 - April 2020: Promoted to President and Editor of The News Tribune. Also named Regional Editor for McClatchy's Washington state papers. Announced April 7, 2020 via PR Newswire.
 - 2025 to now: SVP of Local News at McClatchy. Editor of The News Tribune and The Olympian (per RocketReach).
- **Sanctions / criminal / civil:** None located.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Domain is media.** Her power comes from running the only daily newspaper in Pierce County. She also has regional say over three other McClatchy dailies in Washington state.
- **No law-based power.** She has no statutory role. She has real influence on the public-information environment for about 880,000 Pierce County residents.
- **How she wields influence:**
 - **Editorial agenda-setting:** She picks which Pierce County stories get investigative follow-up. She picks which council or county-executive actions get a board nod. She shapes how coverage frames police-accountability, business, and political races.
 - **Board nod power:** The News Tribune board (which she leads) issues primary and general-election nods that swing local races. Past nods include Tacoma mayoral, Pierce County Executive, and school-board races.
 - **Hiring and budget:** As President and Editor she controls local newsroom headcount, beat assignments, and contractor ties.
 - **Cross-paper reach:** As Regional Editor, she sets cross-state newsroom strategy for McClatchy in Washington. She covers the Bellingham Herald, Tri-City Herald, and The Olympian.
- **Key facts:**
 - **Reach:** The News Tribune has the largest print circulation in Pierce County. It also has digital subscriptions. McClatchy's WA cluster reaches about 1 million combined digital readers. Current paid-subscriber counts were not in primary sources (UNVERIFIED).
 - **Ownership chain:** News Tribune is owned by McClatchy LLC. McClatchy is owned by Chatham Asset Management. Chatham is a hedge fund that bought McClatchy out of bankruptcy in 2020 for $312 million. Pedersen does not own equity. Her power is operational and editorial.
 - **Editorial stance:** She has publicly backed local journalism and accountability reporting. Specific 2024 to 2026 Pierce County investigative projects were not enumerated in primary sources (UNVERIFIED).

As President and Editor she controls hiring, beat priorities, and who gets the newsroom's nod in local races. Her power is operational and agenda-setting — not equity ownership. She exercises it inside a Chatham Asset Management–owned newsroom. That newsroom faces the cost pressure typical of post-bankruptcy McClatchy.
- **Conflicts of interest (defense-attorney counter-argument expected):** Possible critique: newsroom picks in the main local daily distort democracy. They lift some candidates and silence others. Counter-defense: newsroom picks are a long-standing newspaper tradition. The board that makes them (which Pedersen chairs) operates apart from the newsroom's reporting side, per standard SPJ and Cox principles.
- **The other reading:** In a fragmented media market where many Pierce County voters get news from social media, The News Tribune's sway is smaller than its historic reach. That reading lowers her weight. The reading that elevates Pedersen: News Tribune remains the cited source-of-record for official Pierce County business. That includes council minutes, court filings, and campaign-finance data. Her board's picks are still covered as news by other outlets. tier3 placement at rank 158 fits — she has influence but not authority.

- **Why he is on the map:** Steve Conway is on this map because he holds office, makes decisions, and is well-connected. ## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why it's on the map:** Sumner-Bonney Lake School District (SBLSD) is a Title 28A state law (RCW) public school district. It serves about 10,000 students in eastern Pierce County. That includes the cities of Sumner and Bonney Lake plus nearby unincorporated areas. It is included for two reasons. First, it makes decisions — it adopts its own budget, levies local property taxes through voter-approved EP&O and Capital levies, and signs contracts with its employees. Second, it is well-connected — it is one of about 15 Pierce County school districts that talks to the County Council about tax collection and to state legislators about funding formulas.
- **Neighbors NOT added to the map:** Bethel, Puyallup, Dieringer, White River, Orting, and Carbonado school districts are peer districts mapped on their own. - **Governing law:** Title 28A RCW. The state's Superintendent of Public Instruction (OSPI) oversees it. The Washington State Board of Education sets learning standards.
- **Board structure:** 5-member Board of Directors. Each is elected from one of 5 director districts. Each serves a 4-year term. Board duties per the district: check progress toward district goals, watch the budget, adopt instructional programs, approve hiring and union contracts, and link families, schools, and the community.
- **Executive leadership:** Superintendent Dr. Laurie Dent, effective July 1, 2016. She earned a doctorate from Northwest Nazarene University in 2018. She got her superintendent certificate from WSU in 2016. She was named 2013 Pierce County Principal of the Year while principal of Liberty Ridge Elementary.
- **Operating posture:** SBLSD publicly posts its budget presentations, monthly budget-status reports, Annual Financial Reports, and enrollment reporting on its website. That fits the OSPI-required reporting.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power from the law (FACT):** As a Washington public school district under Title 28A RCW, SBLSD is a junior taxing district. Pierce County collects property taxes for it. It can: (a) run a public K-12 system, (b) levy voter-approved local excess levies (EP&O and Capital Project levies) under RCW 84.52.053, (c) adopt annual budgets, (d) sign union contracts, and (e) issue bonds with voter approval.
- **Local-levy power (FACT):** Per the district's February 2024 levy Q&A: "The levy accounts for 16 percent of the district's overall budget. The average levy increase in a four-year levy would be $11.31 a month ($136 annually)." This is the district's main local fiscal lever above state funding.
- **Budget size (FACT):** The district's 2025–26 general-fund budget is $136.5 million per the district's Budget page. Spending categories per the FY2022–23 summary: Regular Instruction $78.1M, Special Education $16.6M, CTE $4M, Compensatory Education $6.8M, Community Services $2.6M, and Support Services $28.1M.
- **Hiring power (FACT):** The Board of Directors hires and supervises the Superintendent, approves all hiring decisions, and approves union contracts. The Board is the district's ultimate employer of record.

 - **inst ↔ econ:** SBLSD is one of the largest employers in Sumner and Bonney Lake. The annual budget is about $136.5M and payroll is the biggest line.
 - **inst ↔ community:** Union bargaining shapes teacher and staff pay across all district schools.

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** Sumner-Bonney Lake School District is a Title 28A RCW public K-12 district with a $136.5M general-fund budget (2025–26). It serves about 9,900 to 10,000 students across Sumner, Bonney Lake, and unincorporated east Pierce County. Its discretionary fiscal power comes from voter-approved local excess levies (EP&O and Capital Project / Technology). The district says those levies fund 16% of its total budget. The rest comes from state funding. Its hiring power is significant locally: the 5-member Board hires and supervises the Superintendent, adopts the annual budget, and approves union contracts.
- **Conflicts of interest:** Three flags. (1) The Board is elected from 5 director districts. But Board members represent the whole district, not just their sub-area. So one Board member from a small area can sway district-wide policy. (2) Local levy money is collected through Pierce County. That creates a fiscal dependency on county collection accuracy and timing. (3) The district's reliance on local levies (about 16% of total) makes it vulnerable to state-funding-formula changes. When the state underfunds basic education, the district must turn to voters for relief. That is a structural pressure, not a discretionary one.
- **The other reading:** A defense-attorney reading would say SBLSD is procedurally constrained. Board meetings follow the Open Public Meetings Act. Budgets and AFRs are posted publicly. Levy votes are public elections. The Board's power is set by statute, not by choice. The Superintendent and staff operate under policies adopted by an elected board. The opposing reading: school-board elections in Pierce County usually draw very low turnout (often under 25% even in contested races). So the actual power of a Board member is closer to that of an appointed official than a competitive elected one. Incumbents rarely face a real challenge. Union-aligned candidates (SBL EA, Puget Sound Energy (PSE), and others) face a friendly field. The levy dependency on Pierce County Council collection is a passive but real board overlap.
- **Confidence:** High. Structural facts (Board makeup, Superintendent, levy share, budget size, statutory framework) match the district's own website with multiple pages. FY2022–23 spending matches the Budget Summary page. The February 2024 levy outcome (yes/no vote tally) is UNVERIFIED in this pass.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- Pierce County Superior Court is on this map for two reasons: it holds office, and it makes big decisions. It is the only trial court in Pierce County with full authority over serious cases. Its judges hear all felonies, big civil cases over about $100,000, real estate fights, tax disputes, divorce, and probate. It also hears appeals from lower courts.
- The judges are elected. They have wide power to decide sentences, civil awards, and family cases.
- Pierce County District Court is on the map as a separate node. State appeals courts are mapped separately. The county clerk's office is not on the map because it only keeps records.

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** Pierce County Superior Court
- **Entity type:** Government — a trial court with full jurisdiction, part of the state court system
- **Governing law:** Washington State Constitution Art. IV § 6; state law (RCW) 2.08 and 2.12; Pierce County's own local rules
- **Tax ID number (EIN) or business registration:** N/A (government entity)
- **Parent and related bodies:** Part of Washington's state court system. Pierce County pays for the building, staff, and operations. The State of Washington pays the judges' salaries.
- **Locations:** Main courthouse at 930 Tacoma Ave S., Tacoma. Juvenile Court at Remann Hall, 5501 6th Ave., Tacoma.

## 2. Their career and offices
- **Presiding Judge:** Susan Adams (Dept. 11). Elected May 2020. She is the Presiding Judge-Elect for 2025–2026. She sits on the Executive Committee. She chairs the Civil Protection Order Committee. She is a Trustee of the Superior Court Judges Association.
- **Court Administrator:** Chris Gaddis (handles press for court news).
- **Deputy Court Executive (Juvenile Court):** Hiring search underway, posted July 2026.
- **Full judge roster (23 judges):** The court has 23 elected judges across 23 departments. The 2025 group photo lists: Stanley Rumbaugh, Philip Sorensen, Michael Schwartz, Grant Blinn, Karena Kirkendoll (retired March 2026), Shelly Moss, Timothy Ashcraft, Sabrina Ahrens, Alicia Burton, Clarence Henderson Jr., Matthew Thomas, Susan Adams, Diana Kiesel, Thomas Quinlan, Andre Peñalver, Jennifer Andrews, Joseph Evans, Angelica Williams, TaTeasha Davis, Philip Thornton, Rebecca Reeder, Ingrid McLeod, and Scott Peters.
- **Commissioners:** 10 court commissioners. They handle specific matters like emergency orders, juvenile cases, probate, and protection orders. Hannah Gurewitz was hired in May 2026.
- **Board overlap:** Stanley Rumbaugh appears in the power graph as a separate node (weight 4, judge). No other judges are graph nodes today.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Statutory authority:** The state constitution gives the court full power over felonies, serious civil cases, real estate title fights, tax legality, divorce, probate, and naturalization. It can issue court orders to compel witnesses, review lower courts, and free wrongfully held people. Source: WA Constitution Art. IV § 6.
- **Size and reach:** Pierce County has about 920,000 people. The court is the second-busiest superior court in Washington State, behind only King County. Judges set sentences in felony cases, order civil remedies, and decide family and probate cases.
- **How judges are chosen:** All 23 judges are elected in nonpartisan contests. They serve four-year terms. If a seat opens between elections, the governor appoints a replacement from a list vetted by the county bar association. No judge can serve past age 75.
- **Cases and enforcement:** The court hears felony cases brought by the Pierce County Prosecuting Attorney (`pa-office`/Mary Robnett). It also hears major civil cases, family law, and probate. Judges enforce orders through contempt powers, court orders, and sentencing. Specific yearly case numbers are not published in an easy-to-find place.

| Who wins | Parties with better-paid lawyers; the PA's office in criminal cases; repeat institutional players like insurance companies and government agencies. Judge Stanley Rumbaugh won the WSAJ 2026 Judge of the Year award. | #5, #9 |

## 4. Their money
- **2026–2027 biennial budget (Pierce County):** Superior Court: $51.7M. Juvenile Court: $54.9M. Assigned Counsel (free lawyers for poor defendants): $50.3M. Together, courts and legal services make up about 8% of county spending. Public safety is 18%. The General Fund ($967.4M) pays about 76% of law enforcement, courts, and justice costs.
- **Funding sources:** Pierce County's General Fund pays for buildings, staff, operations, and assigned counsel. Washington State pays judge salaries, set by law based on county size. Filing fees and court costs recover some costs. The state also funds specific programs like therapeutic courts.
- **Tax status:** N/A (government entity)
- **Property holdings:** County-City Building (930 Tacoma Ave S.) and Remann Hall (5501 6th Ave.) — both county-owned.
- **Levy/bond history:** The court cannot issue its own levy or bond. The County Council approves its budget.

## 5. How they touch government
- **Pierce County Council** (`county-council`): Approves the court's budget (weight 5 in graph). The council does not run court operations, but it sets the funding level.
- **Governor of Washington** (`bob-ferguson`): Fills judicial vacancies (weight 5). Gov. Ferguson, elected Nov 2024, appoints to vacancies in counties over 100,000 people.
- **Pierce County Prosecuting Attorney** (`pa-office` / Mary Robnett `mary-robnett`): The PA prosecutes all felony cases in the court (weight 5/4). This is the most common government contact — the PA files most of the court's criminal cases.
- **Keith Swank** (`keith-swank`): Listed in the graph as "enforces" (weight 4). Likely a law enforcement officer who carries out court orders. UNVERIFIED in this pass.
- **Federal District Court (WDWA/Tacoma)** (`federal-district-court`): Federal review of state convictions through habeas corpus petitions (weight 3).
- **Court of Appeals Division II** (`court-appeals`): Hears appeals from Superior Court (weight 4).

- **Other oversight:** The Washington Supreme Court oversees court administration. The State Court Administrator's Office and the Commission on Judicial Conduct handle discipline.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- The Tacoma City Council is on the map for two reasons: it holds office, and it makes big decisions. It governs Tacoma (about 220,000 residents), the biggest city in the county and the county's economic core.
- The council writes city laws, adopts a two-year budget of about $4.7 billion, and confirms the mayor's top appointments. Tacoma uses a council-manager system. The council sets policy. The city manager runs the city.
- The council sits on screens at places like the Pierce Transit Board, Sound Transit Board, and the Tacoma-Pierce County Board of Health. This makes it a key power node.
- Not on the map: the city manager (executes policy, appointed by council). The city attorney (gives legal advice). Individual council members get their own pages where they matter (Anders Ibsen, Kristina Walker). Advisory boards and ethics boards do not make decisions.

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** Tacoma City Council (City of Tacoma)
- **Entity type:** Government — city council (the law-making body of a first-class city)
- **Governing law:** Tacoma City Charter (set up the council-manager system in 1952); state law (RCW) 35 (cities and towns); Tacoma Municipal Code
- **Tax ID number (EIN) or registration:** N/A (government entity)
- **Parent and related bodies:** The City of Tacoma — an independent city government. It is not under Pierce County.
- **Meeting location:** Tacoma Municipal Building, 747 Market Street, 1st Floor, Tacoma, WA 98402
- **Website:** tacoma.gov/government/departments/city-council

## 2. Their career and offices
- **Structure:** 9-member council: 1 Mayor + 5 District Council Members + 3 At-Large Council Members
- **Government type:** Council-Manager (since 1952). The council sets policy and appoints the city manager, who runs city operations.
- **Current roster (as of Aug 2026):**

- **Joe Bushnell**: Position 5. Deputy Mayor. Vice Chair of Government Performance and Finance Committee. Vice Chair of Economic Development Committee.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Statutory authority:** The council writes city laws, adopts the two-year budget, confirms mayoral picks (city manager, police chief, department heads), and controls land-use rules (zoning, permits, subarea plans). The mayor can veto council laws. Six of nine council members can override a veto.
- **Budget control:** The 2025–2026 two-year budget is $4.7 billion total. The General Fund faces a projected $40M structural deficit. Priority-based budget is $2B of $4.7B. The council approves the budget the mayor proposes.
- **Appointment powers:** The council confirms mayoral picks for city manager, police chief, fire chief, and department director jobs. The mayor appoints committee members and chairs, subject to council approval.
- **Jurisdiction:** City of Tacoma (about 220,000 residents, about 62 square miles). Tacoma is the county's largest city. Its policy choices on land use, economic development, and public safety affect the whole region.
- **Domain overlaps:** Government (law-making, budget), Economic (economic development policy, business rules), Political (elected officials, campaign networks), Institutional (board seats on regional bodies).

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |

| Who benefits | Residents of Tacoma (about 220,000) get city services funded by the budget. Businesses benefit from economic development policy and zoning decisions. Developers benefit from land-use approvals. Contractors benefit from city contracts. | #3, #8, #9 |
| Who sits | 9 elected officials (mayor + 8 council members). 5 standing committees, each with 4 members plus 1 alternate. The mayor appoints committee members, confirmed by the council. | #1, #6, #7 |
| Who governs | The council as a body adopts laws and the budget. The mayor proposes the budget and chairs meetings. The city manager runs policy. Committee chairs (Rumbaugh, Diaz, Hines, Walker) control policy pipelines. | #6, #7, #10 |
| Who wins | Groups that show up to testify and lobby (labor, business, environmental groups). Developers with land-use proposals before the council. Connect Tacoma levy (Prop 1, $200M) passed by voters in Aug 2026 after council action. | #3, #8, #11 |

## 4. Their money
- **2025–2026 biennial budget:** $4.7 billion total (approved Dec 10, 2024). Priority-based budget: $2B of $4.7B. The rest includes internal funds, utility funds, and debt service.
- **General Fund:** Faces a projected $40M structural deficit. Expenses are about $2.5M higher than expected. Revenues are about $3.5M below projections. The city has done a mid-biennium budget adjustment (Mid-Mod) to close the gap.
- **Funding sources:** Sales tax, property tax, utility taxes, business licenses, intergovernmental revenues (state and federal grants), user fees, and the Connect Tacoma levy ($200M over 10 years plus $120M in grants, approved Aug 2026).
- **Tax status:** N/A (the council is itself a taxing body)
- **Property holdings:** City-owned buildings, parks, roads, and infrastructure. Specific portfolio UNVERIFIED.
- **Levy/bond history:** Connect Tacoma: Safe Streets and Sidewalks Levy (Proposition 1) — 10-year, $200M levy approved by voters Aug 4, 2026. Past levies UNVERIFIED in this pass.

- **Verdict:** The Tacoma City Council controls a $4.7B two-year budget and makes laws for the county's biggest city. The council's power works through the full body passing laws, adopting the budget, and confirming mayoral picks. In the council-manager system, the council sets direction while the manager runs it — so the council's power is agenda-setting and oversight, not administration. Council members' seats on regional boards (Pierce Transit, Sound Transit, Board of Health) extend the council's reach beyond city limits. The $40M General Fund deficit limits new spending.

That makes it slow and consensus-driven, with limited ability to act fast. The mayor's veto (overridden by 6/9) is a weak tool. The $40M deficit caps new spending. fields.graph_description: Housing authority administering federal vouchers, public housing, and redevelopment in Tacoma.
fields.profile:
## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- THA is the main public housing agency for the City of Tacoma. It runs thousands of housing units. It also hands out federal housing vouchers. It is a key partner in big city projects like Salishan. Its choices shape land use, affordable housing, and community growth across Pierce County's largest city.
- THA is on the map because it has power from running a big organization. It controls federal housing money and a large redevelopment budget.
- A few related groups sit outside this map. Pierce County runs its own housing programs in a different area. Lakewood and Bremerton have their own housing agencies. They do not work inside Pierce County's main power structure, so they are left out.

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** Housing Authority of the City of Tacoma. It does business as Tacoma Housing Authority, also called THA.
- **Entity type:** THA is a public housing agency. It is a part of government. It was set up under Washington state law. It is not a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. It is not an LLC. It is a quasi-governmental agency.
- **Governing law:** A Washington state law says THA must have a five-person Board of Commissioners. The Mayor of Tacoma picks each member. They serve five-year terms. Since 1998, one of the five members must be a current THA housing aid recipient (Source 1).
- **tax ID number (EIN):** UNVERIFIED — could not find the EIN in public records.
- **Parent/subsidiaries:** THA has no parent group. It runs as an independent agency. It manages tax-credit partnerships, like Hillside Terrace and Bay Terrace, through its property arm.
- **MTW designation:** THA takes part in the Moving to Work (MTW) program. This is run by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Only a few agencies nationwide get this status. It lets THA design its own housing plans (Source 6).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power held — statutory authority:** THA has the legal power to run housing aid programs in Tacoma. It manages federal HUD money. It runs public housing units. It gives out Housing Choice Vouchers (HCVs). It controls about 3,552 Section 8 vouchers. It also gives out special vouchers: VASH, FUP, FYI, NHT, and EHV (Source 4).
- **Market share / scale:** THA is the biggest housing authority in Pierce County. Its Board adopted the FY2026 budget on January 28, 2026. The FY2022 budget had about $55.3 million in revenue and $50.8 million in spending. It added 57 new Project-Based Voucher units (Source 5). The FY2026 budget covers departments: Asset Management & Real Estate Development ($4,081,892), Client Support & Empowerment ($2,954,327), Executive ($904,800), Finance ($2,733,284) (Source 2).
- **Redevelopment authority:** THA ran the largest housing redevelopment in Tacoma's history. It was the $200 million Salishan project. THA tore down 855 public housing units from the World War II era. It then rebuilt a mixed-income neighborhood on 188 acres. HUD gave THA a $35 million HOPE VI grant in 2001. THA picked Lorig Associates as its development partner (Source 7).
- **Budget controlled:** THA controls an annual operating budget in the tens of millions. Most of the money comes from HUD. Monthly cash payments were $11,792,969 in November 2025 (Source 2).
- **Appointment/veto powers:** The Board of Commissioners approves the yearly budget. It signs off on contracts and payments. It hires and fires the Executive Director. It sets policy. The Mayor of Tacoma picks the Board members. So the Mayor has indirect control over THA through these picks.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Low-income Tacoma residents who receive THA housing assistance (vouchers, public housing units); developers who partner with THA on redevelopment projects (e.g., Lorig Associates, 1DROP, LMC Construction). | 3, 7 |
| Who sits | Board of Commissioners: Stanley Rumbaugh (Chair, attorney, former Pierce County Superior Court judge); Dr. Minh-Anh Hodge (Vice Chair, Tacoma School District administrator); Athena Dunn (Commissioner, public health advocate, appointed 2025); Rev. Ronelle Jones (Commissioner, pastor, appointed 2026); Nathe Lawver (Commissioner, Pierce County Central Labor Council AFL-CIO Secretary-Treasurer). | 1 |
| Who governs | Executive Director April Black (first woman to lead THA in its 81-year history, appointed 2021; previously Deputy Executive Director for 6 years). Board Chair Stanley Rumbaugh has served on the Board since 1998. | 1, 3 |
| Who wins | THA has successfully secured major federal grants (HOPE VI $35M) and MTW designation. Its development partners benefit from THA-controlled project-based voucher allocations and tax-credit partnerships. Labor is represented on the Board via Nathe Lawver (AFL-CIO). | 1, 7 |

## 5. How they touch government
- **Federal (HUD):** HUD is THA's main funder. THA gets HUD money for Section 8, HCV, public housing, VASH, FUP, FYI, NHT, and EHV vouchers. THA sends its MTW plan to HUD each year for approval. Congress's FY2026 budget gave THA more voucher money (Source 6).
- **City of Tacoma:** The Mayor picks THA Board members. THA works with the city on land use, redevelopment, and community growth.
- **Pierce County Council:** THA works with Pierce County on regional housing, human services, and law and justice issues (connection weight 3).
- **Tacoma City Council:** THA works with the Tacoma City Council on redevelopment projects (connection weight 3).
- **Contracts and grants:** THA partners with private developers on housing redevelopment. Its partners include Lorig Associates, 1DROP, LMC Construction, and Brawner. THA has also gotten state money for supportive housing.
- **Lobbying:** THA lobbies at the federal level through CLPHA, the Council of Large Public Housing Authorities. Executive Director April Black joined the CLPHA board in September 2023 (Source 3).

## 6. Other seats they hold
- **Board overlaps:**
 - Stanley Rumbaugh (Chair) is a founding partner at the law firm Rumbaugh, Rideout, Adkins and Wallace. He is a former Pierce County Superior Court judge. He served 10 years on the Bates Technical College Board of Trustees. He is a World Trade Council director. He sits on the WA State Association for Justice Board of Governors.
 - Dr. Minh-Anh Hodge (Vice Chair) directs Second Language Acquisition, Elementary Education and Leadership at Tacoma Public Schools.
 - Nathe Lawver (Commissioner) is Secretary-Treasurer of the Pierce County Central Labor Council AFL-CIO. He is a member of LiUNA Laborers' Local 252. He chairs United Way of Pierce County. He sits on the Pierce County Workforce Board, the Greater Tacoma Community Foundation Executive Board, and the Pierce County Economic Development Board.
 - Rev. Ronelle Jones (Commissioner) is Senior Pastor at True Vine Community Church COGIC. She is International VP of the COGIC Youth Department.
- **Executive Director board overlaps:** April Black joined the CLPHA Board of Directors in September 2023. She had been THA Deputy Executive Director for six years under longtime Executive Director Michael Mirra.
- **Development partnerships:** Lorig Associates worked on Salishan. 1DROP, LMC Construction, and Brawner worked on the Salishan-Hillside renovation in 2026.

- Inclusion rule: **well-connected + decision-making**. Tacoma Police Union Local #6, I.U.P.A. is the certified union for Tacoma police officers, detectives, and sergeants. It bargains with the city. It also gives money to local campaigns. The graph links it directly to Kelly Chambers ($2,400). That puts Local 6 on the Pierce County political-power map.
- Adjacent but excluded: Tacoma Police Management Association Local #26 (sergeants and lieutenants). Tacoma Firefighters Union Local 31 ("Active in Democracy" PAC). AFSCME and SEIU 1199NW (other unions). All are labor actors, but they are not the same node.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Tacoma Police Union Local #6, I.U.P.A. (International Union of Police Associations).
- **Entity type:** Labor union. Local chapter of IUPA. Also linked with Washington Council of Police and Sheriffs (WACOPS).
- **tax ID number (EIN) / UBI:** No public 501(c)(5) EIN verified in the federal tax agency (IRS) files (UNVERIFIED). Unions under 29 U.S.C. § 159 are usually 501(c)(5) tax-exempt.
- **Address:** PO Box 11265, Tacoma, WA 98411-1265 (per union website).
- **Phone / email:** 253-272-2119; tacomalocal6@gmail.com.
- **Bargaining unit:** Sworn officers, detectives, and sergeants below lieutenant. Lieutenants and above are in Tacoma Police Management Association Local #26.
- **Governing law:** state law (RCW) 41.76 (police collective bargaining in Washington). The 2024–2026 contract is the current deal.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Domain = political.** State law gives Local 6 the sole right to bargain for its unit. The union also runs a Political Action Committee (PAC) that funds local campaigns.
- **Statutory authority:** Under RCW 41.76, Local 6 is the sole certified representative for its unit. The city must meet and confer on wages, hours, and working conditions. The 2024–2026 collective bargaining agreement (CBA) runs Jan 1, 2024 – Dec 31, 2026 (filed by City of Tacoma HR/Labor Relations).
- **Market / political power:**
 - Runs a registered Tacoma Police Union PAC. It gives direct contributions under the Washington $1,200-per-candidate local-election cap (per News Tribune 2021 PAC analysis).
 - Records show a $1,000 contribution to a Tacoma City Council candidate in 2018. The $2,400 to Kelly Chambers (Council District 1 / Pierce County Council) is the specific edge in our graph.
 - Endorsements and public statements from President Henry Betts appear on KING 5, the Jason Rantz show, and KNKX. He has criticized Police Chief Avery Moore. These moves shape the public-safety story in local news cycles.
- **Key facts answers:**
 - **Who is funded and endorsed:** Kelly Chambers (graph edge), past council candidates (per News Tribune 2021). Full 2024 endorsement list is UNVERIFIED.
 - **PAC spending:** No standalone summary on the state campaign-finance agency (PDC) page (UNVERIFIED on totals, but individual contributions are verified through secondary reporting).
 - **Party-machinery control:** None. Police labor usually leans Republican, but Local 6 has backed both parties in primaries. Not a partisan-machine actor.
 - **Candidate recruitment / training output:** None documented.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- Tacoma Public Utilities (TPU) is the city’s electric, water, and rail company. It serves about 187,000 homes and businesses across central Pierce County, including Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM), the big military base near Tacoma.
- TPU is on this map for four reasons: it holds a public office (the city gave it the right to be the only electric and water provider in its area); it makes big decisions (its board sets rates and runs the city’s largest budget); it has a long record (130 years in operation); and it is well-connected (its CEO sits on national utility boards, and its rail arm moves freight for the Port of Tacoma).
- **Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates:** The 5-member Public Utility Board is not a separate node — it is covered below as the group that governs TPU. Tacoma City Council is a separate node. Puget Sound Energy (PSE) is the main private power company in the region and is mapped on its own. The state’s utility regulator (the Washington Utilities and Transportation Commission, or UTC) is excluded — TPU is not under it. The Tacoma-Pierce County Economic Development Board (EDB) is a separate node. Click! Network was TPU’s cable and internet arm — UNVERIFIED whether it still operates under TPU after the 2024 sale.

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** Tacoma Public Utilities. It is a department of the City of Tacoma. Its three divisions are Tacoma Power, Tacoma Water, and Tacoma Rail.
- **Entity type:** A department of city government, not a private company. Voters created it in 1893 when they bought out a private firm called Tacoma Light & Water Company. It does not aim to make a profit for owners. It runs on money from the bills customers pay, not from taxes.
- **Tax ID (EIN)/registration:** It uses the City of Tacoma’s EIN. There is no separate EIN because it is a city department, not its own company.
- **Parent/subsidiaries:** The parent is the City of Tacoma. The three operating divisions are Tacoma Power (electricity), Tacoma Water (drinking water), and Tacoma Rail (a short freight railroad serving the Port of Tacoma, Lakeview, and the Frederickson industrial area).
- **Ownership chain:** Public. The City of Tacoma owns it. There are no private shareholders. Money left over goes back into the system.
- **Governing law:** The Tacoma City Charter and Washington State laws on city utilities. The state regulator (UTC) does not oversee TPU because it is a city utility.
- **Founded:** 1893, when voters bought the old private company. The first big dam (Mayfield Dam) came online in 1929. The rail division was added later.
- **Headquarters:** Public Utilities Building, 3628 South 35th Street, Tacoma, WA 98409.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power held:** TPU has the power of a city-owned monopoly. In its service area, it is the only legal electric, water, and rail provider. It is the largest department in Tacoma’s city government. Its power comes from: the city charter (the law that gives it the franchise); market share (about 187,000 customers over a 180 square-mile electric service area); self-rule (it answers to the City Council, not the state regulator); its wires and dams (2,286 miles of power lines plus a large hydro dam system); and freight rail (it runs the trains in and out of the Port of Tacoma, a key shipping hub).
- **Government domain overlap:** TPU is a government body that also acts like a big business. It collects its own money (about $1.2 billion a year in the 2025–2026 budget). Its board and the City Council approve its budget. It spends money on pipes, wires, and rails across Pierce County.
- **Budget:** About $1.2 billion a year for 2025–2026 (a two-year budget). Tacoma Power alone reported $516.5 million in operating revenue in 2024.
- **Jobs controlled:** Between 1,001 and 5,000 workers (the LinkedIn range). Tacoma Power alone has about 805 workers. Citywide, the utility had about 1,777 workers in 2018.
- **Rate authority:** The 5-member Public Utility Board recommends rates and the budget. The Tacoma City Council gives final approval. For 2025–2026, the Council approved a 6.5% electric rate hike and a 6.3% water rate hike.
- **Land/real-estate:** TPU owns a set of old dams (Mayfield, Cushman, and others), 2,286 miles of power lines (1,524 above ground, 862 below), and rail track in and around the Port of Tacoma and Frederickson.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | TPU’s 166,000–187,000 customers get not-for-profit electric, water, and rail service. A typical home pays about $100 a month for power. JBLM and large factories get steady, publicly owned power. The Port of Tacoma relies on Tacoma Rail to move freight. | #1, #2, #3 |
| Who sits | TPU’s CEO is Jackie Flowers (since 2018). The 5-member Public Utility Board is nominated by the Mayor and approved by the City Council. Flowers also serves on the steering committee of the Large Public Power Council, co-chairs the American Public Power Association (APPA) Climate Change Task Force, chairs the Grid Forward Board, and sits on the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber and EDB boards. | #4, #5 |
| Who governs | The Public Utility Board sets rates and policy for Tacoma Power, Water, and Rail. The Tacoma City Council gives final budget approval (state law requires it). Through Tacoma Rail, TPU controls freight movement at the Port of Tacoma — a key bottleneck. TPU’s big project choices (dams, the Click! Network sale, new meters) shape Pierce County’s infrastructure for decades. | #2, #3, #4 |
| Who wins | TPU customers win from not-for-profit rates. Big commercial and industrial users win from steady power. The City of Tacoma wins because TPU is its biggest department and supports the local economy. The 2025–2026 rate hike passed the Council without big fights — TPU’s rate-setting power keeps winning there. | #1, #3 |

## 9. Who they are connected to
- Graph connections (from `evidence/29-power-graph-v2.json`):

| Connected entity | Relationship | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| Pierce County Council (`county-council`) | municipal | 4 |

**Network analysis:** TPU has only a few listed ties, but the ties it has are strong. Its link to PSE (weight 2) matters because TPU (public, customer-owned) and PSE (private, foreign-pension-owned) are structural opposites — they cover different areas of Pierce County and only meet at the borders. Its link to the Pierce County Council (weight 4) reflects shared work on water service for unincorporated areas, power lines, and rail rights-of-way. The graph undercounts two big ties: the Port of Tacoma (Tacoma Rail is its freight arm — weight UNVERIFIED in the graph) and JBLM (TPU is JBLM’s electric provider — weight UNVERIFIED). TPU’s rank (77/163) understates its power: a $1.2 billion city utility is bigger than most other economic groups on this map.

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** Tacoma Public Utilities runs the city’s electric, water, and rail service for about 187,000 customers across central Pierce County. It has a $1.2 billion two-year budget and between 1,001 and 5,000 workers. Its power comes from being the only legal provider in its area (a city monopoly since 1893) and from owning 2,286 miles of power lines, a set of dams, and the freight railroad at the Port. It answers to its own Public Utility Board and the Tacoma City Council — not the state regulator — which gives it more freedom to set rates than private utilities like PSE have.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags:** TPU’s not-for-profit setup shields it from some abuses private utilities face, but it also answers to no outside rate regulator. CEO Jackie Flowers sits on several outside boards (Large Public Power Council, APPA, Grid Forward, the Chamber, the EDB). She runs TPU and also sits on regional boards that push for the same industrial customers TPU serves — a possible conflict. The defense: utility CEOs often hold such seats to represent their city in national policy. The Public Utility Board’s 5-year appointed terms (not elected) keep rate decisions away from voters. That is good for expertise, but limits public say. The 2025–2026 6.5% rate hike passed without a fight, showing the current setup usually goes TPU’s way.
- **Analysis of alternatives:** The opposing view is that TPU is held in check by the City Council’s budget approval, by public-notice rules, and by customers’ option to move (limited — there is no other electric provider in the area). Under this reading, TPU is a well-run public utility with proper checks. But the 2024–2025 rate cycle shows a different picture: TPU’s board approved the rate hike on October 23, 2024, and the City Council approved the budget in November 2024. Both votes were largely pro-forma, with no real changes. The real story is that TPU has far more freedom to set rates than its private peer PSE has before the UTC.
- **Confidence:** Medium-High. TPU’s legal form, governing setup, leadership, customer base, and rate process are confirmed by primary TPU and City of Tacoma sources (reliability 0.95), backed by Wikipedia (reliability 0.8). Tacoma Power’s 2024 operating revenue ($516.5M) comes from a primary financial report. Main unverified items: TPU’s specific Pierce County land holdings, the exact number of rail customers Tacoma Rail served in 2024, and Click! Network’s status after the 2024 sale (UNVERIFIED).

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Inclusion rule:** Tacoma Public Schools (TPS) is on this map because it holds office and makes decisions. It is the largest school district in Pierce County. It has 28,272 students across 69 schools (2023-24). It runs a large budget (with a $30M shortfall for 2025-26) and hires hundreds of staff. Its elected board sets education policy for tens of thousands of families. The superintendent, Josh Garcia, is one of the highest-paid public officials in Tacoma at $342,038 (per OpenPayrolls). The district's school-bond link with Pierce County Council (graph edge weight 4) and its partnership with MultiCare Health (weight 3) spread its reach into county finance and healthcare.
- **Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates:** Puyallup School District is the second-largest in the county and is a separate entity. Franklin Pierce Schools is a separate district (linked through Lance Goodpaster on the Greater Tacoma Community Foundation board). Bethel School District is separate. Clover Park School District is separate (linked through Alice Phillips). These districts are outside the boundary at the current tier.

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** Tacoma Public Schools (also Tacoma School District No. 10)
- **Entity type:** Public school district (government entity)
- **Location:** Central Administration Building, 601 South 8th Street, Tacoma, WA 98405 (sources #1, #5)
- **Governing law:** state law (RCW) 28A (Common School Code); Washington State Board of Education rules; Tacoma School Board policies
- **EIN / registration:** N/A — government entity, not a separately registered organization
- **Parent:** None; independent school district run by an elected board
- **Board composition:** 5 members, elected at-large to 6-year terms (sources #2, #3)

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Statutory authority:** As a public school district, TPS can levy taxes (with voter-approved bonds and levies), run schools, hire and fire staff, set curriculum, and manage facilities. The board approves budgets and sets policy.
- **Budget and fiscal power:** TPS is facing a $30 million shortfall for the 2025-26 school year, which means "major position eliminations" (source #4). A $10 million shortfall is projected for 2026-27 (source #4). The district's budget process has public hearings and board votes, giving the board real fiscal power.
- **Enrollment and scale:** 28,272 students across 69 schools (2023-24). Minority enrollment 70%. About 43.1% of students are economically disadvantaged (source #6). That makes TPS the largest educational institution in Pierce County.
- **Superintendent power:** Superintendent Josh Garcia runs day-to-day operations. His salary is about $342,038 (source #7). That makes him one of the highest-paid public officials in the region. His three-year contract started at $292,750 when he was first hired in 2012 (source #8).
- **Domain overlaps:** Institutional (education), political (elected board, bond elections), economic (major employer, budget authority), health (MultiCare partnership).

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why it is on the map:** Tacoma Weekly is one of a few print news outlets that cover Pierce County government and local politics. It is on the map for two reasons. First, it is named in Washington State Public Disclosure Commission (PDC) actions. That shows a paper-trail link to political coverage. Second, it serves as a low-cost place to publish legal notices. The City of Tacoma runs some legal ads in it. It is part of the legal-notice system in Pierce County.
- **Other papers NOT on this map:** The News Tribune (Tacoma's daily paper, owned by McClatchy). KING 5 / KOMO / KCPQ (Seattle-Tacoma TV stations). The Stranger and Seattle Weekly (Seattle papers that sometimes cover Pierce County). Tacoma Ledger and other newer digital outlets. Gig Harbor Now (a separate small paper on the Key Peninsula).

## 1. Who they are
- **Name:** Tacoma Weekly (newspaper).
- **Type:** A for-profit community newspaper.
- **Owner:** Matt Nagle is the publisher and editor. The paper comes out under Pierce County Community Newspaper Group (PCCNG). PCCNG calls itself "a locally owned and operated newspaper organization."
- **Address:** P.O. Box 7185, Tacoma, WA 98417.
- **History:** Started in 1987 as the Tacoma Monthly. Renamed Tacoma Weekly in 1994. Has used broadsheet format since 2001.
- **Old owner:** John Weymer was the prior publisher. Weymer had over $170,000 in court judgments against him and his business since 1995. His business paid $9,157.06 in wage-theft claims to the Washington Department of Labor and Industries (L&I) over two years. In 2019 a judge ruled Weymer owed $5,000 to the Grand Cinema for failing to deliver a paid printing job.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Reach (FACT):** About 10,000 copies each week. Distributed on Wednesdays to "hundreds of businesses and public spaces in the Tacoma area."
- **Legal notices (FACT):** Tacoma Weekly runs a "Submit Legals" portal. Governments and people can publish legal notices there. That is a quasi-official role under Washington newspaper-of-record laws.
- **Editorial problems (FACT):** In September 2021, the Washington State Public Disclosure Commission (PDC) fined Tacoma Weekly $15,000. The PDC found the paper offered political candidates a news story or endorsement in exchange for money. The paper ran cover stories for two paying candidates under a staff member's byline without saying they were paid ads. This kind of finding raises real questions about Tacoma Weekly's reliability as a news source.
- **Editor and owner (FACT):** Publisher Matt Nagle is also the editor. Editorial and ownership are in one person.
- **Domain overlap:**
 - **Media and government:** Legal notices, political coverage, and the 2021 PDC fine put the paper at the meeting point of local government, elections, and campaign-finance rules.
 - **Media and business:** A small for-profit paper. Its payroll and contracts have been in court (wage-theft claims, the Grand Cinema judgment).
- **FACT vs INFERENCE:** The paper's reach, founding, and PDC fine are FACT. Whether Tacoma Weekly is really a "community newspaper" in the sense of doing solid accountability reporting is INFERENCE. It may be more of a place for legal notices and ads. The sources reviewed do not say directly.

| Who sits | Matt Nagle is publisher and editor. PCCNG is the parent group. Old publisher John Weymer is no longer in that role. | Sources 1, 3 |
| Who governs | Matt Nagle controls editorial and business calls. PCCNG is the publishing body. | Sources 1, 3 |
| Who wins | The 2021 PDC finding shows two paying political candidates got cover-story placement that non-paying candidates did not get. Those two candidates are the documented "winners" of the paper's favor. | Source 1 |

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** Tacoma Weekly is a free weekly community paper with about 10,000 readers a week. It has used broadsheet format since 2001. Matt Nagle is the publisher under the Pierce County Community Newspaper Group (PCCNG). Its real power is (a) a low-cost place for legal notices, and (b) a place where local advertisers and political candidates can buy favorable coverage. The second use was flagged in a 2021 Washington State Public Disclosure Commission action. The PDC fined the paper $15,000 for offering news-story placement to paying candidates without saying so. The paper is on the Pierce County power map not because of a big audience (10,000 is modest) but because legal notices and political access are places where the paper has real say.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags:** The 2021 PDC finding shows a pattern of selling news coverage to political candidates without disclosure. Editorial and revenue were mixed on purpose. This is the main trust concern for any use of Tacoma Weekly as a source of civic news. On top of that, old publisher John Weymer's track record of judgments ($170K+ since 1995, including wage-theft claims and a failed printing job) is a red flag about business practices. Whether current publisher Matt Nagle has kept or fixed those practices is UNVERIFIED.
- **Analysis of alternatives:** A defense reading would say the 2021 PDC fine was a single case settled without admitting broader wrongdoing. The paper kept publishing. Current publisher Matt Nagle is different from old publisher John Weymer. The opposing reading is that the PDC fine is a sign of a structural problem in community-newspaper business models. With no paywall and small ad budgets, the urge to monetize political coverage is built in, not a one-off. A paper whose 2021 conduct included undisclosed paid political coverage should be cross-checked with other outlets before being trusted for any contested civic fact in this investigation.
- **Confidence:** Medium — circulation, founding, format, publisher, and PDC fine verified against Wikipedia and the paper's own website; the Wikipedia article references PDC and court records that were not directly extracted in this pass, so the PDC-fine detail is at one degree of remove from the primary record; UNVERIFIED for the specific 2021 PDC case number and any subsequent PDC actions against the paper under current ownership.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why it is on the map — from holding office / institutional:** Tacoma Community College is on the map as a public college in Pierce County. It has a large budget (about $84M a year). Its Board of Trustees is appointed by the Governor and makes policy. Board members connect the school to major Pierce County power players (MultiCare, United Way, Pierce County Executive's office, Puyallup Tribe). Its inclusion is from holding office (it runs a public institution with a budget and land) and well-connected (board members link it to MultiCare, United Way, Pierce County government, and tribal government) — Laumann, Marsden & Prensky 1983.
- **Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates:** The TCC Foundation (a separate 501(c)(3) supporting organization) is treated as part of TCC, not profiled separately. The Washington State Board for Community and Technical Colleges (SBCTC) is the statewide coordinating body and is excluded as a state-level entity outside Pierce County.

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** Tacoma Community College (also called TCC).
- **Type of entity:** A public community college district. One of 34 community and technical college districts in Washington State. It is a government entity, not a nonprofit or private company.
- **tax ID number (EIN)/registration:** Not publicly available in sources checked. As a public entity, it is part of the Washington State public higher education system.
- **Parent/subsidiaries:** TCC is a standalone college district. It is coordinated by (not a subsidiary of) the Washington State Board for Community and Technical Colleges (SBCTC), which sends state money to individual colleges. The TCC Foundation is a separate 501(c)(3) supporting organization.
- **Ownership:** Public entity of the State of Washington. A 5-member Board of Trustees governs it. The Governor appoints trustees, and the State Senate confirms them.
- **Governing law:** state law (RCW) 28B.50.100. The Board sets and reviews college policies, oversees management, sets direction, approves budgets, and protects the school's finances.
- **Established:** 1965.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Statutory authority:** The Board of Trustees holds authority under RCW 28B.50.100. It sets college policy, approves budgets, sets direction, and oversees management. The Governor appoints trustees to 5-year terms. The State Senate confirms them. This is a Governor appointment — political patronage at the state level.
- **Budget size:** FY2023 total expenses: $83,971,405 (per the TCC FY23 Financial Report). Major categories: instruction ($31,7M), student services ($12.5M), institutional support ($10.1M), operations/maintenance ($9.7M), scholarships/fellowships/aid ($9.3M), academic support ($6.0M), auxiliary enterprises ($4.5M). Net position at end of FY2023: $105.9M.
- **Students:** About 9,912 students (per the FY2023 report). Other sources report different numbers depending on the date and method. TCC serves about 9,000 to 10,000 students a year.
- **Revenue sources:** Per the FY2023 report: 42% state money (through SBCTC), 24% tuition and fees, 19% local funds and grants, 8% auxiliary, 6% other, 1% federal. The state is the largest single source. TCC's budget depends on state legislative choices.
- **Tax status:** Public entity. It does not pay income tax. It is funded through state appropriations (tax dollars), tuition, grants, and auxiliary revenue.
- **Board roster and overlaps:** See Section 6 for board overlaps.
- **Government share of revenue:** About 42% state (the largest source), plus about 1% federal grants and about 19% local/grant funding. Government funding is most of TCC's revenue.

## 5. How they touch government
- **State funding:** TCC's main government link is with the Washington State Legislature (through SBCTC) for biennial budget appropriations. The 2025 Legislature kept $28.6M for the college system. TCC's government relations page tracks legislative requests.
- **Board appointments:** The Governor appoints trustees, and the Senate confirms them. This is a direct political link. Current board members were appointed by Governors Inslee (Bernstein 2017, Ponepinto 2019, Santiago 2022, Wortham 2020) and Ferguson (Strobel 2026).
- **Lobbying:** TCC advocates through its Government Relations office and the Trustees Association of Community and Technical Colleges. Specific lobbying costs are not confirmed.

- **Land use:** TCC's campus development (new buildings, parking, facilities) is subject to local land-use rules. Recent capital projects include the Center for Innovative Learning & Engagement and an EMS lab (per the 2023 annual report).
- **Rules that apply to TCC:** Washington State audit (State Auditor's Office), SBCTC oversight, federal education rules (Title IV financial aid, accreditation), and local building and zoning codes.

## 1. Who they are
- **The bottom line:** Tacoma Community College is a public community college with moderate institutional power. It has an $84M annual budget, about 9,912 students, and a Governor-appointed Board of Trustees. Its power is mostly institutional. It runs a college, a budget, a campus, and a workforce pipeline. It influences policy through its Board. Board members hold overlapping seats with MultiCare (2 members), United Way (CEO as Board Chair), the Pierce County Executive's office (Andrew Strobel), the Puyallup Tribe (Strobel's former role), Tacoma Public Utilities (Wortham), and the WA State LGBTQ Commission (Santiago). The TCC Foundation Board adds more overlaps with KeyBank, BECU, TAPCO Credit Union, and Virginia Mason Franciscan Health. That makes TCC a key institutional link between health care, banking, government, tribal, and nonprofit sectors in Pierce County.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags:** Trustee Andrew Strobel's dual role — Strategic Advisor to Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello AND former Puyallup Tribe Planning Director — could conflict when TCC matters touch county policy or tribal relations. Trustee Lois Bernstein's dual service on the TCC Board of Trustees AND the TCC Foundation Board could blur the line between public governance and private fundraising. Two MultiCare executives on the Foundation Board (Michael McDonald, Dr. Scott Meehan) plus Bernstein (retired MultiCare) create a strong MultiCare-to-TCC overlap — relevant if TCC's health training programs or campus health services touch MultiCare's interests.
- **Analysis of alternatives:** The opposing reading: TCC is a standard community college with standard board appointments. The overlaps reflect the natural makeup of Pierce County civic leadership, not deliberate power-building. Board members are Governor-appointed (not self-selected), and their multi-board service is typical of civic leaders in mid-sized cities. TCC's $84M budget is modest compared to MultiCare ($7.2B) or Joint Base Lewis-McChord ($12.1B impact). TCC is a mid-tier institution, not a power center. Its 42% state funding dependency means its fiscal health is controlled by the Legislature, not by its board.
- **Confidence:** Medium — primary sources (TCC website, WA Governor's office, TCC financial report) confirm the board composition, trustee terms, budget, enrollment, and presidential leadership. The board overlap analysis is based on documented board memberships. The significance of these board overlaps for actual policy influence is inferential — no specific instance of board overlap-driven policy change has been documented. The financial data is from FY2023 and may not reflect current-year figures.

- **open questions & leads:**.
 - Current-year (FY2025 or FY2026) budget and enrollment figures would update the FY2023 data.
 - TCC's specific capital project funding sources (state capital budget vs. local bonds vs. donations) would clarify the funding overlaps.
 - Andrew Strobel's appointment (January 2026) is recent — his impact on board decisions and county-tribal-TCC relations warrants monitoring.
 - The MultiCare-to-TCC board overlap (3 members across Trustee + Foundation boards) and whether TCC's nursing/allied health programs create a training pipeline that benefits MultiCare's workforce needs.
