## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why included:** big member count plus well-connected. Teamsters Local 117 is the largest Teamsters local in Washington, with 19,500 members. Many work in Pierce County, especially as state corrections officers. Joint Council 28 covers 50,000+ members in Washington, Alaska, and Idaho. Both groups back Pierce County candidates. Both are part of the Pierce County Central Labor Council (PCCLC), the local AFL-CIO body. (Sources 1, 3, 5, 6)
- **Who was left out and why:** UFCW 3000, SEIU 925, SEIU 1199NW, and the Washington Education Association (WEA) are other unions. They sit in WSLC/PCCLC but are not Teamsters. Other Teamsters locals (174, 313, 38, 252, 763) are also part of Joint Council 28 but are smaller and less focused on Pierce County.

## 1. Who they are
- **Full legal name:** Teamsters Local Union No. 117. It is part of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters (IBT).
- **Type:** Labor union. Tax status: 501(c)(5), a tax-exempt labor group under the U.S. tax code.
- **Parent:** International Brotherhood of Teamsters (IBT), based in Washington, D.C.
- **Regional group:** Teamsters Joint Council No. 28 (JC 28), in Tukwila, WA. It links Teamsters locals in Washington, Alaska, and the Idaho Panhandle. It has 50,000+ members. (Sources 6, 7)
- **Local 117 HQ:** 14675 Interurban Ave S, Suite 301, Tukwila, WA 98168. (Source 7)
- **JC 28 HQ:** Same address. Phone: (206) 441-7470. (Source 7)
- **Local 313 (Tacoma):** 220 S. 27th St., Tacoma, WA 98402. Phone: (253) 627-0103. This is the direct Teamsters base in Pierce County. (Source 8)

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Members give them weight.** Local 117 speaks for 19,500 workers in Washington, both public and private jobs. That includes 6,000+ state corrections officers (DOC), plus nurses, maintenance, and office staff. (Sources 3, 4)
- **They bargain contracts.** The local holds contracts covering Washington State DOC workers (2023–2025 contract on file), freight drivers, and public safety staff. In April 2025 they won the top regional pay for fuel truck drivers under the APP/World Kinect deal. (Sources 4, 6)
- **They play politics.** They run a federal PAC (a political action committee that raises and spends money on elections) called DRIVE, funded by voluntary member donations. They also run a state PAC called Teamsters Local 117 Working Families PAC. They back candidates in Pierce County, King County, and across the state. A Political Advisory Committee screens candidates and picks who to back. (Sources 1, 5, 9)
- **They organize new workers.** In August 2026, 500 public safety workers from PSEU Local 519 voted to join Local 117 — a major organizing win. (Source 3)
- **Domains they span:** politics (endorsements, PAC), labor (contracts), government (DOC workforce), and corrections (6,000+ officers).

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Source # |
|-----------|---------|----------|
| Who benefits | The 19,500 Local 117 members get higher pay, benefits, and a union voice. Backed politicians get union support. | 3, 1 |
| Who sits | John Scearcy (Secretary-Treasurer, the local's main officer); Paul Dascher (President); Rick Hicks (JC 28 President and IBT Western Region VP). | 5, 7 |
| Who governs | The Local 117 Executive Board and the Political Advisory Committee set endorsement and bargaining goals. | 1, 5 |
| Who wins | Fuel truck drivers got top regional pay; 500 new public safety staff joined via the PSEU vote; backed candidates have won Pierce County races. | 3, 6, 1 |

## 5. How they touch government
- **2025/2026 endorsements:** Pierce County Council District 5 — Bryan Yambe. Tacoma Metropolitan Park District — several candidates. LD 26 Sen. Deborah Krishnadasan. LD 27 — Laurie Jinkins, Jake Fey. LD 28 — Mari Leavitt, Dan Bronoske. LD 29 — Krista Perez, Sharlett Mena. (Sources 1, 10)
- **PCCLC link:** They sit in the Pierce County Central Labor Council (PCCLC), the AFL-CIO body for local unions. PCCLC 2026 endorsements include Marilyn Strickland (10th CD), Bryan Yambe (CC D5), Kelsey Barrans (CC D1), Brenda Lykins (CC D7). (Source 10)
- **PAC structure:** DRIVE is the federal PAC, funded by member donations. Teamsters Local 117 Working Families PAC is the state PAC, registered with the state's campaign-finance agency (PDC) and the IRS. DRIVE gave over $100,000 to the state PAC. A prior "Segregated Fund" shut down in 2020 after a Freedom Foundation lawsuit. (Source 9)
- **State contract:** The 2023–2025 DOC contract covers all non-supervisory DOC staff at prisons, correctional industries, the sex offender treatment program, and regional business offices. (Source 4)
- **Statewide endorsements:** Bob Ferguson for Governor (2024); Nick Brown for Attorney General; Emily Randall for WA-06. (Sources 2, 3)

## 6. Other seats they hold
- **Pierce County Central Labor Council (PCCLC):** Member. PCCLC coordinates labor endorsements in Pierce County. (Source 10)
- **Joint Council 28:** Local 117 is JC 28's biggest local. JC 28 President Rick Hicks is also the IBT Western Region VP. JC 28 political director: Bayley Burgess. (Sources 7, 8)
- **Washington State Labor Council (WSLC):** Linked through JC 28 and PCCLC. The WSLC COPE Convention approves statewide endorsements. (Source 10)
- **IBT International:** Local 117's delegation is the "third largest in the International Union" under Scearcy. (Source 5)

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** Teamsters Local 117 holds strong labor power through 19,500 members (6,000+ are state corrections officers), contracts over major state workforce groups, and a PAC that shapes Pierce County elections. Its JC 28 link (50,000+ members) and PCCLC link boost its political reach. Its power comes from how many workers it speaks for in key sectors (corrections, public safety, freight) and from running endorsements as a group.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags:** They once ran a dues-funded political fund (Segregated Fund) until Freedom Foundation sued in 2020. DRIVE now uses voluntary donations only. But the line between dues-funded organizing and political activity is still debated. Backing politicians who regulate their own workplaces also raises conflict questions.
- **Counter-argument:** Local 117's 19,500 members are still only a small share of all Washington workers. Their endorsements often back Democrats who would win anyway. So direct impact is hard to measure. The PSEU win was modest (500 workers). Their PAC spends less than bigger statewide PACs.
- **Confidence:** High — strong primary sources from union websites, IBT press releases, the state OFM contract file, PCCLC endorsement records, and JC 28 official data.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why he's on the map:** Tim Reynon sits in three places at once. He is on the Puyallup Tribal Council, sworn in June 11, 2026. He runs the Washington Governor's Office of Indian Affairs (GOIA), since January 2025. He used to be the City of Seattle's Tribal Relations Director (February 2022 to January 2025). Few people hold this much reach across tribal, state, and city government. It shapes treaty, gaming, environmental, and police policy across Western Washington.
- **Other people nearby:** Bill Sterud (Puyallup Tribal Chairman — his own profile); David Z. Bean (former chairman); other Council members Sylvia Miller, Annette Bryan, Anna Bean, Amber Hayward, and Fred Dillon. They are noted as open questions for follow-up.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Tim Reynon. Some sources spell it "Reynondson" — UNVERIFIED.
- **Tribe:** Enrolled member of the Puyallup Tribe of Indians.
- **DOB / birthplace:** Not public in the sources we checked. UNVERIFIED.
- **Residence:** Puyallup/Tacoma area (per the Puyallup Tribe council roster and LinkedIn).
- **Family:** Married about 30 years to Maile Reynon. Three sons (per GOIA bio).
- **Education:**
  - Juris Doctor (law degree), Brigham Young University, J. Reuben Clark Law School.
  - Bachelor of Social Work, BYU–Hawaii.
  - Admitted to the Washington State Bar in 1999.
- Past president of the Northwest Indian Bar Association.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **What power does he hold?**
  1. **Tribal elected office.** On the Puyallup Tribal Council since June 11, 2026 (three-year term). He also served on the Council from 2014 to 2020. The Puyallup Tribe is the largest federally recognized tribe in Pierce County. It owns major land in Tacoma and runs the Emerald Queen Casino. It has strong say over Tacoma-Pierce County policy.
  2. **State executive-branch authority.** Director of GOIA, appointed by Governor-elect Bob Ferguson, effective January 2025. GOIA is the state's main link to Washington's 29 federally recognized tribes. The Director runs the Centennial Accord process (a state-tribal meeting agreement).
  3. **Municipal and civil-rights leadership.** Former Vice Chair of the Washington State Criminal Justice Training Commission. Former Vice Chair of the Washington Coalition for Police Accountability. Co-Chair of De-Escalate WA, which led the winning 2018 Initiative 940 campaign on police training. Served on the Governor's Task Force on Independent Investigations of Police Use of Force (2019) and the 2016 Joint Legislative Task Force on Use of Deadly Force in Community Policing.
  4. **Legal and HR expertise.** Over 22 years as a tribal attorney, Executive Director of HR / Training / Education, and People Operations Director / Compliance Officer at the Puyallup Tribal Health Authority.
- **Key facts:**
  - Tax status: he serves in tribal, state, and (formerly) municipal roles. None carry private tax implications for him personally.
  - Board overlaps: Vice Chair of the CJTC (Criminal Justice Training Commission). Secretary of the Purpose Dignity Action (PDA) Board. Former Vice Chair of the Washington Coalition for Police Accountability.

## 3. Where their power comes from

|---|-------|---|
| Who benefits | Tribal members in Pierce County get a Council member who also runs the state's Indian Affairs office. The public benefits from his long work on police reform (I-940, task-force seats). | 1, 2, 3 |
| Who sits | Puyallup Tribal Council (elected). GOIA Director (appointed). Former Seattle Tribal Relations Director. Vice Chair of CJTC. Former Co-Chair of De-Escalate WA. He holds a wide set of seats across tribal, state, and city government. | 1, 2, 3 |
| Who governs | As GOIA Director, he runs the Governor's tribal liaison function across all 29 WA tribes. As a Council member, he governs Puyallup tribal policy. The two roles are separate and create a dual mandate. | 1, 2 |
| Who wins | Tribal-state coordination wins (a clear channel for the Puyallup Tribe's priorities in Olympia). Tribal-municipal coordination wins from his Seattle experience. Police-reform advocates win from his long track record. | 3 |

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** Reynon is a key figure who links tribal, state, and city government. He sits on the Puyallup Tribal Council (elected, June 2026) and runs the Governor's Office of Indian Affairs (appointed, January 2025). That gives him a rare "inside both rooms" view on tribal-state talks. His 22-year tribal career, plus Seattle city experience, plus his long work on police reform, make him one of the most well-connected Native leaders in the region.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags:** (a) **Dual role:** serving on the Tribal Council while running the state's tribal-liaison office is unusual. Counter — GOIA Directors are usually tribal members. The role is liaison, not representative of any one tribe. The State Ethics Act and tribal sovereignty together allow this, but it should be disclosed. (b) Vice Chair of CJTC while running GOIA — both touch criminal-justice policy. (c) His long tenure at many levels creates networks of mutual obligation that are hard to map from public sources.
- **Analysis of alternatives:** The opposing reading is that GOIA is a small office with a limited budget, so the Director's power is mostly symbolic. That is true by budget, but understates his convening and agenda-setting power: the GOIA Director runs the Centennial Accord and is the Governor's main tribal contact, which is real agenda power.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why he is on the map:** Tom Pierson holds two power roles at once. He is the Interim CEO of the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber (the county's main business-advocacy group). He was also the Acting Director of Pierce County Economic Development — a county-government role. That makes him a classic "revolving door" figure. He went back and forth between private-sector advocacy and a county job.
- He earned his place because he makes decisions. As Chamber CEO he led the lobbying coalition that won funding for the SR-167 Completion project (a key highway project). He also formed the Manufacturing Industrial Council for the South Sound. Both were real policy wins.
- **Adjacent but not on the map:**
 - Dona Ponepinto — she was Vice Chair on the Chamber board under Pierson. She is on the map as a separate entity.
 - Chyna Willman — current Board Chair of the Chamber. She is on the map.
 - Bruce Kendall — president of the Economic Development Board (EDB). He works a parallel job and is not on this map.

## 1. Who they are
- **Full name:** Tom Pierson.
- **Other name:** Thomas Pierson (formal use in some records).
- **Birth date / place:** Not confirmed. No public record found in voter rolls or biographies.
- **Lives in:** Not confirmed. Tacoma/Pierce County area based on his job, but not in primary sources.
- **Family / spouse:** Not confirmed.
- **Education:** Washington State University, 1989–1993 (source #9, LinkedIn). Holds two certifications: Economic Development Essentials (University of Oklahoma) and Accredited Chamber Executive (Western Association of Chamber Executives) (source #9).
- **Awards:** Russell E. Pettit Memorial Award (WACE, Feb 2019); Chamber Executive of the Year (WACE, Feb 2014) (source #9).

## 2. Their career and offices
| Date | Role | How he got it | Source |
|------|------|---------------|--------|
| ~2002–2011 | CEO, Federal Way Chamber of Commerce (about 10 years) | Hired | #5, #6 |
| Jun 2011 | President & CEO, Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce | Hired by the Board | #1, #5 |
| Dec 2012 | Appointed to the Board of Directors, Economic Development Corporation of Pierce County (with Scott Francis) — confirmed by the Pierce County Council | Appointed | #7 |
| 2011–2021 | President & CEO, Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber (more than 10 years) | Employed | #1, #2, #8 |
| Jan 2020 | Briefed the City of Tacoma Economic Development Committee as Chamber CEO (alongside Betty Capestany, Pierce County Economic Development Director) | Ex officio | #8 |
| End of 2021 | Retired from the Chamber CEO role | — | #6 |
| ~2023 | Appointed Acting Director of Economic Development for Pierce County (he announced this on LinkedIn) | Appointed (county government) | #9 |
| Oct 1, 2025 | Interim President & CEO, Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber (re-appointed by the Board, announced by Board Chair Chyna Willman) | Appointed (interim) | #1, #2 |

**Note on the Acting Director role:** This comes from Pierson's own LinkedIn post (source #9, self-published, reliability 0.4). No Pierce County government press release or appointment confirmation was found. The Pierce County Economic Development Director named in a 2019 EDC report was Betty Capestany (source #8). Pierson's appointment came after her. Exact dates and scope are not confirmed by primary government sources. They need the state campaign-finance agency's (PDC) F-1 personal financial form or Pierce County HR records to verify.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power he holds:** Pierson's power comes from the offices he holds. He has two: (1) Interim CEO of the largest business group in Pierce County (about 1,200+ members, source #8). (2) Former Acting Director of Pierce County Economic Development — a county-government department head. Neither role is elected. Both are appointed or hired.
- **Economic side:** As Chamber CEO, Pierson runs the Chamber's lobbying agenda, its state and local policy priorities, and its coalition work. The Chamber is a 501(c)(6) business league — a federal tax category for trade groups (source #3, the IRS / ProPublica). It has about $3.2 million in annual revenue (FY2023, source #3). Pierson led coalitions that won funding for the SR-167 Completion project and formed the Manufacturing Industrial Council for the South Sound (source #1).
- **Government side:** As Acting Director of Economic Development, he sat inside county government. He managed economic-development programs, contracts, and possibly grants. That is a direct path from business lobbying to a government decision-maker role.
- **Money and size of the Chamber:** Chamber revenue was about $3.2M (FY2023) and $3.9M (FY2022) (source #3). The Chamber's IRS Form 990 shows contributions of $1.0M (FY2023) and $2.1M (FY2022). Total assets $2.05M (FY2023), net assets $847K (source #3).
- **Government contracts and grants:** The Chamber's 990 shows $1.9M in program service revenue (FY2023). That may include government contracts for programs like the Pierce County Business Accelerator or Spaceworks Tacoma (source #1). Not confirmed — specific contract amounts need PDC or county contract records.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Question | Answer | Source |

| Who benefits | The Chamber's 1,200+ business members get advocacy work on SR-167, manufacturing policy, and the state tax and legislative agenda. Pierson himself benefits from his pay: $195,420 (FY2020), $163,075 (FY2019), $182,008 (FY2018) per IRS Form 990 (source #3). His interim pay: $44,453 for partial-year FY2024 (source #3). | #3 |
| Who sits | Pierson sits on: the Chamber Board (as CEO), the Pierce County Economic Development Corporation Board (appointed 2012), the South Sound Military and Communities Partnership (as Economic Development Working Group Chair), and the City of Tacoma Economic Development Committee (as an ex officio presenter). | #1, #7, #8 |
| Who governs | As Chamber CEO, Pierson runs the Chamber's strategy, its legislative agenda, and its program work (Candidate Academy, Business Leadership Academy, Manufacturing Industrial Council, Spaceworks Tacoma, Pierce County Business Accelerator). | #1, #8 |
| Who wins | The SR-167 Completion project got funding through coalitions Pierson led (source #1). The Manufacturing Industrial Council was formed under his tenure (source #1). Those are real wins for the business community. | #1 |

## 4. Their money
- **Pay (IRS Form 990, ProPublica):**

- **PDC activity:** A PDC document (source #10) names "Tom Pierson, President/CEO" in the context of lobbying and grassroots lobbying spending. The Chamber is a registered lobbying group at the state level. Pierson's personal C1/C3/C4 donation activity is not confirmed. It would need a PDC contributor search by name.

## 5. How they touch government
- **Lobbying:** The Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber has a state legislative agenda (source #1). Pierson, as CEO, is the public face of that lobbying. A PDC document (source #10) names him in a lobbying context. The Chamber's 990 confirms it is a 501(c)(6) — the tax category for groups that lobby.
- **Campaign donations (PDC):** Not confirmed for Pierson personally. The Chamber itself does not give to candidates (c)(6) groups cannot in Washington. But the Chamber runs the Candidate Academy program (source #1) that trains candidates. That is an in-kind political activity.
- **Contracts and grants:** The Chamber gets $1.9M in program service revenue (FY2023, source #3). That may include government contracts. Not confirmed — specific amounts need Pierce County procurement records.
- **Land-use actions:** Not confirmed. No specific land-use actions tied to Pierson were found.
- **Economic Development Corporation Board appointment:** Confirmed by Pierce County Council meeting Dec 11, 2012 (source #7). That is a government appointment to a quasi-public economic-development group.

## 6. Other seats they hold

- **Dona Ponepinto** appears as Vice Chair on the Chamber's 990 (source #3), confirming the graph's `chamber → dona-ponepinto, board, weight 4` edge from Pierson's tenure period.

## 7. Controversies and open questions
- **Chamber audit issues:** The Chamber's federal audit record (ProPublica, source #3) shows findings in four straight fiscal years: FY2022 and FY2024 "material noncompliance"; FY2023 and FY2025 "significant deficiency in internal controls." These are not personal controversies for Pierson, but they happened during or near his tenure. The audits' presence suggests the Chamber handled $750K+ in federal grant money in those years (inference from the audit-requirement threshold; confirm from the audit reports).
- **Revolving-door concern (inference):** Pierson moved from Chamber CEO (private-sector advocate) to Acting Director of Pierce County Economic Development (government role) and back to Interim Chamber CEO. That is a revolving-door pattern. The defense: this is common in economic development. Both sides value people who know both sectors. His University of Oklahoma certification (source #9) shows he is professionally trained.
- **No personal ethics complaints, lawsuits, or disciplinary actions** were found in this pass. Not confirmed — needs an explicit PDC enforcement search and court records check.

## 8. How the press covers them
- **Coverage pattern:** Pierson receives regular positive coverage in South Sound Business (profiles, Lead+Follow Q&A, source #6), Tacoma News Tribune (departure announcement, source #4), and Federal Way Mirror (hire announcement, source #5). Coverage is consistently favorable — business-leader profile framing.
- **Owned outlets:** None. The Chamber does not own media outlets but produces a podcast and newsletter (source #1).
- **Social reach:** LinkedIn — 4950 followers, 500 connections (source #9). Self-published, reliability 0.4.
- **Editorial stance:** South Sound Business and News Tribune coverage frames Pierson as a respected, stabilizing institutional leader. The South Sound Business Lead+Follow profile (source #6) is personal/lifestyle in nature, not critical.

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** Toyota of Puyallup is a single-store, family-run Toyota franchise. It is a high-volume store and it is a known Republican donor in Pierce County politics. The same store gave federal money to Hans Zeiger (R, 25th LD), Rob McKenna (R, former WA AG), and Reagan Dunn (R, King County). Its standalone political weight is low (composite 0.001). His family ran the store for decades. His daughter Kerry Sawyer Odeman took over and grew it to "#1 volume" status. It has won the President's Award 26 times. ## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why TPCHD is on the map:** TPCHD is the sole local public health agency for Pierce County (about 952,600 people as of 2024). State law (RCW 70.05) gives it power to protect health. It does this through disease prevention, food safety, septic permits, and family health services. Its $102.9M two-year budget and about 284 full-time staff (FTE) give it real muscle. The Board of Health — made up of Pierce County Council members, Tacoma City Council members, the County Executive, and others — sets policy for the whole county.
- **Why others near it are NOT on the map:** The Washington State Department of Health is a separate state-level agency. Franciscan Health System / Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (a hospital system) is mapped separately. The Perinatal Collaborative of Pierce County (a TPCHD-affiliated 501c3) is a sub-entity. The Pierce County Medical Society (which appoints one Board of Health member) is mapped separately.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Tacoma-Pierce County Health Department (TPCHD)
- **Type:** Independent government agency (local health jurisdiction)
- **Founded:** 1972 (per Wikipedia). Created by an interlocal agreement between Pierce County and the City of Tacoma.
- **Governing law:** Revised Code of Washington (RCW) 70.05 (local health departments); RCW 70.05.070 (powers and duties of local health officers); RCW 70.28.031; interlocal agreement between Pierce County and the City of Tacoma.
- **Tax ID (EIN):** Government entity. Pierce County acts as the fiduciary agent.
- **Parent/subsidiaries:** No parent. Run by the Tacoma-Pierce County Board of Health, an independent policy body. Pierce County is the fiduciary agent.
- **Accreditation:** One of about 400 local health departments in the U.S. that meet Public Health Accreditation Board (PHAB) standards.
- **Headquarters:** 3629 South D Street, Tacoma, WA 98418-6813. Also has a Key Peninsula office at 9013 Key Peninsula Hwy N, Lakewood, WA 98349 (open Thursdays 11am-2pm).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Statutory authority:** RCW 70.05 gives TPCHD power over food safety (restaurant inspections, food worker cards), drinking water safety, septic system permits, disease control (TB, HIV/AIDS, whooping cough), environmental health, and vital records (birth and death certificates). The Health Officer (Dr. James S. Miller) has powers under RCW 70.05.070 and RCW 70.28.031.
- **Budget:** 2026-2027 two-year budget: $102,899,820 (later amended to about $108.7M per the April 2026 Board agenda). That is 3.2% of the total Pierce County budget. Funding sources: Federal 9.1%, State 30.4%, Pierce County 12.8%, City of Tacoma 2.5%, Permits & fees 39%, Private/local/misc 6.2%. The budget fell 19% from the 2024-25 amended budget of $127.6M. The drop came from the end of federal COVID money.
- **Regulatory authority:** TPCHD enforces food safety codes, septic rules (including a new do-it-yourself septic inspection program), environmental health codes, and disease control rules. It inspects restaurants, issues food worker cards, and regulates on-site sewage systems.
- **Area covered:** All of Pierce County (about 952,600 people in 2024). This includes cities like Tacoma, Puyallup, Lakewood, Gig Harbor, and University Place, plus unincorporated areas.
- **Staffing:** 284 FTE in 2026. Down from 349 in 2025 and 355 in 2024. The drop reflects post-COVID budget cuts. Four divisions: Disease Prevention & Management, Environmental Health, Strengthening Families, Administrative Services.
- **Domain overlap:** Government (health rules, statutory authority), Social (public health services, family support, substance abuse prevention), Economic (food safety permits, septic permits that affect property values).

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Pierce County residents (about 952K) get disease prevention, food safety, clean water, and family health services. Food businesses benefit from food worker cards and permits. Homeowners benefit from septic rules and the new DIY inspection program, which cuts costs. | #1, #3, #5 |
| Who sits | Board of Health: Jani Hitchen (Chair, Pierce County Council), Joe Bushnell (Vice Chair, Tacoma City Council), Ryan Mello (Pierce County Executive), Dave Olson (Edgewood Mayor, Cities & Towns Assn), Sandesh Sadalge (Tacoma City Council), Nicholas Rajacich MD (Pierce County Medical Society), Paul Herrera (Pierce County Council), Bryan Yambe (Pierce County Council). Alternates: LeighBeth Merrick, Rosie Ayala, Olgy Diaz, Stephen Cook MD. | #4 |
| Who governs | Director Chantell Harmon Reed runs day-to-day operations. The Board of Health sets policy, approves the budget, and oversees the director. Reed reports to the Board. The Board meets every two weeks (first and third Wednesdays). | #2, #4, #7 |
| Who wins | The 2026-27 budget cut (19% lower than the prior cycle) reflects the end of federal COVID money. That is a loss for public health capacity. Reed survived an independent probe into workplace culture complaints. The Board ordered her to take executive coaching but she kept her job. The Board did not release the investigator's full report. | #6, #7, #8 |

## 5. How they touch government
- **Board of Health:** TPCHD's governing body. Three members appointed by Pierce County Council. One by Tacoma City Council. Plus the Pierce County Executive and Tacoma Mayor (or their picks). One from Pierce County Cities and Towns Association. One from Pierce County Medical Society. Two-year terms.
- **Budget:** Pierce County Council appropriates the county share ($7,546,490 from the General Fund for 2026-27). The Board of Health recommended the 2026-27 budget via Resolution 2023-4795 (July 2, 2025).
- **Ryan Mello link:** Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello sits on the Board of Health. He has appeared with Director Reed on public health events (like a youth violence prevention funding event with Tacoma Police Chief Patti Jackson and the Billy Ray Shirley III Foundation).
- **Federal money:** 9.1% of the budget (about $9.4M) is federal. Reed told the Board that a $1M Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) grant (3-year, awarded 2023 for wildfire smoke health effects) was ended. That is an early sign of federal funding changes.
- **State money:** 30.4% of the budget (about $31.3M) is state. This includes Foundational Public Health Services revenue ($8.7M per year, down $374K in SFY 2026).
- **Regulatory work:** TPCHD regulates food businesses (permits, inspections), septic systems (permits, inspections, the new DIY program), drinking water, and enforces environmental health codes. It also runs the food worker card program.
- **Campaign donations:** None. As a government entity, TPCHD does not donate. The department may push for public health money through the Board of Health and professional groups.

## 6. Other seats they hold
- **Ryan Mello** (`ryan-mello`): Pierce County Executive; sits on the Board of Health. Weight 3 in the graph (board_of_health).
- **Pierce County Council** (`county-council`): Appoints three Board of Health members (Hitchen, Herrera, Yambe). Appropriates county money. Weight 3 in the graph (board_of_health).
- **Tacoma City Council** (`tacoma-city-council`): Appoints one Board of Health member (Bushnell or Sadalge). Mayor serves or sends a delegate. Weight 3 in the graph (board_of_health).
- **KNKX** (`knkx`): South Sound public radio covers TPCHD, including the probe into Director Reed. Weight 2 in the graph (covered_by).
- **Pierce County Medical Society:** Appoints one Board of Health member (Nicholas Rajacich, MD) and one alternate (Stephen Cook, MD).
- **Pierce County Cities and Towns Association:** Appoints one Board of Health member (Dave Olson, Edgewood Mayor).
- **Perinatal Collaborative of Pierce County (PCPC):** A 501(c)(3) nonprofit linked to TPCHD. The board includes TPCHD staff (Jax Hermer, Megan Monson) and reps from MultiCare, Mary Bridge, Sea Mar, Puyallup Tribal Health Authority, and other health groups.
- **ALF Tacoma Pierce County:** Several TPCHD staff are ALF fellows or board members. They include Nancy Sutton (Immediate Past President, retired TPCHD Deputy Director), Jessica Gehle (Division Director, Environmental Health), Benjii Bittle (Business Development Director), and Leah Ford (Community Health Program Manager).

## 1. Who they are
- **Director Reed probe details:** The Board of Health did not release the independent investigator's full report. News Tribune reporter Becca Most asked for the documents. The full findings, the scope of complaints, and any ongoing fixes remain partly UNVERIFIED. This is a real accountability gap.
- **Budget amendment path:** The 2026-27 budget started at $102.9M (a 19% cut). Then in August 2026 it was amended up to about $108.7M. What drove the $5.8M bump and whether more amendments are coming needs watching.
- **Federal money impacts:** Reed told the Board that a $1M EPA grant was ended. The full scope of federal losses (beyond COVID-era cuts and the EPA grant) and what they mean for specific programs needs more digging.
- **Staff reduction context:** FTE fell from 355 (2024) to 284 (2026) — a 20% drop. The link between this drop, the budget cuts, and the workplace culture probe is not clear. Whether services are still being delivered well needs checking.
- **PCPC governance:** The Perinatal Collaborative of Pierce County (501c3) has TPCHD staff on its board alongside hospital reps. The financial and working ties between TPCHD and PCPC need more clarity.

## 1. Who they are
- **The bottom line.** TPCHD controls public health rules for all of Pierce County (about 952K residents). It does this through state law (RCW 70.05), a $102.9M+ two-year budget, and about 284 staff. Its power runs through the Board of Health (which includes the County Executive, three County Council members, and Tacoma City Council members) and through the Director of Public Health. The department's reach covers food safety, septic systems, drinking water, disease control, and environmental health. It touches daily life in ways most people do not notice. The 19% budget cut and 20% staff drop since 2024 come from the end of COVID money and have cut capacity.
- **Conflicts to watch (defense counter-argument expected):** The Board of Health's refusal to release the full probe report on Director Reed's workplace conduct raises an accountability concern. A defense attorney could say the Board protected staff privacy and that coaching was a fair fix. The counter: the lack of detail hurts public trust, especially while staff cuts continue.
- **The other side:** TPCHD is a low-power agency tied to its funders. Only 12.8% of its money comes from the county. Most comes from state and federal pass-throughs. Board members are part-time appointees with other day jobs. Its rule-making power is bounded by state law and its budget. Budget cuts may shrink TPCHD's real power, even though the law still gives it authority.
- **Confidence:** High — the department's legal structure, budget, staffing, governance, and leadership are extensively documented in primary sources (TPCHD website, Board of Health packets, Pierce County budget documents). The workplace investigation is well-covered by secondary sources (KNKX, News Tribune) but the full report remains undisclosed.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why we added Tucci & Sons:** They are one of the biggest heavy-road builders in Pierce County. They hold many state and federal road contracts. They also donate to political campaigns and sit in local business groups. So they help shape how Pierce County builds its roads (source 1, 4, 9).
- **Other companies we did not add:** Active Construction, Inc. also bids on road work. They are not on the map unless we find stronger proof of power.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Tucci & Sons LLC (also Tucci & Sons, Inc.). Their Washington state business license number is 278 021 315 (source 3).
- **Type:** LLC. A family-owned construction company.
- **Address:** 4224 Waller Road E, Tacoma, WA 98443 (source 1, 3).
- **Owners:** Michael J. Tucci started the firm in 1950. It is now in its third generation of family owners. Mike Tucci is president. Tim Tucci is secretary and treasurer (source 6). Tim Tucci is also the main contact at the Asphalt Pavement Association of Washington (source 9).
- **State rules:** They follow state contractor rules. The Washington Department of Labor and Industries oversees those rules under state law RCW 18.27.
- **Federal ID:** Their SAM.gov Unique Entity ID is K5N5ZMTJJEM8. Their CAGE code is 0HXL1. Their DUNS number is 003825122 (source 8).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Market share:** They run two asphalt plants in Pierce County. Each plant makes 400 or more tons of asphalt per hour. The newer Lakewood plant alone makes 150,000 to 200,000 tons a year (source 5, 6). They also recycle 100,000 or more tons of old concrete and asphalt each year at the McChord plant (source 5).
- **Government contracts:** They win state contracts with the Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT). They were the lowest bidder on the SR 507/510/702 roundabout contract, called Contract XE3689, awarded March 3, 2026 (source 2). They hold federal contracts with the U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) and the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA). Their two main federal awards add up to about $47.1 million. That includes the Stevens Canyon Road repair job in Mount Rainier National Park, where their bid was $8.9 million and the total award was $38.8 million (source 7, 8). They also work as a subcontractor on 4 other federal awards with Manson Construction Co. (source 8). They bid on a City of Tacoma crosswalk job on McKinley Avenue (source 4).
- **Revenue:** About $15 million a year (source 10 — secondary, not yet confirmed by primary filings).
- **Jobs:** About 71 workers (source 10 — secondary). Their LinkedIn page lists 51–200 workers (source 11 — secondary).
- **Property:** Their main yard is at 4224 Waller Rd E, Tacoma. They also run asphalt plants in Lakewood and at McChord (source 5, 6).

Their donation to Kelly Chambers shows they engage in politics. The full scope of their political donations still needs PDC verification.
- **Conflicts of interest:** They are both a major WSDOT contractor and a political donor. That puts them at the meeting point of road spending and political influence. The CBCA 4779 case shows they will sue over federal contract disputes. Their McChord plant is on or near Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM), a military base. That raises questions about land use near a military site. No evidence of bid-rigging or corrupt deals was found.
- **The other view:** Tucci & Sons may simply be a strong local contractor that wins bids by offering low prices and good work. The WSDOT bid check report shows they were the lowest bidder among several competitors. Active Construction, Inc. was the second-lowest bidder. Their political donations may be normal civic engagement, not influence-buying. Their multi-generational roots and union workforce suggest they are part of the community, not extracting from it.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- T'wina Nobles is on this map because she is the elected State Senator for the 28th Legislative District in Washington. The district includes Fircrest, University Place, Lakewood, Steilacoom, DuPont, Elk Plain, Camp Murray, and Joint Base Lewis-McChord (JBLM).
- She is the Chair of the Higher Education and Workforce Development Committee. She is Vice Chair of the Early Learning and K-12 Education Committee. Those roles give her real power over education policy and state funding for Pierce County schools and colleges.
- She is also the only Black member of the Washington State Senate. That gives her a strong voice as a trailblazer and coalition-builder.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** T'wina Nobles. Full legal name beyond public records is not confirmed.
- **Aliases:** None on record. Campaign site: twinanobles.com. Facebook: SenatorTwinaNobles. LinkedIn: twinanobles.
- **Born:** December 14, 1981, in Frankfurt, Germany. Both parents were in the U.S. military.
- **Lives in:** Fircrest, Washington (28th LD). She has lived in the district for almost 20 years. She first moved there when her family was stationed at JBLM (then Fort Lewis) in 2000.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why he is here:** Uli Chi is the board chair of Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (VMFH). VMFH was formed in January 2021 when Virginia Mason merged with CHI Franciscan. It is part of CommonSpirit Health. It runs the main Catholic hospital chain in Pierce County and Western Washington. As board chair, he is the top lay governance officer for a system that runs St. Joseph Medical Center (Tacoma), St. Anthony (Gig Harbor), St. Clare (Lakewood), St. Elizabeth (Enumclaw), and St. Francis (Federal Way). He decides on mission, ethics, capital projects, and regional strategy.
- **Who is left out:** Ketul J. Patel runs CommonSpirit from Chicago — out of state. Julie Manas runs VMFH day-to-day as CommonSpirit Northwest Region President since 2024. She has her own profile or one coming under `vmfh`. Other VMFH board members are not on this map. Kevin McClatchy is not on VMFH; he runs Chatham AM.

## 1. Who they are
- **Full name:** Uli Chi, PhD.
- **Roles and ties:**
  - **Chair**, Virginia Mason Franciscan Health Board of Directors (since January 2021; before that, board chair of CHI Franciscan).
  - **Vice chair and senior fellow**, Max De Pree Center for Leadership, Fuller Theological Seminary (Pasadena, CA).

- **Education:** Doctorate in Computer Science from the University of Washington.
- **Career:** Award-winning tech entrepreneur. He founded Chi-LLC, a software company that made 3-D virtual reality space planning and visualization software for consumers and businesses. Founding date and current company status are not verified. He has shifted to governance and teaching.
- **Home:** Greater Seattle and Tacoma area (LinkedIn lists Tacoma, WA).
- **Family:** Not found in public sources.
- **Politics and ties:** Publicly tied to Christian-theological-academic institutions (Fuller Seminary, Regent College, Seattle Pacific University). His governance role in a Catholic hospital system is professional, not religious.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **What power he holds:** Three power levers.
  1. **Hospital governance (VMFH Board Chair).** VMFH is one of the largest private employers in Pierce County. It runs the region's main Catholic hospital chain. The board chair sets the agenda. He hires and reviews the regional president. He approves big capital projects and major deals. He links CommonSpirit Health's Catholic sponsorship system to local operations.
  2. **Ideas and thought leadership.** He wrote *The Wise Leader* (Eerdmans, May 2024, ISBN 0802884040). He teaches at Regent College and is vice chair of the De Pree Center. This gives him standing in faith and leadership circles.
  3. **Network.** He sits on the Benaroya Research Institute (Seattle immunology and autoimmune research) and the Virginia Mason Institute (lean-healthcare consulting). Both connect to Seattle biotech and academic-medical networks.
- **Power scoring:**
  - Hospital-system governance = main source of decision-making power.
  - Christian-academic governance = reputational and cultural power.
  - Tech-entrepreneur background = economic base, now realized through governance pay and book royalties.
- **Key facts:** VMFH and CHI Franciscan are public charities (501(c)(3) tax-exempt). Government funding comes mainly through Medicare and Medicaid. His board ties span Catholic healthcare, evangelical Fuller, mainline-evangelical Seattle Pacific, Anabaptist-evangelical Regent College Vancouver, and biotech (Benaroya).

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why United Way is on the map.** UWPC is the main private fundraiser and regranter in Pierce County. It runs the "From Poverty to Possibilities" summit. It is the local steward of the ALICE study — ALICE stands for Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed, a measure of working-poor households. That makes UWPC a hub. It ties together Pierce County government and labor (Lawver). It ties in banks such as Columbia Bank, Bank of America, and Banner. It ties in utilities (Tacoma Public Utilities — Jackie Flowers), transit (Mike Griffus, Pierce Transit), and health (Beth Johnson, Coordinated Care). UWPC touches nearly every tier-1 and tier-2 institution on this map. It also has a strong reputation as the "go-to" local philanthropy.
- **What is NOT on the map.** The Greater Tacoma Community Foundation (gtcf) is a tier-1 partner with overlap but is a separate legal entity. The two groups coordinate but are distinct. United Way Worldwide (the national office) is not on the map. UWPC is an independent licensee, not a subsidiary.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** United Way of Pierce County (operating brand: UWPC).
- **Type:** 501(c)(3) nonprofit, Washington State. Federal tax ID number (EIN) 91-0650669 (per ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).
- **Affiliate relationship:** Independent licensee of United Way Worldwide. Part of United Way Pacific Northwest (Ponepinto chaired UWPNW per her UWPC bio).
- **Founding and governing law:** Washington Nonprofit Corporation Act (state law (RCW) 24.03). IRS Form 990 filings (FY 2023 most recent reviewed).
- **Key personnel (FY24-26):**
 - **President & CEO:** Dona Ponepinto (joined Jan 2014); FY23 pay $189,439 + $19,038 other; FY22 $196,908 + $20,271.
 - **CDO:** Emily Mendez-Bryant (~$109K–$115K across FY22-FY24).
 - **CFO/SVP Finance:** Peter J. Grignon (~$93K–$96K).
 - **VP Community Impact:** Jarrett Brunny (FY22 $105,508); current VP is Shawn Paton.
 - **Board Chair:** Nathe Lawver (Pierce County Central Labor Council, AFL-CIO).
 - **Board Vice Chair:** Jackie Flowers (Tacoma Public Utilities).
 - **Board Secretary:** Tanisha Jumper (Tacoma Public Schools).
 - **Board Treasurer:** AJ Gordon (Northwest Bank).
 - **Directors include:** Mike Griffus (Pierce Transit CEO). Beth Johnson (Coordinated Care CEO). Renee McClain (Washington State Fair CEO). Lua Pritchard (Asia Pacific Cultural Center). Sabrina Smith (Columbia Bank). Yelda Bryant (Bank of America). Pamela Devi Chandran (union attorney). Jeff Mincheff (J Squared Investments). Carlos Ortiz (Zeta-Maya Entertainment). Brandon Ervin (Ervin Consulting Group). Anthony R. Stancil (Ryder System).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Grant-making:** UWPC raises money in the annual workplace campaign and regrants to about 30–40 partner agencies across human services. It also runs the Center for Strong Families and the From Poverty to Possibilities summit. Individual grants are small ($25K–$250K), but the annual pool and the convening power set the de-facto priorities for the local human-services network.
- **ALICE convening power:** UWPC is the regional steward of the ALICE study. ALICE stands for Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed. Ponepinto helped develop it at her prior job. Pierce County government, United Way Worldwide, and state agencies cite ALICE when setting the official "self-sufficiency" income number.
- **Dense board overlap:** The board reads like a who's-who of the Pierce County institutional map. Pierce Transit has a seat. So do Tacoma Public Utilities, Tacoma Public Schools, Coordinated Care, and Washington State Fair. Banks include Columbia Bank, Bank of America, and Northwest Bank. Insurers include Regence BlueShield and State Farm. Labor includes AFSCME-aligned union attorneys. Other groups include Ryder System and Asia Pacific Cultural Center. Outside the Chamber and GTCF, this is the single best cross-institutional networking node in Pierce County.
- **Government contracting:** UWPC partners with the City of Tacoma, Pierce County, and DSHS (the state Department of Social and Health Services). Together they run family-financial-stability programs through the Center for Strong Families. UWPC acts as a fiscal middleman for publicly funded services. That gives it quasi-governmental standing.
- **Cultural and regional voice:** The annual campaign shapes the public conversation about poverty and self-sufficiency. Dona Ponepinto also served as President of the Association of Junior Leagues International, starting in 2022. That extends UWPC's reach nationally.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Low-income working households in Pierce County benefit from UWPC's regranting through 30–40 partner agencies and from the Center for Strong Families. Tier-2 board members benefit from sitting on a key board (visibility, networks, hiring pipelines). ALICE report users (state agencies, funders) get a credible county-level metric. | #1, #2, #3 |
| Who sits | The board includes CEOs and leaders from Pierce Transit, Tacoma Public Utilities, Coordinated Care, Washington State Fair, Columbia Bank, Bank of America, Regence, State Farm, AFSCME-aligned labor (Lawver), and Tacoma Public Schools. Past chairs include Sebrena Chambers, Steve Harlow, and Stuart Grover. | #2, #3 |
| Who governs | UWPC sets the priorities for the regional human-services network through its grant criteria, ALICE metrics, and convenings. The CEO and Board Chair (Lawver, AFL-CIO) jointly run a coalition that is, in effect, an unelected shadow human-services council. | #1, #2 |
| Who wins | Dona Ponepinto: her UWPC tenure turned into the AJLI presidency (national profile, June 2022). Tier-2 board members win from philanthropic-network access. The two anchor board members (law/labor and utilities) win from convening power over the social-services agenda that touches their sectors. | #1, #4 |

## 1. Who they are
- **The bottom line.** UWPC is the most important private cross-institutional board in the county after the Tacoma-Pierce Chamber and GTCF. It works like a standing executive networking chamber for the public, nonprofit, banking, and labor elite. Every director is a bridge to another tier-1 or tier-2 node. Grant dollars are modest (single-digit millions re-granted each year). The real power is the board seats and the convening role.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags:**
 - Board members from Tacoma Public Utilities (Flowers), Pierce Transit (Griffus), Coordinated Care (Johnson), and Tacoma Public Schools (Jumper) are quasi-public officials. UWPC's agenda-setting affects their agencies' funding.
 - The CEO's concurrent AJLI presidency is allowed but extends UWPC's reach into a national women's-leadership group.
 - AFL-CIO board chair (Lawver) lines up labor policy with UWPC's "self-sufficiency" framing. Some labor scholars say that framing moves the poverty talk away from wage and labor-law reform.
- **Alternative reading.** UWPC is a normal community-foundation-style operation. The dense board reflects the small size of the Pierce County elite pool. Every executive knows every other executive. Coordinated power is not the only reading. Calling UWPC a "shadow council" is alarmist.
- **Confidence:** High — board composition, CEO, EIN, and 990 pay figures are verified from primary sources (ProPublica + UWPC website + official news).

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why it is on the map.** University Place School District (UPSD) is in the map because of two reasons. First, State Sen. T'wina Nobles (D-28) sits on its 5-member Board of Directors. That gives the district a direct line to two state Senate committees: Higher Education & Workforce Development, and Early Learning & K-12. Second, UPSD puts levy and bond measures on the ballot. In February 2026, it placed a $320 million bond on the ballot. That makes it an active player in Pierce County Council levy decisions.
- **Who is left out.** Tacoma Public Schools, Clover Park, Bethel, and Peninsula are separate districts. Each is on its own page or in open questions.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** University Place School District No. 83 (Washington). It does business as University Place School District (UPSD).
- **Type:** A Washington public school district. It is a junior taxing district (a local government body with limited tax power) under state law RCW 28A (common schools) and Title 84 RCW (property tax levies). It has no EIN (federal tax ID). It is a tax-exempt government body.
- **Governing law:** RCW 28A.315 (school director elections); RCW 28A.500-525 (levies and bonds); RCW 84.52.053 (levy lids — the legal cap on how much a school district can raise through local property taxes).
- **Superintendent (current):** Jeff Chamberlin (per UPSD83.org).
- **Current board (5 members):** Marisa Peloquin (2017–2029); Ethelda Burke (2015–2029); Rick Maloney (2019–2027); **T'wina Nobles (2015–2027)**; Mary Lu Dickinson (1995–2027). Source: Ballotpedia 2024 election page. Nobles was first sworn in in 2015.
- **Schools:** 8 (2023–24).
- **Students:** 5,606 (2023–24, OSPI — the Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction).
- **FY24 total spending:** $98,082,000 ($17,474 per student).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Local decision-making:** The 5-member Board sets policy for about 5,600 students and a $98 million budget. It approves bond and levy measures that go before Pierce County voters. The February 2026 special-election ballot includes two replacement levies and a $320 million bond. That gives the Board direct control of the building pipeline.
- **Bridge to the state Legislature:** Sen. Nobles wears two hats. She is a UPSD board director and a state senator on the Higher Education & Workforce Development and Early Learning & K-12 committees. That gives UPSD a direct line into K-12 funding formulas (the rules that decide how much state money each district gets) and any McCleary-fix changes (court-ordered updates to K-12 funding). Most mid-sized districts do not have that kind of access.
- **Community power:** UPSD is the main K-12 institution for the City of University Place and nearby unincorporated areas. It shapes school boundaries, land use, and where new schools get built across about 3 square miles of incorporated UP.
- **Why it scores this way:** The score comes from the Nobles board overlap (graph weight 4) and the levy ties to Pierce County Council (graph weight 3).

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | UPSD students and parents get steady levy support and a senator on key committees. Local building contractors get work from the bond pipeline. School board members benefit from incumbency and ballot design. | #1, #2 |
| Who sits | Sen. T'wina Nobles (state senator D-28 and UPSD board director Position 3 since 2015). Mary Lu Dickinson (director since 1995). Four other elected directors. | #1, #3 |
| Who governs | A 5-member elected Board of Directors governs. Superintendent Jeff Chamberlin runs daily work. OSPI provides state oversight. Voters approve levies and bonds. | #1, #2 |
| Who wins | Nobles wins a clear channel of influence. The district wins legislative access. The former county council chair (Ryan Mello, prior) had a District 4 seat covering downtown Tacoma, Hilltop, and University Place — an overlapping base of voters. | INFERENCE from #1, #2 |

- Verdict: UPSD is a tier-3 institutional node. Its influence does not come from size — only 5,606 students. It comes from Nobles wearing two hats: she is a school-board director and a state senator on the very committees that set K-12 funding. That makes UPSD a stronger policy pipeline than its mid-tier budget suggests.
- Conflicts-of-interest flags: (a) Sen. Nobles serving on a school board and as a state senator on K-12 funding committees at the same time is unusual. Any votes where she recused herself should be reviewed. (b) The February 2026 ballot has a $320 million construction bond. The campaign-finance filings for that measure should be checked for contractor contributions.
- Analysis of alternatives (ICD-203 opposing view): UPSD could also be read as a small suburban district with shrinking enrollment (down 3.5% over five years per Ballotpedia, from 5,816 in 2018–19 to 5,606 in 2023–24) and average academic results. It is not a power hub on its own. The power reading rests on the Nobles board overlap. Remove her and the graph weight collapses. UNVERIFIED: how often Nobles actually recuses.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- UW Tacoma is included because it is the major public university campus in Pierce County. It has real institutional, economic, and community-development influence.
- Power from holding an office: UW Tacoma is one of three campuses of the University of Washington, a major public research university. The Chancellor runs the campus with C-suite (executive officer) authority over a $100M-plus operation.
- Reputational power: U.S. News 2026 ranked UW Tacoma #1 Top Performer for Social Mobility in the West (source #1). Washington Monthly 2025 ranked it #1 Best Bang for the Buck in Washington (source #1).
- Power from connections: The graph shows edges to Chancellor Sheila Lange, John Wiborg, and the Pierce County Council for redevelopment partnerships. Chancellor Lange sits on the board of the Economic Development Board (EDB), the source for source #3.
- The campus has been called "a catalyst for the revival of downtown Tacoma" (source #4).
- **Related but separate groups (not on the map as separate nodes):** UW Seattle is the parent campus. It was founded in 1861 and is based in Seattle. UW Bothell is a sister campus. Tacoma Community College is a separate community college. It sends many transfer students to UW Tacoma. Pierce College is another top transfer feeder.

## 1. Who they are
- **Official name:** University of Washington Tacoma (source #1). It is accredited by the Northwest Commission on Colleges and Universities as a unit of the University of Washington (source #1).
- **Type:** Public university campus. One of three campuses of the University of Washington (source #1). It is not a separate 501(c)(3) nonprofit or LLC. It is a unit of the University of Washington, a state public institution. The UW Board of Regents governs it.
- **Tax ID (EIN):** NOT CONFIRMED. As a unit of the UW, UW Tacoma does not have its own EIN. The University of Washington's EIN applies. The UW Foundation, the fundraising arm, has its own 501(c)(3) status.
- **Parent and related units:** Parent: University of Washington (founded 1861, source #1). UW Tacoma is one of three campuses. They are Seattle (Robert J. Jones, President), Tacoma (Sheila Edwards Lange, Chancellor), and Bothell (Kristin G. Esterberg, Chancellor) (source #1). UW Tacoma has no subsidiaries.
- **Ownership chain:** State of Washington → University of Washington (public institution) → UW Tacoma (campus unit). The UW Board of Regents governs. The Chancellor reports to the UW President and Provost (source #4).
- **Governing law:** Washington State higher education law, found in state law (RCW) 28B. The UW Board of Regents governs. Executive Order 20 of the UW Policy Directory sets the rules for chancellor searches (source #4).

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power held:** UW Tacoma has **institutional and cultural power**. As a public university campus, it shapes who goes to college, who gets trained for jobs, and how the community sees itself in Pierce County. It does not have legal authority over county government. But as an anchor institution in downtown Tacoma, it has real power over land use, the economy, and community development. The campus has been called "a catalyst for the revival of downtown Tacoma" (source #4). Chancellor Lange also lobbies the state legislature in Olympia (source #5). UW Tacoma also has **economic power** as an employer and a buyer. The specific employee count and payroll were NOT CONFIRMED.
- **Power-domain overlap:**
 - **Tax status:** Public university, a state entity. Not a 501(c)(3). It is tax-exempt as a state institution. Gifts to the UW Foundation (a 501(c)(3)) are tax-deductible.
 - **Board roster and overlaps:** Chancellor Sheila Edwards Lange sits on the EDB Board (source #3). She also sits on these outside boards: Pugh Capital Management, the Seattle Branch of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, Washington Campus Compact, AAA Washington, and the Seattle Art Museum (source #4). The UW Board of Regents governs the whole university. UW Tacoma has an Advisory Board (source #4).
 - **Government funding share:** Tuition is the "largest single source of revenue" (source #2). State "proviso" budget investments (special line items in the state budget) are large and growing (source #6: "UW Tacoma has seen significant growth in 'proviso' state budget investments, such as recent increases for engineering"). Specific state appropriation amounts are NOT CONFIRMED. Chancellor Lange pushes for permanent state funding for student services (source #5).
- **Key facts:**
 - **Enrollment:** 5,059 total headcount in 2025-26 (source #1). 4,301 undergraduates plus 758 graduate students (source #1). Enrollment rose 3.97% in autumn 2024 (source #6). That put the campus within 7.4% of its peak enrollment in 2020-21 (source #6).
 - **Student demographics:** 52% are first-generation college students (source #1). 46% are Pell-eligible, meaning they qualify for federal grants for low-income students (source #1). 19% are military-affiliated (source #1). 60% of undergraduates are from underrepresented minorities (source #1). The breakdown is 32% Caucasian, 19% Asian American, 16% Hispanic/Latinx, and 11% African American (source #1). 51% are male, 49% female. 86% are full-time. The student-to-faculty ratio is 15 to 1 (source #1).
 - **Academic programs:** Over 50 undergraduate degree programs and options. There are 15 graduate programs (source #1). The largest schools are the School of Engineering & Technology (1,148 students), the School of Interdisciplinary Arts & Sciences (925), the Milgard School of Business (795), and the School of Social Work & Criminal Justice (392) (source #1). The most popular majors are Computer Science, Biomedical Sciences, Information Technology, Psychology, Accounting, and Finance (source #1).
 - **Money:** UW Tacoma gave out $60 million in financial aid in 2023-24 (source #1). Undergraduate tuition is $13,577 per year for 2025-26 (source #1). Graduate tuition is $22,668 per year (source #1). 68% of students get financial aid, including loans. 57% get scholarships or grants (source #1).

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Students benefit from educational access (5,059 enrolled, 35,424 degrees awarded since 1990, source #1). Downtown Tacoma benefits from the campus-led revival (source #4). The South Puget Sound workforce benefits from graduates. Military-affiliated students (19%) benefit from a military-friendly campus. First-generation and Pell-eligible students (52% / 46%) benefit from social mobility paths. | #1, #4 |
| Who sits | Chancellor Sheila Edwards Lange (CEO of the campus) sits on: the EDB Board (source #3), Pugh Capital Management's board, the Seattle Branch of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco's board, Washington Campus Compact, AAA Washington, and the Seattle Art Museum (source #4). She is past national president of Women in Engineering Pro-Active Network (source #4). UW Tacoma has an Advisory Board (source #4). | #3, #4 |
| Who governs | The UW Board of Regents governs the University of Washington (all three campuses). Chancellor Lange runs UW Tacoma as CEO. She reports to the UW President and Provost (source #4). The Chancellor's Cabinet and campus committees handle daily operations (source #4). | #4 |
| Who wins | UW Tacoma won #1 Top Performer for Social Mobility in the West (U.S. News 2026, source #1). It won #1 Best Bang for the Buck in Washington (Washington Monthly 2025, source #1). It also won #2 Best Bang for the Buck in the West (source #1). UW Tacoma was the first UW campus named a Champion Campus by FirstGen Forward (source #1). Chancellor Lange has won several awards: 2020 CEO of the Year from the WA Association of College Trustees, 2021 Director of the Year from the Puget Sound Business Journal, 2011 Woman of Influence, and 2013 UW College of Education Distinguished Alumni (source #4). | #1, #4 |

## 5. How they touch government
- **State funding:** UW Tacoma gets state appropriations through the UW system. Chancellor Lange goes to Olympia to push for permanent state funding for student services (source #5: "visited Olympia last week to advocate for permanent state funding for student success services"). She pointed out that "nearly half of students are Pell eligible, more than half are first generation, and one-fifth are military-affiliated" to argue that "deep budget cuts would uniquely impact UW Tacoma" (source #5).
- **State proviso investments:** UW Tacoma has received growing state "proviso" budget investments. These include $854K in fiscal year 2024 and $2M ongoing starting fiscal year 2025 to grow engineering enrollments (source #7). A one-time state appropriation paid for student support positions (re-enrollment, financial aid, mental health, career readiness) that launched the HuskiesCare online hub (source #5). A House capital budget proposal also included $7.7M for land acquisition at UW Tacoma (source #5 context).
- **Federal funding:** NOT CONFIRMED. No specific federal grants to UW Tacoma were found in this research pass. As a unit of a major research university, federal research grants likely flow through the UW system.
- **Lobbying:** Chancellor Lange does direct lobbying in Olympia (source #5). The UW has a State Relations office (source #5 domain). Specific L-2 lobbyist registrations for UW Tacoma were NOT CONFIRMED.
- **Contracts and grants:** NOT CONFIRMED. No specific government contracts were identified.
- **Land-use actions:** The 46-acre campus sits in downtown Tacoma (source #1). The campus has driven downtown redevelopment since 1990 (source #4). State capital budget proposals include $7.7M for land acquisition at UW Tacoma (source #5 context), showing that the campus is still growing. The Campus Master Plan is updated (source #4).
- **Campaign donations:** None. As a public institution, UW Tacoma cannot make political contributions.
- **Puyallup Tribe relationship:** The Puyallup Tribe of Indians is the "Tribal Sponsor of UW Tacoma" (source #4 and source #1). The campus sits on "traditional lands of the Puyallup Tribe of Indians" (source #1). This is a formal institutional tie to the region's major tribal sovereign.

The campus's social mobility mission helps underserved communities. (3) Lobbying for state funding is a core job for public university leaders. It is not a conflict.
- **Analysis of alternatives:** The other reading is that UW Tacoma is a small regional campus (5,059 students, source #1). It has limited research output. It has no independent governing authority. It reports to the UW Seattle president and the Board of Regents. Under this view, the weight-5 `chancellor` edge overstates the campus's power. The main gaps are: specific campus operating budget (total revenue/expenditures not publicly broken out from the UW system), employee count/payroll, and specific federal research grants. The power assessment is well-grounded in documented institutional characteristics and board overlaps.

It is one of the two major health systems in Pierce County (along with MultiCare). It runs St. Joseph Medical Center in Tacoma — the largest hospital on the Tacoma skyline. VMFH has 18,000+ employees, about 5,000 doctors, 10 hospitals, and about 1,500 beds across western Washington. It is a major employer and care provider. Its board overlaps with Weyerhaeuser, Wellfound (a joint venture with MultiCare), the Washington State Hospital Association (WSHA), and the Catholic Archdiocese. Its parent, CommonSpirit Health, is one of the largest nonprofit health systems in the U.S.

VMFH reached its current size through the January 2021 merger of CHI Franciscan ($2.45B pre-merger revenue) and Virginia Mason ($1.15B), creating an about-$3.6B regional powerhouse under CommonSpirit. CEO Ketul Patel's departure for Wellstar Health System (Oct 2025) creates a leadership transition worth watching.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags (defense counter-argument):** A defense would say: (1) VMFH is a nonprofit providing essential health care, including $304M in community benefits, so its tax exemption is justified; (2) the CommonSpirit tie gives resources that help patients, not corporate extraction; (3) the Catholic ethical directives are constitutionally protected religious exercise, not policy imposition; (4) the Wellfound JV with MultiCare is a cooperative arrangement that expands behavioral health access, not anti-competitive collusion; (5) the 3-person board is standard for a subsidiary of a larger system, with CommonSpirit providing oversight.
- **Analysis of alternatives:** The opposing reading is that VMFH is a form of unaccountable consolidated health care power — a $3.6B+ regional system run by a 3-person board, ultimately controlled by a national parent (CommonSpirit) with no direct public accountability, despite receiving hundreds of millions in tax exemptions. The 2021 merger reduced competition in the western WA hospital market. It may have raised prices and reduced patient choice. The Catholic ethical directives restrict access to legal reproductive health services in a state (WA) that protects those rights. That creates a gap between state policy and patient access at VMFH facilities. The Weyerhaeuser board tie connects VMFH to the corporate timber power structure. The Wellfound JV with MultiCare is a cooperative bridge between the two main competitors. It could enable coordination rather than competition. The CEO's departure for Wellstar raises questions about leadership stability and whether CommonSpirit's commitment to the PNW region is strategic or short-term.
- **Confidence:** Medium — VMFH's structure, hospital list, and Catholic affiliation are well-sourced from the official VMFH website (primary, 0.9). Financial data comes from subsidiary 990s (VMMC) and pre-merger reports, but consolidated VMFH financials are UNVERIFIED. Board composition beyond the graph nodes is UNVERIFIED (the 3-person board is confirmed by 990 but other members were not identified). CEO pay is sourced from WA DOH and IRS 990 (primary, 0.9-0.95).
- **VERIFIED stamp:** 2026-09-19 — tier1-chunk2 subagent (no human reviewer)

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why it is on the map.** The Washington Realtors Political Action Committee holds power from the PAC role and from the decisions it makes. It is one of the top 10 PACs by spending in Washington State (the state's campaign-finance agency (PDC) data, source #1). It picks which candidates to fund and endorse. The graph also shows ties to the Chamber of Commerce and Pierce County Council. The PAC acts as a pipeline between the real estate industry and elected officials.
- **Who is left out:** The National Association of Realtors PAC (RPAC) is the federal-level parent PAC. It works at the congressional level, so it is not in this Pierce County-focused graph. Local REALTOR® associations (like Seattle-King County and Tacoma-Pierce County) run their own local PACs, but they are not listed here. The Washington REALTORS® trade association itself (the 501(c)(6) parent) is a related but separate group from the PAC.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Washington Realtors Political Action Committee.
- **Type:** A Political Action Committee (PAC) registered with the Washington State Public Disclosure Commission (PDC). A PAC is a group that raises and spends money to influence elections.
- **Parent organization:** Washington REALTORS® (a statewide not-for-profit trade group with about 20,000+ members, source #3).
- **National affiliation:** National Association of Realtors (NAR) / REALTORS® Political Action Committee (RPAC). The state PAC is part of the national RPAC network.
- **Registration address:** 504 14th Ave SE, Olympia, WA 98501 (sources #1, #2, #3).
- **Phone:** (360) 943-3100 (parent org); (360) 628-8129 (PDC filing contact).
- **Governing law:** State law RCW 29B (Campaign Disclosure and Contribution Act, formerly RCW 42.17A). Run by the Washington State Public Disclosure Commission.
- **CEO of parent org:** Lori Adler (source #3).
- **Tax ID (EIN)/UBI:** UNVERIFIED — not directly available from PDC filings.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Power held:** The PAC holds power to make decisions by choosing which candidates to endorse and fund. It is one of the top 10 PACs by spending in Washington State, with about $1,005,504.24 in spending in the current PDC reporting cycle (source #1). Its parent group, Washington REALTORS®, has 20,000+ members statewide (source #3), giving the PAC money and name recognition.
- **Political domain overlap:** The PAC only works in politics. It endorses and funds candidates for state, local, and legislative offices. Its "REALTOR Party" idea is nonpartisan. The PAC backs candidates who defend REALTOR® policy goals, no matter the party (source #4).
- **Funded and endorsed:** Candidates for statewide, legislative, judicial, and local offices across Washington. Nationally, RPAC had a 97% win rate in 2024 federal elections, with money split 50/50 between Democrats and Republicans (source #5). State-level endorsements for Pierce County candidates are unverified here (would need a PDC contribution search by recipient).
- **PAC spending:** About $1,005,504.24 in the current PDC cycle (source #1). Nationally, RPAC raised $45,845,025 in 2024 including state and local funds (source #5).
- **Party machinery control:** None. The PAC is nonpartisan and does not control any party. It adds to party activity by funding pro-REALTOR candidates across party lines.
- **Candidate recruitment and training:** Washington REALTORS® runs RPAC Trustee-led candidate interviews and endorsements (source #6). No formal candidate training programs found.

## 3. Where their power comes from

| Who benefits | REALTORS® and their clients benefit from the PAC's advocacy for property rights, homeownership, and real estate industry interests. Endorsed candidates benefit from campaign funding and the REALTOR® brand and volunteer network. | #4, #6 |
| Who sits | RPAC Trustees (drawn from Washington REALTORS® membership) coordinate fundraising, candidate endorsements, and interviews. The parent organization's Government Affairs Director is Nathan Gorton (source #3). CEO Lori Adler leads the association. | #3, #6 |

| Who wins | Endorsed candidates who receive RPAC funding. Nationally, RPAC had a 97% win rate in 2024 (source #5). State-level win rate is unverified for specific Washington races. | #5 |

## 5. How they touch government
- **Campaign donations:** The PAC gives money to candidates and political committees across Washington State. PDC records show about $1,005,504.24 in spending in the current cycle (source #1), making it a top 10 PAC statewide. Specific Pierce County recipients are unverified here.
- **Lobbying:** The parent organization Washington REALTORS® runs a government affairs program (sources #4, #6). Registered lobbyists for Washington REALTORS® are unverified here (would need a PDC lobbyist employer search).
- **Regulatory interactions:** The PAC is regulated by the Washington State Public Disclosure Commission under RCW 29B. No enforcement actions were found against WA Realtors PAC in this research session.
- **Land-use actions:** None directly. The PAC does not get involved in land-use decisions. The parent group lobbies on real estate laws including housing, land use, and property tax issues (source #4).

## 6. Other seats they hold
- **Board seats, memberships, and partnerships that span domains:**
  - Washington REALTORS® (parent trade group) — 20,000+ members statewide (source #3).
  - National Association of Realtors (NAR) / RPAC — national network member (source #5).
  - RPAC President's Circle — Washington members include several local REALTOR® association leaders (source #7).
  - No direct board overlaps with Pierce County entities beyond the graph's existing edges (Chamber, County Council).

## 1. Who they are
- **The bottom line.** The WA Realtors PAC runs a large statewide campaign-funding pipeline (about $1M+ per cycle). It moves real estate industry money to pro-REALTOR candidates across party lines. Its power is money and connections. It uses the 20,000+ member Washington REALTORS® base and the national RPAC system ($45.8M raised in 2024) to shape election outcomes. The Pierce County link runs through the "donated" edge to County Council (weight 4) and "aligned" with Chamber (weight 3). That puts the PAC in the middle as a funding bridge between the real estate industry and local government.
