## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why it is here:** The WEA-PAC is the political action committee (PAC) of the Washington Education Association (WEA), the state's largest teachers' union. It is the main political money arm for K-12 school employees in Olympia. The graph links it to two Pierce County nodes: Pierce County Democrats (weight 3) and Ryan Mello (weight 4). WEA-PAC moves union and Democratic money into Pierce County elections. The WEA claims 6 of its members sit in the state legislature and 55+ more sit on local school boards and in local offices. That is a real candidate pipeline.
- **Who is NOT on this page:** The NEA Fund for Children and Public Education (NEA-FCPE) is the federal PAC for the National Education Association. WEA-PAC works with it but stays a state and local PAC. PIE (Public School Employees of Washington) is a separate PAC for classified school employees. PIE is not on this page either.

## 1. Who they are
- **Full legal name:** Washington Education Association Political Action Committee (WEA-PAC). Registered with Washington's Public Disclosure Commission (PDC). Committee ID: co-2025-20621 (current 2025 registration); also listed as co-2023-20621 in the 2023 cycle.
- **Type:** State political action committee, registered under Washington law RCW 42.17A (the state's campaign-finance law). It is part of the Washington Education Association (WEA), which is the state arm of the National Education Association (NEA).
- **Parent and affiliates:** WEA-PAC is the political arm of WEA. WEA gives WEA-PAC a lot of in-kind support (staff time, office space, supplies). A PDC enforcement case (#139384) found that "WEA-PAC receives significant in-kind contributions from WEA that sustains its operation." NEA-FCPE is the federal PAC; WEA-PAC works with it on candidate recommendations.
- **Laws it follows:** Washington RCW 42.17A (Campaign Disclosure and Contribution). At the federal level, FECA (the Federal Election Campaign Act) and IRS rules for 527 political groups. Contacts: WEA-PAC coordinators Samantha Casne (253-765-7161) and Emily Hansen (206-412-4406); email WEAPAC@washingtonea.org.
- **Members and money in:** WEA members can sign up for monthly payroll-deduction donations: $2.25, $5, or $10.50 per month. They can also add $1 per month for NEA-FCPE.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Endorsing and recruiting candidates (decision-making):** WEA-PAC's stated goal is to "recommend and elect pro-public education, pro-labor candidates to office — regardless of party affiliation." Its track record claim: 6 WEA members in the state legislature and 55+ WEA members on local school boards and in local offices. That pipeline is the PAC's clearest claim to power — it turns endorsements into actual wins.
- **Independent spending and in-kind spending (decision-making + money):** 2023 PDC filings show WEA-PAC spent $968,027.15 in-kind, $250,040.25 in monetary contributions to other PACs, and $20,410.00 in independent expenditures. 2025 totals: $780,778.25 to other PACs and $754,947.72 in-kind. The Washington Observer Substack reports WEA-PAC spent $3.75 million in a recent year (the cycle is UNVERIFIED in this pass).
- **Partisan tilt (well-connected):** A Freedom Foundation analysis says WEA-PAC gave 63% of member contributions to Democratic candidates, totaling nearly $5 million. Another 35% went to support the union itself — likely for member-mobilization work. The "bipartisan" line in WEA's own mission statement is disputed by who actually got the money.
- **Compliance and enforcement history:** PDC enforcement case #139384 (Washington Education Association Political Action Committee) required WEA-PAC to fix its campaign-finance reports. Freedom Foundation says the filings "claimed WEA-PAC received under-the-limit contributions from nearly 27,000 unidentified contributors — six times as many as it reported."
- **Why it scores where it does:** The graph shows WEA-PAC tied to Pierce Dems (weight 3) and Ryan Mello (donated weight 4). WEA-PAC is a top-10 political spender in Washington and outpaces nearly every other PAC in the state.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Question | Answer |
|----------|--------|
| Who benefits | WEA-PAC's recommended candidates win (mostly Democrats). WEA itself gets in-kind support and a stronger pipeline of friendly lawmakers. K-12 union members see better contracts and laws from the lawmakers it helps elect. |
| Who sits | WEA-PAC is run by WEA's internal PAC structure. Coordinators Samantha Casne and Emily Hansen staff it. The WEA-PAC board roster is not public. |
| Who governs | WEA-PAC does not govern — it influences. It targets the Washington State Legislature, statewide offices (Governor, Attorney General, Superintendent of Public Instruction), and local school-board races. It also shapes the Washington Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction (OSPI), the State Board of Education, and K-12 funding formulas. |
| Who wins | Short-term: the candidates WEA-PAC backs. Medium-term: WEA members win better contracts and pro-education laws. Long-term: critics (Freedom Foundation, school-choice reformers) say WEA-PAC locks in union control over K-12 policy at the cost of parental choice. Defenders say WEA-PAC is a fair counter to corporate school-reform money. The "who wins" question is disputed in this case. |

## 9. Who they are connected to

|---|---|---|
| Pierce Dems (`pierce-dem`) | aligned | 3 |
| Ryan Mello (`ryan-mello`) | donated to | 4 |

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** WEA-PAC is a tier-3 political node with structural power. It is the top K-12 labor PAC in Washington. It runs the candidate pipeline for school-board races, state legislative seats, and pro-labor statewide offices. The graph weights understate its size: WEA-PAC's 2023 in-kind spending alone ($968K) is bigger than many entities' full contribution profiles in this dataset. Its 2025 PAC-to-PAC figure ($781K) puts it in the top tier of Washington PACs.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags:** (a) PDC enforcement case #139384 found that WEA-PAC's pre-2024 reporting broke the rules — "27,000 unidentified contributors" — and the fix came under PDC order. That is a real compliance problem for a group claiming $5M in pro-Democratic giving. (b) WEA's "regardless of party affiliation" line is misleading, since 63% of contributions went to Democrats per Freedom Foundation. The 35% in in-kind spending to WEA itself suggests the PAC also works as a member-mobilization slush fund, not just a candidate-support vehicle. (c) The Pierce Dems ↔ WEA-PAC ↔ Ryan Mello graph links suggest a clear Pierce County Democratic / WEA-PAC / candidate pipeline. It is worth mapping, not necessarily illegal.
- **Other view:** WEA-PAC could also be seen as a defensive union PAC fighting back against corporate school-reform dollars (charter-school advocacy, parental-choice PACs). The Freedom Foundation analysis is partisan. The PDC data behind it is not. The fair read is that WEA-PAC operates at the same scale as a big corporate trade-association PAC, with strong incumbent-protective effects on Washington K-12 policy.
- **Confidence:** **Medium** for spending figures (PDC is primary); **Medium** for partisan-share claim (single secondary source, Freedom Foundation, with admitted perspective bias); **High** for who they are legally and PDC enforcement-case fact pattern.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Inclusion rule (well-connected + decision-making):** Wellfound is the **only freestanding adult inpatient psychiatric hospital in Pierce County**. That regional monopoly makes it the gatekeeper for involuntary and voluntary adult inpatient behavioral-health beds. Its two parents are MultiCare Health System and Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (formerly CHI Franciscan). Both parents are tier-1 nodes in this map. The joint venture was formed through their shared "Alliance for South Sound Health" agreement in 2014.
- **Related but separate groups (not on the map):** Western State Hospital is in Lakewood. It is run by DSHS (the Department of Social and Health Services, a state agency). It handles civil and forensic long-term commitments. Online therapy platforms like Talkspace and Cerebral are not Pierce-specific. Mary Bridge Children's mental-health services have a separate EIN and a separate site.

## 1. Who they are
- **Operating name:** Wellfound Behavioral Health Hospital. **Parent / legal entity:** Alliance for South Sound Health. It is a Washington nonprofit corporation with EIN **47-4654897** (per the IRS, through Charity Navigator). It was registered in 2014.
- **Entity type:** 501(c)(3) nonprofit hospital. Charity Navigator confirms the 501(c)(3) status: "501(c)(3) organization... EIN 47-4654897... 3402 S 19TH ST, TACOMA WA 98405-2487." (NPI 1003462033; state hospital license required under state law, RCW 70.41.)
- **Owners and parents:** 50/50 joint venture between **MultiCare Health System** (`multicare`) and **Virginia Mason Franciscan Health** (`vmfh`; formerly CHI Franciscan Health, a CommonSpirit Health subsidiary until Catholic Health Initiatives separated in 2024–2025). The joint venture is run by an Alliance for South Sound Health board.
- **Founding and operating documents:** The joint venture agreement was signed in 2014 ("Alliance for South Sound Health"). Construction finished in 2019. The hospital admitted its first patients on May 7, 2019.
- **CEO:** Maureen Womack (named at opening). She is the CEO of the joint-venture entity and the public face of the hospital.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Legal authority:** Wellfound is a licensed acute-care psychiatric hospital under RCW 70.41. The Washington State Department of Health has designated it as a Medicare and Medicaid facility. It is also a designated facility under the Involuntary Treatment Act (ITA), state law RCW 71.05. That makes it the county's main destination for ITA involuntary holds.
- **Market position (regional monopoly):** Before Wellfound opened, Pierce County had **2.8 inpatient psych beds per 100,000 residents**. That was the lowest of any urban county in Washington. The state average was 8.6. The national average was 26.1. After Wellfound opened, the county had 16.3 beds per 100,000, "almost double the state average." For adult acute inpatient care in Pierce County, Wellfound is the only option.
- **Power from parent companies:** Both parents are tier-1 anchors. MultiCare is the dominant nonprofit health system in the South Sound. Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (VMFH) and CHI Franciscan are the second-largest and a Catholic health system. Their joint venture creates a high barrier for any other health system that wants to build competing inpatient capacity. Joint planning agreements, certificate-of-need rules (state approval to build new hospital capacity), and shared doctor rosters make a third-party competitor too expensive to pursue.
- **Cultural influence:** At the opening, the heads of both parents and the Wellfound CEO spoke publicly. They framed the hospital as a "community solution" to a public-health crisis. In the press, every story about Pierce County behavioral-health capacity defaults to Wellfound.
- **Veto power:** In effect, yes. Any county-level decision to expand psychiatric capacity (such as a proposed DSHS facility or a competing nonprofit's certificate-of-need application) cannot move forward without Wellfound or Alliance agreement. ## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Inclusion rule — power and decision-making.** West Pierce Fire & Rescue is Pierce County Fire District No. 3. It is a junior taxing fire district under Title 52 of the Revised Code of Washington (RCW), the state law for fire districts.
- It has voter-approved taxing power over a defined area: Lakewood and University Place, plus a contract for the Town of Steilacoom.
- It controls a $72.8 million revenue budget (FY2024).
- It provides emergency fire and medical services to about 100,000 people across 31 square miles.
- The graph links West Pierce to John Clancy (chair, weight 4) and Central Pierce Fire (peer district, weight 2). Those document its structural ties.
- **Adjacent but excluded:** Central Pierce Fire & Rescue, East Pierce Fire & Rescue, Gig Harbor Fire & Medic One, and the Pierce County Fire Training Consortium are mapped as adjacent. South Pierce Fire & Rescue and the Puget Sound Regional Fire Authority are peer districts not mapped at this tier. The cities of Lakewood and University Place are separate municipalities.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** West Pierce Fire & Rescue (WPFR). Legally, Pierce County Fire District No. 3, established in 1944.
- **Entity type:** Government — a junior taxing special-purpose fire protection district under Title 52 RCW, set up as a municipal corporation under RCW 41.24.010.
- **Formation history.** Lakewood Fire (District No. 2) and University Place Fire (District No. 3) merged on March 1, 2011 to form West Pierce Fire & Rescue. The original District No. 3 had been around since 1944. The merged district kept that legal identity.
- **Service area:** Lakewood and University Place (full service). Town of Steilacoom (contracted). 31 square miles. Just over 100,000 people.
- **Board of Fire Commissioners:** Five commissioners, elected at-large, six-year terms. As of 2026: John Clancy (Position 2, Board Chair, 2022–2027); Scott Casebolt (Position 3, 2024–2029); Dave Durr (Position 4, Vice Chair, 2022–2027); Marshal (Scott) Dellinger (Position 5, 2026–2031); Alan Billingsley (Position 1, 2026–2031).
- **Executive leadership:** Fire Chief Ryan McGrady. Deputy Chiefs Mike Boltz and Hallie McCurdy.
- **WSRB rating:** Class 3 from the Washington Survey and Rating Bureau (WSRB) as of the 2019 re-rate. (Class ratings go from 1 (best) to 10; lower numbers mean better fire protection and can lower insurance costs.) The Town of Steilacoom is also Class 3 because WPFR serves it.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Statutory authority.** As a fire district under RCW Title 52, WPFR can levy voter-approved property taxes (Regular Fire Levy, EMS Levy), issue general obligation bonds with voter approval, and contract for fire-protection services. An elected Board of Fire Commissioners governs the district under RCW 52.14.
- **Taxing authority (FY2024 budget revenue):** Regular Levy $24.4 million. EMS Levy $8.1 million. M&O (Maintenance and Operations) Levy $17.0 million. GEMT Funds $4.3 million. Fire Protection Contracts $1.66 million. Plus intergovernmental revenue, transport fees ($2.5 million), and reserves. Total revenue: $72.8 million.
- **Budget control (FY2024):** Total appropriated expense: $63.8 million. Operations divisions: Suppression $29.0 million; EMS $12.0 million; Administration $4.5 million; Training/EMS Training $2.1 million; Community Risk Reduction $2.6 million; Logistics/Facilities $1.8 million; Fleet $1.75 million; IT $2.2 million; SS911 $0.65 million. Plus capital projects ($1.83 million), infrastructure ($1.75 million), grants ($0.76 million), debt service ($1.4 million), and reserve deposits ($0.2 million). Beginning fund balance $10.9 million. Ending balance $9.0 million.
- **Operational scope:** Six fire stations staffed 24 hours a day. About 17,721 incidents a year (2022 figure). Services: fire suppression, EMS and transport, technical rescue, hazardous materials response, marine operations, fire prevention, inspections and code enforcement, and fire and life-safety education.
- **Contracted service relationships:** WPFR has service contracts with DSHS (Western State Hospital), Clover Park Technical College, Pierce College, Pierce County (Chambers Creek Properties, Lakewood Community Center, Steilacoom Ferry Landing), Pierce Transit, Lakewood Water District, Clover Park School District, University Place School District, and the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (American Lake facility, outside the district).
- **Domain overlaps:**
  - **Government ↔ Economic:** Taxing power over property. Large purchasing power for trucks and supplies. Contracts with school districts, hospitals, and transit.
  - **Government ↔ Institutional:** Interlocal agreements (formal cooperation contracts) with peer fire districts through the Pierce County Fire Training Consortium.
  - **Government ↔ Social:** Emergency response and life-safety service to about 100,000 residents. Mutual-aid agreements with neighbors.

## 3. Where their power comes from

| Who sits | A five-member elected Board of Fire Commissioners governs the district. Current roster: John Clancy (Position 2, Board Chair); Scott Casebolt (Position 3); Dave Durr (Position 4, Vice Chair); Marshal (Scott) Dellinger (Position 5); Alan Billingsley (Position 1). Fire Chief Ryan McGrady runs operations. | Sources 1, 2 |
| Who governs | The Board of Fire Commissioners manages business affairs, sets levies, approves the budget, and hires and supervises the Fire Chief. RCW 52.14 gives the Board legislative authority over district affairs. | Sources 1, 3 |
| Who wins | Voters in the WPFR service area keep low-density fire-EMS coverage with WSRB Class 3 ratings (which lower commercial insurance premiums). The Board wins re-election in non-competitive races. Contractors win stable public-sector revenue. | Sources 1, 3 |

## 1. Who they are
- **Verdict:** West Pierce Fire & Rescue controls a $72.8M revenue / $63.8M expense fire district that delivers critical life-safety services to ~100,000+ residents across Lakewood and University Place. Its power is fundamentally fiscal and operational: it levies property taxes, contracts for service, and dispatches fire/EMS resources. The Board of 5 elected commissioners holds the legislative authority; the Fire Chief (Ryan McGrady) executes operations. WPFR's market position is structurally protected by geographic monopoly (the district's boundaries are exclusive for fire-EMS service), but constrained by the 1% property-tax cap (Washington's I-747/Levy Lid), voter approval requirements for levy lid lifts, and WSRB ratings oversight.
- **Conflicts-of-interest flags:** The Board's authority over the district's budget and contracts creates standard procurement-conflict potential. Some commissioners have business interests connected to construction (Dave Durr — painting contractor; Bart Dalton — financial advising at Edward Jones; John Sheeran — defense attorney; John Clancy — former Cardinal Health/manpower sales) — these are common in junior-taxing districts but should be disclosed. The 2011 merger consolidated two districts and increased market concentration, which reduces competitive pressure on service delivery costs. FY2024 includes a planned non-voter-approved bond issuance (~$16.5M, 20-year life) which would commit future tax revenue without explicit voter sign-off — UNVERIFIED whether voter approval was secured or whether it proceeds under existing statutory authority.
- **Analysis of alternatives :** An opposing reading: WPFR is one of several Pierce County fire districts, and its power is bounded by geographic scope and the political limits of property-tax-funded services. The Class 3 WSRB rating is not the best achievable (Class 1 is top) — improving it would require additional capital investment. Service contracts with peer entities (Western State Hospital, school districts) reduce direct tax pressure but create dependency. The merger with University Place eliminated a competing fire department and likely reduced service-delivery competition, but voter approval in both jurisdictions was required for the merger.
- **Confidence:** High — primary budget PDF (West Pierce official, FY2024) and the official Elected Officials page corroborate board composition, financial scale, and operational scope. Some biographical details (commissioner career paths from LinkedIn) are secondary. The 2024 budget's mention of a planned non-voter-approved bond issuance is FACT from the document; whether the issuance ultimately proceeded requires verification beyond this pass.

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why included:** Weyerhaeuser is on the map because it holds office-level economic power, makes major decisions, and is well-connected. It is one of the largest private landowners in Pierce County and Washington State. It holds large amounts of timberland. Its decisions about land use, jobs, and political donations affect the region. It belongs to the Tacoma-Pierce County Chamber of Commerce. It donated to local candidates, including Mary Robnett. The company's roots go back to 19th-century federal land grants that shaped the region's economy.
- **Adjacent but NOT included:** Green Diamond Resource Company (`green-diamond`, already on the map). Hampton Resources. Plum Creek Timber (bought by Weyerhaeuser in 2016). Smaller timber operators in Pierce County are left out because they own less land and have less political influence.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Weyerhaeuser Company (NYSE: WY)
- **Type:** Real estate investment trust (REIT). Publicly traded on the NYSE under the ticker WY. The company became a REIT in 2010. It paid shareholders a special $5.6 billion dividend as part of that change.
- **SEC CIK number:** 0000106535
- **Headquarters:** Seattle, WA (moved from Federal Way, WA)
- **Founded:** 1900, by Frederick Weyerhaeuser. The company started in a Tacoma field office. It began by buying 900,000 acres of Washington timberland from the Northern Pacific Railway.
- **Ownership:** Publicly traded. Held by large investors. No single shareholder controls the company.
- **Governing law:** Delaware General Corporation Law. Operates as a REIT under IRC §856 of the federal tax code.

## 2. Their career and offices
- **CEO/President:** Devin W. Stockfish (since January 2019). He also sits on Weyerhaeuser's board. He has a J.D. from Columbia University and a B.S. in mechanical engineering from the University of Colorado. He joined Weyerhaeuser in 2013. Before that, he was VP and Associate General Counsel at Univar Solutions, a lawyer at Starbucks Corp. and K&L Gates LLP, and an engineer at Boeing. He was elected to the Xcel Energy board of directors on January 23, 2025.
- **CFO:** David M. Wold (SVP & CFO).
- **SVP & Chief Administration Officer:** Denise Merle.
- **SVP Timberlands:** Travis Keatley.
- **SVP & Chief Development Officer:** Rehad Hossain.
- **Board of Directors (2024/2025 proxy):** Rick R. Holley (Independent Non-Executive Chairman), Devin W. Stockfish (CEO, not independent), Nicole W. Piasecki, Mark A. Emmert, Lawrence A. Selzer, Kim Williams, Sara Grootwassink Lewis, Deidra "Dee" Merriwether, Al Monaco, James C. O'Rourke, Rick Beckwitt (joined around 2024, former president/CEO of Lennar Corporation).
- **Board overlaps:** Devin Stockfish → Xcel Energy board (Jan 2025). Mark A. Emmert is the former president of the University of Washington (linked to the education side of the map). No direct board overlap with Pierce County entities beyond what is listed in §9.

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Sources of power:**
  - **Market power:** The largest integrated timber and forest products company in North America. It owns or manages millions of acres of timberland across the U.S. In Washington state, it owns or manages about 1.3 million acres and runs two mills, two nurseries, and its Seattle headquarters.
  - **Land use power:** As a major landowner, Weyerhaeuser's choices about logging, land sales, and development shape Pierce County's environment, economy, and land use.
  - **Political power:** The Weyerhaeuser political action committee (PAC) gave $389,500 to federal candidates in 2023–2024 (63.41% to Republicans, 34.02% to Democrats). At the state level, Weyerhaeuser has donated to Washington candidates. That includes $2,000 to Mary Robnett, the Pierce County Prosecutor. The company is also listed as a $1,200 donor to Washington gubernatorial candidates.
  - **Economic size:** $7.1 billion in net sales (2024). About 9,400 employees worldwide. Adjusted EBITDA was $2.3 billion in 2023. The 2025 Adjusted EBITDA was $1.021 billion. Net earnings in 2025 were $324 million.
- **Why power crosses domains:** The economic side (timberland, jobs) meets the political side (campaign donations, lobbying) and the institutional side (Chamber of Commerce membership).
- **Key facts:**
  - **Revenue and ownership:** $7.1 billion in net sales (2024). Publicly traded REIT.
  - **Market position:** Largest private timberland owner in North America.
  - **Government contracts/grants:** None found today. Note: The map edge `federal_land_grant` between Weyerhaeuser and the Pierce County Council refers to the company's 19th-century roots. The original 900,000 acres came from the Northern Pacific Railway, which got federal land grants. This is a historical fact, not a current funding relationship.
  - **Jobs controlled:** About 9,400 worldwide. Washington state jobs at the county level are UNVERIFIED.
  - **Land holdings:** About 1.3 million acres in Washington state (per a 2021 Seattle Times report). About 2.6 million acres in the Pacific Northwest (including Oregon) after the 2013 Longview Timber purchase. Pierce County-specific acreage is UNVERIFIED.

## 3. Where their power comes from
| Indicator | Finding | Evidence (source #) |
|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Shareholders (over $6 billion returned 2021–2025 via dividends and buybacks), local communities through jobs and taxes, employees through wages | #1, #5, #10 |
| Who sits | Devin Stockfish (CEO) sits on the Weyerhaeuser and Xcel Energy boards. Rick Holley (chair) and other independent directors also serve. | #3, #7 |
| Who governs | A board of 11 directors. The REIT structure requires paying out 90% of taxable income to shareholders. | #5, #8 |
| Who wins | Political candidates get Weyerhaeuser PAC donations. Timber-friendly land use policies help the company. | #9, #10 |

## 4. Their money
- **Revenue:** $7.1 billion in net sales for FY2024. $7.7B in 2023. $10.2B in 2022.

- **Net earnings:** $324M (2025). $396M (2024). $839M (2023). $1.88B (2022).
- **Funding sources:** Product sales (timber, wood products), real estate sales, climate solutions. No government grants found.
- **Tax status:** REIT — pays out 90%+ of taxable income to shareholders. No corporate-level tax on qualified REIT income. Dividends are mostly taxed as capital gains to shareholders.
- **Shareholder returns:** Over $6 billion returned to shareholders 2021–2025 through dividends and buybacks. Base quarterly dividend $0.19 per share (2023). The company aims to give back 75–80% of Adjusted FAD through dividends and buybacks.
- **Long-term debt:** $5.3 billion (investment-grade balance sheet).
- **Property holdings:** Millions of acres of timberland across the U.S. About 1.3 million acres in Washington. The company sold about $850 million in non-core timberlands from 2022–2025. It spent over $1.2 billion on strategic acquisitions in the same period.

## 5. How they touch government
- **Lobbying:** Weyerhaeuser runs a federal PAC (Weyerhaeuser Co PAC, FEC ID C00007948). Federal contributions 2023–2024: $389,500 to candidates (63.41% Republican, 34.02% Democrat). - **Land-use actions:** Weyerhaeuser manages timberland under Washington State Forest Practices Rules (state law RCW 76.09). The company has sold non-strategic timberlands in southwest Washington. It must follow the federal Clean Water Act and state salmon habitat protections.
- **Regulatory interactions:** The company is regulated by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the Washington Department of Natural Resources, and the Washington Department of Ecology. ## 0. Why this person or group is on the map
- **Why it is on the map — from holding office + decision-making:** WSHA is the main trade group for Washington State hospitals. That includes major Pierce County health systems (MultiCare, Virginia Mason Franciscan Health). Its lobbying, political action committee (PAC) spending, and regulatory advocacy directly affect health care policy and funding in Pierce County. (Sources 1, 3)
- **Adjacent but EXCLUDED candidates:** Washington State Medical Association (WSMA) — a separate group for doctors. American Hospital Association (AHA) — the national counterpart. Both are adjacent but not the subject here.

## 1. Who they are
- **Exact legal name:** Washington State Hospital Association
- **Type of entity:** A 501(c)(6) business league / trade association (Source 4)
- **tax ID number (EIN):** 91-0584257 (Source 4)
- **Founded:** 1961 (Source 5)
- **HQ:** 1201 3rd Avenue, Suite 1601, Seattle, WA 98101 (Source 1)
- **Parent/subsidiaries:** Washington Hospital Services (WHS) is the services arm of WSHA. It offers group purchasing and business solutions. (Source 6)
- **Governing law:** IRC 501(c)(6); Washington State nonprofit corporation law.
- **2024 finances:** Total revenue $17,096,686. Total expenses $19.8M. Total assets $33.5M. Net assets $26.6M. (Sources 4, 5)

## 3. Where their power comes from
- **Statutory/regulatory power:** WSHA has no direct statutory authority. But it has strong influence through lobbying the state legislature and Congress, advocating with regulatory agencies (WA State Health Care Authority, CMS), and building coalitions. It represents 100+ hospitals. That includes nonprofit, investor-owned, county, state, and military hospitals. (Sources 1, 3)
- **Market power:** WSHA is the unified voice of WA hospitals. It has outsized influence on health care policy. Its member hospitals control billions in annual revenue and employ tens of thousands in WA. (Source 3)
- **Political power:** WSHA runs the Hospitals for a Healthy Future PAC (HHFPAC). The PAC raised more than $236,000 in 2024. The 2025 goal is $275,000. Washington Hospital Services (a WSHA subsidiary) gave $200,000 and $143,190 to HHFPAC in 2022. (Sources 7, 8)
- **Domain overlaps:** Political (PAC, lobbying) + Health care (member hospitals) + Government (regulatory advocacy, Medicaid policy).

## 3. Where their power comes from

|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| Who benefits | Member hospitals benefit from WSHA's advocacy on Medicaid funding, regulatory relief, and payment rates | 3, 7 |
| Who sits | Board chaired by Florence Chang (President, MultiCare Health System, Tacoma) — a direct Pierce County link | 3 |
| Who governs | WSHA sets legislative priorities and PAC spending strategy. It lobbies the state legislature and Congress | 1, 3, 7 |
| Who wins | HHFPAC helps elect "health care champions." WSHA pushed successfully on Medicaid directed payment programs | 2, 7 |

## 5. How they touch government
- **Lobbying:** Registered federal lobbyists (LDA filings) — multiple lobbyists including Matthew Levin, Elizabeth Fortunato, and Nina Flink. (Source 2)
- **PAC spending:** Hospitals for a Healthy Future PAC (HHFPAC) — raised more than $208,000 in 2022, more than $236,000 in 2024. The 2025 goal is $275,000. Washington Hospital Services gave $343,190 to HHFPAC in 2022. (Sources 7, 8)
- **Federal advocacy:** WSHA leaders and members went to Capitol Hill (May 2025) to push on Medicaid funding and directed payment programs (Safety Net Assessment Program). (Source 3)
- **State lobbying:** Active in the WA State Legislature on hospital funding, workforce, and regulatory issues. Publishes annual legislative summaries. (Source 7)

## 6. Other seats they hold
- **Board of Directors:** Chaired by Florence Chang (President, MultiCare Health System, Tacoma) — a direct board overlap with MultiCare. Chair-Elect: Eric Moll (CEO, Mason Health). Secretary-Treasurer: Joel Gilbertson (Chief Executive, Providence Central Division). Cassie Sauer is President/CEO of WSHA. (Source 3)
- **Virginia Mason Franciscan Health (VMFH)/CHI link:** Ketul Patel, CEO of Virginia Mason Franciscan Health, became WSHA board chair in October 2024. (Source 3)
- **AWPHD:** Non-voting representative from the Association of Washington Public Hospital Districts. (Source 3)
- **WSMA:** Non-voting representative from Washington State Medical Association (John Scott, UW Medicine). (Source 3)
- **AHA:** Jon Hersen serves as AHA RPB Delegate. (Source 3)

## 0. Why this person or group is on the map

It is the most populated district in Pierce County. She is on the map for three reasons. First, she holds office as a state senator. She is vice chair on several committees. She also chairs the Senate Members of Color Caucus. Second, she makes decisions. She votes on state laws. She helps negotiate the Capital Budget. She represents about 157,468 people. Third, she is well-connected. The Pierce County Council appointed her. The graph ties her to Pierce Dems and the County Council. She also used to work for Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal.
- A few related names sit outside this map. Jeannie Darneille was the D-27 senator before Trudeau. She has retired from the legislature and is not profiled. Pramila Jayapal was Trudeau's old boss. Jayapal is now in the U.S. Congress and is out of scope. The two D-27 House members may get their own profiles if needed.

## 1. Who they are
- **Legal name:** Yasmin Ayesha Christopher Trudeau.
- **Aliases:** Yasmin Trudeau is her common name. Yasmin A. Christopher uses her maiden name.

- **Current residence:** Tacoma, WA (Source 2, ERFC bio: "She lives in Tacoma with her husband, 2 children, and cat, Mr. Jinx").

 - J.D., Seattle University School of Law, 2014 (Sources 1 and 3).

It is unverified here, but the state's capital budget is usually $2-6 billion per two-year cycle.
